data.description: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.

A rare benign vascular tumor of the heart composed of proliferating blood-filled vascular channels. It may arise in the ventricular myocardium and often shows progressive contrast enhancement on cardiac MRI.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging appearance of a well-defined vascular-appearing lesion with progressive enhancement
Histology showing vascular channels within fibrous stroma

data.description: A benign tumor composed predominantly of fibroblasts and dense collagen, usually arising within the ventricular myocardium. It is more common in children but can rarely occur in adults.
symptoms_in_common: Fibrous tissue visible on histologic staining
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent vascular channels on histology
Progressive vascular-type contrast enhancement typical of a hemangioma
Grossly yellow-tan soft appearance rather than a firm fibrous mass

data.description: The most common primary benign cardiac tumor, usually arising in the left atrium from the interatrial septum. Ventricular myxomas are uncommon and may cause obstruction or embolization.
symptoms_in_common: Female patient in the typical adult age range
symptoms_not_in_common: Left ventricular myocardial location rather than the usual left atrial septal location
Vascular-channel histology rather than myxoid stroma with stellate cells
Progressive enhancement pattern suggestive of a vascular tumor

data.description: A malignant endothelial-cell tumor of the heart that most often arises in the right atrium and may invade surrounding structures or metastasize. It can have hemorrhagic and highly vascular imaging features.
symptoms_in_common: Cardiac mass with vascular characteristics on imaging
Can occasionally be detected before symptoms develop
symptoms_not_in_common: Left ventricular location; angiosarcoma usually involves the right atrium
No constitutional symptoms, pericardial effusion, or signs of invasive disease
Well-circumscribed benign-appearing lesion
Histology without reported malignant cellular atypia, necrosis, or infiltrative growth

data.description: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

data.diagnosis: Splenic infarction associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
data.description: Ischemic injury of splenic tissue from impaired splenic arterial perfusion or thrombosis; Mycoplasma pneumoniae can rarely cause a prothrombotic inflammatory state and extrapulmonary vascular complications.
symptoms_in_common: Acute left upper quadrant abdominal pain
Pain worsened by deep breathing or lying down
Mild cough and sputum compatible with an atypical respiratory infection
Imaging appearance of focal peripheral splenic lesions compatible with infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: No leukocytosis

data.diagnosis: Splenic infarction due to splenic arterial or venous thrombosis
data.description: A splenic infarct occurs when blood flow to part of the spleen is blocked, commonly producing peripheral wedge-shaped areas of ischemia on imaging. Causes include thrombosis, emboli, infection, hematologic disease, and hypercoagulability.
symptoms_in_common: Pleuritic worsening of pain with deep breathing
Imaging findings suggestive of focal splenic ischemic lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild cough
Whitish sputum

data.description: A splenic abscess is a localized bacterial, fungal, or parasitic infection within the spleen. It can cause fever, inflammatory marker elevation, and left upper quadrant pain, with focal splenic lesions on ultrasound or MRI.
symptoms_not_in_common: No leukocytosis
Mild cough
Whitish sputum

data.diagnosis: Left lower lobe pneumonia with diaphragmatic pleurisy
data.description: Lower-lobe pneumonia can irritate the diaphragm and present with upper abdominal pain rather than prominent respiratory symptoms, particularly in children.
symptoms_in_common: Upper abdominal pain can occur from diaphragmatic irritation
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominant focal left upper quadrant abdominal pain
Splenic focal lesions on imaging

data.description: Epstein-Barr virus infection can enlarge or inflame the spleen and, rarely, lead to splenic infarction through transient hypercoagulability or altered splenic blood flow.
symptoms_in_common: Possible splenic infarct-like lesions on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported sore throat
No reported lymph node enlargement
No reported fatigue
Mild cough and whitish sputum are not typical dominant features
No reported leukocytosis or atypical lymphocytosis

data.description: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

A hepatic abscess caused by invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection, often occurring months to years after travel to endemic regions. It can cause fever, inflammatory-marker elevation, diarrhea, and pleuritic upper abdominal or diaphragmatic pain.
symptoms_in_common: Marked neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein
Left diaphragmatic discomfort on deep inspiration
Travel to Vietnam, an endemic region for amoebiasis, 18 months earlier
Focal hepatic lesion on CT consistent with a liver abscess
Negative blood cultures, which can occur in amoebic liver abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized myalgia and arthralgia are less characteristic
No reported right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain
No hepatomegaly or jaundice

data.description: A localized bacterial infection within the liver, commonly caused by enteric organisms such as Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, streptococci, or anaerobes. It typically produces fever, neutrophilia, high inflammatory markers, and a focal liver lesion on imaging.
symptoms_in_common: Loose stools that may indicate a gastrointestinal source
Hepatic lesion on CT compatible with an abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood cultures were negative, although this does not exclude pyogenic liver abscess
No localized right-upper-quadrant pain
No jaundice or abnormal liver biochemistry
Generalized arthralgia is not a typical dominant feature

data.diagnosis: Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection)
data.description: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in northern Australia and parts of Southeast Asia. It can cause acute febrile illness with abscesses in the liver, spleen, lungs, or other organs.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to Western Australia, where melioidosis can occur
Tachypnoea and sensation of breathing difficulty
Marked neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein
Hepatic focal lesion compatible with an abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: She appeared clinically well despite severe inflammatory markers
No diabetes, chronic kidney disease, hazardous alcohol use, or other stated melioidosis risk factor
Normal chest radiograph despite respiratory symptoms
Negative initial blood cultures

data.diagnosis: Fascioliasis (acute hepatic infection with Fasciola species)
data.description: Fascioliasis is a parasitic liver infection acquired by ingesting contaminated water or aquatic plants. During the acute hepatic migratory phase it can cause fever, abdominal or pleuritic pain, and focal liver lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Discomfort near the diaphragm on inspiration
symptoms_not_in_common: No eosinophilia was reported; severe neutrophilia is more typical of bacterial infection
No reported ingestion of watercress or untreated water
Loose stools are not a prominent typical feature
Very high C-reactive protein and acute severe inflammatory presentation are less typical

data.diagnosis: Portal pylephlebitis with hepatic microabscesses from intra-abdominal infection
data.description: Pylephlebitis is septic thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system, usually arising from an intra-abdominal infection such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, or bowel infection. It may produce liver abscesses and systemic inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Loose stools suggesting a possible gastrointestinal infectious source
Hepatic lesion or lesions on CT that may represent septic embolic microabscesses
Pleuritic diaphragmatic discomfort from hepatic inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear abdominal tenderness or focal abdominal pain was reported
No documented source such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, or inflammatory bowel disease
Blood cultures were negative
Normal liver biochemistry

data.description: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

data.diagnosis: OPA1-associated hereditary spastic paraplegia with dominant optic atrophy (DOA-plus syndrome)
data.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic OPA1 variants, characterized by slowly progressive bilateral optic neuropathy/optic atrophy and upper-motor-neuron spastic paraplegia; additional neurologic features may occur.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive visual decline beginning around age 50
Bilateral optic disc pallor and retinal nerve fiber layer thinning on ocular imaging
Sustained ankle clonus and brisk reflexes
Maternal history of blindness and parkinsonism/dementia, supporting inherited mitochondrial disease
No major brain or spinal cord lesions evident on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands are not a typical feature, although they may be incidental
Preserved pupillary light reflexes despite optic neuropathy are less prominent than in severe optic atrophy

data.description: An immune-mediated central nervous system demyelinating disease that can cause progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory disturbance, bladder dysfunction, and optic neuritis or optic neuropathy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very slowly progressive bilateral visual decline over approximately 10 years rather than a typical acute/subacute optic neuritis episode
Bilateral optic atrophy with a strong maternal history of blindness suggests inherited optic neuropathy
MRI shown does not demonstrate characteristic demyelinating brain or spinal cord lesions
Family history of Parkinson's disease with dementia is not typical of multiple sclerosis
Late onset of visual symptoms and spasticity is less typical for classic relapsing multiple sclerosis

data.description: A genetic, often mitochondrial, complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by SPG7 variants. It commonly causes progressive lower-limb spasticity and may include optic atrophy, ataxia, neuropathy, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Normal limb power with increased tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Optic neuropathy/optic atrophy with reduced visual acuity and dyschromatopsia
Lack of explanatory structural spinal cord disease on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Maternal inheritance pattern and maternal blindness are more suggestive of OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy or mitochondrial inheritance than typical recessive SPG7 disease
No reported cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, or external ophthalmoplegia
CSF oligoclonal bands are not typical of SPG7-related disease

data.description: 14-year-old female with generalized pruritus, scleral icterus/mild mucocutaneous jaundice, and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities for over 2 months. She denied fever, abdominal pain, or distension. Past history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne. She had taken Chinese herbal medicines for about 9 months. Physical examination showed clear consciousness, facial acne and pigmentation, soft nontender abdomen, and no lower extremity edema.

An autosomal-recessive ATP7B-related disorder of impaired biliary copper excretion, causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. The reported homozygous ATP7B c.2333G>T (p.Arg778Leu) pathogenic variant, Kayser-Fleischer ring, and basal-ganglia MRI abnormalities strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Basal ganglia MRI signal abnormalities consistent with copper deposition
symptoms_not_in_common: Acne is not a classic manifestation
No reported neurologic symptoms such as tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, or behavioral change
No abdominal pain or abdominal distension

data.diagnosis: Drug-induced liver injury from Chinese herbal medicines
data.description: Liver injury caused by herbal or traditional medicines may produce hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed hepatitis with jaundice and pruritus. Herbal exposure for approximately 9 months is a relevant potential contributor, although it does not explain the ATP7B mutation, corneal ring, or brain MRI findings.
symptoms_in_common: History of prolonged Chinese herbal medicine use
Petechiae and ecchymoses, potentially from impaired liver synthetic function or coagulopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Kayser-Fleischer ring is not typical
Basal ganglia changes suggesting metal deposition are not typical
Pathogenic homozygous ATP7B variant is not explained by drug-induced liver injury
Amenorrhea and menstrual irregularities are not typical primary features
Facial pigmentation is not a typical feature

data.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that often affects girls and young women and can present with chronic hepatitis, jaundice, and progression to cirrhosis if untreated.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses that could occur with advanced hepatic dysfunction
Menstrual irregularities or amenorrhea can occur in chronic liver disease
No fever or abdominal pain is possible in chronic autoimmune hepatitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized pruritus is less characteristic unless there is significant cholestasis
Kayser-Fleischer ring is not typical
Basal ganglia MRI abnormalities due to copper deposition are not typical
Homozygous pathogenic ATP7B mutation is not explained
Long-term Chinese herbal medicine exposure does not specifically support autoimmune hepatitis

data.description: Chronic hepatitis caused by viruses such as hepatitis B or hepatitis C can cause persistent liver inflammation, jaundice, impaired coagulation, and eventual cirrhosis, although this presentation is less specifically supported than Wilson disease.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses that may result from hepatic synthetic dysfunction or thrombocytopenia
Amenorrhea or menstrual irregularities can occur in chronic liver disease
May occur without fever, abdominal pain, or abdominal distension
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized pruritus is not a dominant feature in most chronic viral hepatitis cases
Kayser-Fleischer ring is not typical
Basal ganglia MRI findings suggestive of copper deposition are not typical
Pathogenic ATP7B mutation is not explained
Facial pigmentation and acne are not typical manifestations

data.description: 66-year-old man with a 2-day history of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. Past history included hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; azathioprine 75 mg had been started 10 days earlier. On examination, temperature was 38°C with bilateral tender knees and patellar tap. Labs showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated CRP and ESR, mildly elevated rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP, dsDNA, ENA, and anti-ASO; renal function and urinalysis were normal. Chest radiograph was normal, and synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

data.diagnosis: Azathioprine-induced Sweet syndrome (drug-induced acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
data.description: A hypersensitivity-type neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by abrupt fever, neutrophilia, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, and systemic inflammation; it can be triggered by azathioprine soon after initiation.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous rash/plaques on the legs
symptoms_not_in_common: Noninflammatory synovial fluid is not a defining feature
Mildly elevated rheumatoid factor is nonspecific and not typical

data.description: A systemic adverse drug reaction occurring days to weeks after azathioprine exposure, commonly causing fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, elevated inflammatory markers, and neutrophilia; it is distinct from dose-related azathioprine toxicity.
symptoms_in_common: Close temporal relationship to starting azathioprine
symptoms_not_in_common: No gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea
No hypotension or shock
No hepatic or renal deterioration reported

data.description: An immune-mediated drug reaction that typically presents one to two weeks after medication exposure with fever, rash, arthralgias or arthritis, and inflammatory marker elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Onset approximately 10 days after a new medication
symptoms_not_in_common: Neutrophilic leukocytosis is less characteristic than in acute neutrophilic dermatosis
The rash appears to be tender plaques rather than the more typical urticarial eruption
No reported facial edema, lymphadenopathy, or hypocomplementemia
Normal urinalysis without renal involvement

data.description: A panniculitis producing tender erythematous nodules, most often on the shins, often accompanied by fever, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers; it may be associated with drugs, infections, inflammatory disease, or systemic conditions.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous lesions on the lower legs
symptoms_not_in_common: Neutrophilic leukocytosis is not specifically characteristic
The lesions appear more plaque-like than classic deep tender shin nodules
Temporal association with azathioprine more strongly supports a drug hypersensitivity/neutrophilic dermatosis
No identified common trigger such as streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, or inflammatory bowel disease

data.diagnosis: Septic arthritis with cellulitis or bacteremia
data.description: Bacterial infection can cause fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis, painful joint swelling, and erythematous skin lesions; diabetes and immunosuppression increase susceptibility.
symptoms_in_common: Diabetes and recent immunosuppressive therapy as infection risk factors
symptoms_not_in_common: Polyarticular arthralgia is less typical than severe involvement of one infected joint
Synovial fluid was noninflammatory
No bacteria were detected in synovial fluid
No crystals or purulent aspirate were reported
Painful multifocal rash is not typical of uncomplicated septic arthritis

data.description: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.
Bleeding into the retropharyngeal space after neck trauma, producing posterior pharyngeal wall swelling and potentially severe upper-airway narrowing.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall
Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling on flexible endoscopy
symptoms_not_in_common: No cervical spine tenderness

data.diagnosis: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
data.description: Injury to the larynx after blunt neck trauma that can cause edema, internal bleeding, vocal-cord dysfunction, and airway obstruction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling is more characteristic of a retropharyngeal process than isolated laryngeal trauma
No cervical spine tenderness

data.description: A collection of blood within the anterior or deep soft tissues of the neck following trauma, which may expand and compress the pharynx or airway.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising extending to the anterior chest wall
symptoms_not_in_common: Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling specifically suggests deep retropharyngeal extension rather than a superficial isolated soft-tissue hematoma
No cervical spine tenderness

data.diagnosis: Traumatic carotid or vertebral artery injury with expanding neck hematoma
data.description: Blunt injury to a cervical blood vessel, such as arterial dissection, pseudoaneurysm, or vessel rupture, can cause an enlarging neck hematoma and airway compression.
symptoms_not_in_common: No focal neurologic deficits are described
No pulsatile neck mass or bruit is described
Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling is more directly suggestive of retropharyngeal hematoma
No cervical spine tenderness

data.description: 37-year-old man with 3 months of recurrent episodes of weakness, irritability, poor concentration, craving for sweets, foggy sensorium, cold/clammy sweating, fatigue, confusion, and memory loss, worse after fasting for several hours, especially at night and early morning. He gained 30 lb after drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. No significant medical history aside from prior umbilical hernia repair and back surgery; no medications or drug use, social alcohol use, family history of diabetes. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy; other system examinations were unremarkable. Routine labs, HbA1c, endocrine testing, and adrenal testing were normal except for mild prolactin elevation. Glucose was low at 2.4 mmol/L with elevated insulin and C-peptide. MR cholangiopancreatography showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular slightly exophytic lesion between the head and neck of the pancreas.
A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that autonomously secretes insulin, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia (Whipple triad).
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent episodes of weakness, confusion, irritability, poor concentration, and memory loss
Symptoms worse after fasting, particularly overnight and in the early morning
Cold clammy sweating and fatigue during episodes
Craving sweets and drinking cola for symptom relief
Documented hypoglycemia with glucose of 2.4 mmol/L
Inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia
Weight gain from frequent carbohydrate intake
Hypervascular pancreatic lesion in the head/neck region
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild prolactin elevation is not a typical direct feature of insulinoma

data.diagnosis: Endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia due to pancreatic nesidioblastosis
data.description: Diffuse overgrowth or hyperfunction of pancreatic beta cells causing excessive endogenous insulin secretion and recurrent hypoglycemia, more commonly seen after bariatric surgery but possible in adults without surgery.
symptoms_in_common: Neuroglycopenic symptoms including confusion, foggy sensorium, poor concentration, and memory loss
Autonomic hypoglycemia symptoms including sweating, weakness, and irritability
Low blood glucose with elevated insulin and C-peptide
Weight gain due to frequent carbohydrate consumption
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are predominantly fasting and nocturnal rather than mainly postprandial
A discrete 1.8 cm hypervascular pancreatic lesion is more suggestive of insulinoma than diffuse beta-cell disease
No history of bariatric or gastric surgery

data.description: Hypoglycemia caused by insulin secretagogue medications, which increase endogenous pancreatic insulin release and therefore produce elevated insulin and C-peptide levels.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia with confusion, sweating, weakness, and impaired concentration
Low glucose with elevated insulin and C-peptide
Symptoms relieved by intake of sugary drinks
symptoms_not_in_common: He reports no medication use or drug use
No known diabetes requiring glucose-lowering therapy
Presence of a hypervascular pancreatic lesion favors a pancreatic insulin-secreting tumor
Episodes have been recurrent for 3 months without a reported exposure to hypoglycemic medication

data.diagnosis: Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous insulin administration
data.description: Deliberate or inadvertent administration of insulin causing hypoglycemia, usually associated with high insulin levels but suppressed endogenous C-peptide production.
symptoms_in_common: Confusion, sweating, weakness, irritability, and cognitive impairment during low glucose episodes
Low blood glucose with elevated insulin
symptoms_not_in_common: C-peptide is elevated rather than suppressed
He denies medication and drug use
The pancreatic hypervascular lesion suggests endogenous insulin production from a tumor
There is no stated access to insulin or history of diabetes treatment

data.description: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

A hypermobility disorder of the false ribs, usually the 8th to 10th ribs, caused by laxity or disruption of interchondral attachments. The mobile rib cartilage can sublux beneath an adjacent rib and irritate the intercostal nerve, producing focal sharp lower anterior chest-wall pain. The ultrasound appearance of altered relationship/mobility of the 8th rib relative to adjacent ribs supports this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent sharp pain in the lower anterior thoracic wall
Pain localized near the false ribs (7th-9th rib region)
Symptoms provoked by exercise and trunk movement
Pain especially triggered by abdominal crunches
No symptoms during routine daily activities
Atraumatic onset associated with repetitive athletic activity

data.description: Overstretching or repetitive overuse injury of an intercostal muscle, commonly occurring with vigorous exercise, twisting, coughing, or forceful trunk movement.
symptoms_in_common: Atraumatic chest-wall pain after beginning CrossFit
Pain provoked by exercise and abdominal crunches
Absence of symptoms at rest or during normal activities
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging appearance suggesting an abnormal relationship or mobility among the 7th, 8th, and 9th ribs rather than an isolated muscle injury
Pain location specifically in the lower false-rib region is more characteristic of slipping rib syndrome

data.description: A mechanical injury or inflammation involving the cartilage junctions between ribs or between rib cartilage and the sternum, often caused by repetitive loading or forceful movement.
symptoms_in_common: Pain triggered by forceful trunk flexion during crunches
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent sharp lower-rib pain with possible dynamic rib displacement is more suggestive of slipping rib syndrome
No reported direct trauma
No reported persistent focal swelling or tenderness at a costochondral junction near the sternum

data.diagnosis: Rib stress injury or stress fracture
data.description: A repetitive-load injury of a rib that may progress from bone stress reaction to fracture, seen in athletes performing repeated high-intensity upper-body or trunk movements.
symptoms_in_common: Onset after starting high-intensity CrossFit training
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is intermittent and specifically provoked by crunches rather than persistent with most chest-wall movement
No history of direct trauma
No described pain at rest, pain with breathing, or progressive constant pain
Ultrasound findings emphasize relationships among adjacent rib cartilages rather than a cortical fracture defect or callus

data.description: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

67-year-old previously healthy man with a 4-month history of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea, initially treated elsewhere as eosinophilic asthma but worsening despite inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids. No smoking or significant past medical history. On examination, he required 1 L/min nasal cannula oxygen, had decreased breath sounds and fine crackles in the right lower lung field, and no JVP elevation, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest x-ray showed right-sided ground-glass opacities, and high-resolution CT revealed ground-glass opacities with surrounding consolidation in the right lower lung field. Laboratory data showed marked eosinophilia, elevated CRP, and anemia.

data.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
data.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia, abnormal eosinophil maturation, cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities, and possible organ damage from eosinophil infiltration.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal eosinophil precursors and dysplastic myeloid cells on blood smear
Pulmonary ground-glass opacities and consolidation compatible with eosinophilic lung infiltration
symptoms_not_in_common: No significant past medical history
No peripheral edema
No cardiac murmur, gallop, or elevated JVP

data.diagnosis: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene rearrangement
data.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms, often involving PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2 rearrangements, that can cause marked eosinophilia, abnormal myeloid cells, anemia, and eosinophil-mediated lung disease.
symptoms_in_common: Immature eosinophilic cells and abnormal myeloid morphology on smear
symptoms_not_in_common: No hepatosplenomegaly was reported
No lymphadenopathy was reported
No constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats were reported

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with pulmonary involvement
data.description: A disorder of persistent eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated organ injury after secondary causes and defined clonal hematologic neoplasms have been excluded. The lungs, heart, skin, gastrointestinal tract, and nervous system may be involved.
symptoms_in_common: Pulmonary infiltrates with ground-glass opacity and consolidation
Failure to improve with standard asthma therapy
symptoms_not_in_common: Anemia is less typical in idiopathic HES
Dysplastic eosinophil precursors and megaloblast-like cells on smear are more suggestive of a clonal myeloid disorder
Cytogenetic abnormalities are not typical of idiopathic HES
Unilateral right lower-lung predominance is less typical than multifocal or bilateral infiltrates

data.description: An eosinophilic lung disease characterized by subacute cough, dyspnea, wheezing, blood eosinophilia, and pulmonary eosinophilic infiltrates; it is usually corticosteroid responsive.
symptoms_not_in_common: Worsening despite inhaled corticosteroids
Anemia
Abnormal immature eosinophils and dysplastic myeloid cells on blood smear
Cytogenetic abnormalities
Marked unilateral right lower-lobe predominance rather than the more typical peripheral upper-lung infiltrates

data.description: A systemic eosinophilic small-vessel vasculitis typically associated with adult-onset asthma, eosinophilia, sinus disease, neuropathy, skin lesions, and variable pulmonary infiltrates.
symptoms_not_in_common: No chronic rhinosinusitis or nasal polyps reported
No peripheral neuropathy reported
No skin lesions or purpura reported
No renal, cardiac, or gastrointestinal vasculitic manifestations reported
Dysplastic eosinophilic precursors and chromosomal abnormalities are not typical of EGPA
Anemia is nonspecific and not a defining feature

data.description: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

data.diagnosis: Systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), ALK-positive
data.description: An aggressive pediatric T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by large CD30-positive anaplastic lymphoid cells, often ALK-positive, with systemic symptoms and frequent extranodal disease.
symptoms_in_common: Possible gastrointestinal involvement causing blood in stools
Imaging findings suggestive of intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy and extranodal involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe microcytic anemia is not a defining feature, although it can occur from chronic inflammation or gastrointestinal bleeding
Occasional diarrhea is less characteristic
Recent travel to the Dominican Republic is not specifically associated with ALCL

data.description: A rapidly growing high-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly affects children and may present with abdominal masses, bowel involvement, systemic symptoms, and tumor-related anemia.
symptoms_in_common: Occasional blood in stools suggesting possible bowel involvement
Possible abdominal lymphadenopathy or renal involvement on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: One month of recurrent fever may occur but is less prominent than rapidly enlarging abdominal mass symptoms in many cases
Microcytic anemia from gastrointestinal blood loss is possible but not classic
Headache, myalgias, and diarrhea are nonspecific rather than typical presenting features

data.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells that usually presents with painless lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms; extranodal abdominal disease can occur.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated ferritin as an inflammatory marker
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent nearly constant periumbilical and left lower quadrant abdominal pain is less typical
Blood in stools and diarrhea are not typical features
Severe microcytic anemia is more suggestive of chronic gastrointestinal blood loss or inflammatory bowel disease
No palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy is reported

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and causes abdominal pain, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, impaired growth, weight loss, and iron-deficiency anemia.
symptoms_in_common: Poor growth with height and weight near the 1st percentile
Severe microcytic anemia compatible with iron deficiency
Low-grade or recurrent fever can occur during active inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: High recurrent fevers and markedly elevated inflammatory markers may suggest infection or malignancy rather than uncomplicated Crohn disease
Ecchymoses are not typical unless related to malnutrition, thrombocytopenia, or another process
Imaging and biopsy findings suggesting widespread nodal or extranodal lesions would be atypical for isolated Crohn disease

data.description: Tuberculosis involving the gastrointestinal tract, peritoneum, or abdominal lymph nodes can cause prolonged fever, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia, inflammatory marker elevation, and bowel symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to the Dominican Republic, where tuberculosis exposure is possible
symptoms_not_in_common: The illness duration of only one month is relatively short for many cases of abdominal tuberculosis
No cough, known tuberculosis exposure, night sweats, or pulmonary symptoms are reported
Marked ecchymoses are not typical
Pathology consistent with anaplastic lymphoma rather than granulomatous infection would argue against tuberculosis

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.title: Mixed cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma

data.description: 39-year-old man with 4 days of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, fatigue, and lower back pain after returning from a 2-week trip to Tanzania/East Africa. During the trip he had mosquito bites; he ate cooked seafood and a small amount of raw tuna. On the second-to-last day of travel he developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. After returning, he reported weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes. Past history: degenerative knee disease with prior glucocorticoid injections. On exam: fever 38.9°C, facial flushing, mild scleral icterus, and dark brown urine.

data.diagnosis: Plasmodium falciparum malaria (potentially severe malaria with hemoglobinuria)
data.description: Mosquito-borne malaria caused by P. falciparum, which can produce high parasitemia, cyclic fever with rigors, hemolysis, jaundice, acute kidney injury, and dark urine (blackwater fever). The rapid malaria test and blood smear images show findings consistent with P. falciparum ring-form parasites.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to Tanzania, a malaria-endemic region

data.description: A mosquito-borne malaria species that commonly causes intermittent fever, chills, headache, malaise, and gastrointestinal symptoms. It is generally less likely than P. falciparum to cause severe hemolysis, renal failure, or marked hemoglobinuria.
symptoms_not_in_common: Dark brown urine suggestive of substantial hemoglobinuria
Decreased urine output suggesting acute kidney injury
Blurry vision during fever episodes
Blood-smear and rapid-test findings favoring Plasmodium falciparum rather than P. vivax

data.description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, myalgias, jaundice, acute kidney injury, and dark urine.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported freshwater, floodwater, animal urine, or rodent exposure
Blurry vision is not a typical presenting symptom
Blood-smear findings of intraerythrocytic malaria parasites are not typical of leptospirosis

data.description: A mosquito-borne flaviviral illness causing acute fever, severe headache, myalgias, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes liver dysfunction. Severe dengue can cause bleeding, plasma leakage, and shock.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to an area where mosquito-borne infections occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Shaking chills are less characteristic
Dark brown urine from hemoglobinuria is not typical
Decreased urine output is not typical unless severe shock is present
Mild scleral icterus is less typical
No rash, thrombocytopenic bleeding, or severe diffuse muscle and joint pain is reported
Blood-smear findings of malaria parasites are not typical of dengue

data.description: A systemic Salmonella infection acquired through contaminated food or water, causing prolonged fever, headache, malaise, anorexia, abdominal symptoms, diarrhea or constipation, and occasionally hepatitis.
symptoms_in_common: Mild scleral icterus can occur with hepatic involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt fever with shaking chills is less typical than sustained or stepwise fever
Dark brown urine suggestive of hemolysis is not typical
Decreased urine output is not a usual presenting feature
Blurry vision during fever episodes is not typical
Blood-smear findings of intraerythrocytic malaria parasites are not typical of enteric fever

data.description: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

data.diagnosis: Delayed esophageal perforation from cervical spinal hardware erosion
data.description: A late complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which plates or screws erode into the esophageal wall, causing perforation and possible fistulous communication with adjacent infected spaces.
symptoms_in_common: History of cervical spine stabilization with metal plates
Imaging evidence of extensive paraspinal abscess
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia is not caused by the esophageal perforation and predates the current illness

data.description: An abnormal communication between the esophagus and mediastinum that permits leakage of saliva, food material, and bacteria into the mediastinum, resulting in severe mediastinal infection and pus collection.
symptoms_in_common: Endoscopic appearance of mediastinal pus near the upper esophageal opening
Findings compatible with communication between the esophagus and infected mediastinal/paraspinal spaces
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia is unrelated to mediastinitis
The remote traumatic car accident is not a typical presenting feature

data.diagnosis: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with vertebral osteomyelitis and paraspinal abscess
data.description: Infection involving prior cervical fixation hardware and/or adjacent vertebrae, potentially causing osteomyelitis, loosening or migration of hardware, and formation of a large paraspinal abscess.
symptoms_in_common: Large paraspinal abscess extending from the cervical spine to T11
Possible secondary esophageal involvement causing dysphagia and odynophagia
symptoms_not_in_common: Dysphagia and odynophagia are less typical unless the infection extends anteriorly to involve or compress the esophagus
Quadriplegia predates the suspected infection

data.diagnosis: Descending necrotizing mediastinitis secondary to cervical infection or esophageal perforation
data.description: A rapidly progressive deep neck or esophageal infection that spreads along fascial planes into the mediastinum, producing purulent mediastinal collections and systemic infection.
symptoms_in_common: Purulent material in the mediastinal region on endoscopy
Extensive infection extending from the cervical region toward the thoracic spine
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia is not a typical manifestation
Prior cervical metal plates are a predisposing factor rather than a typical symptom

data.description: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

A full-thickness rupture of the esophagus, classically occurring after forceful vomiting, causing leakage of air and gastric contents into the mediastinum and pleural spaces. Imaging is consistent with pneumomediastinum, cervical subcutaneous emphysema, and pleural fluid/air, particularly on the left.
symptoms_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back
Imaging evidence of mediastinal and cervical soft-tissue air
Imaging evidence of left pleural fluid/possible hydropneumothorax
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Normal complete blood count
Normal electrolytes

data.description: Air within the mediastinum, often due to disruption of the esophagus after vomiting. It may extend into the neck and coexist with pleural effusions or pneumothorax.
symptoms_in_common: Chest pain radiating to the back
Imaging evidence of air tracking into the lower neck
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent nausea for 72 hours is not caused by pneumomediastinum itself
Pleural fluid is not always present in uncomplicated pneumomediastinum
Diaphoresis is nonspecific

data.description: A tear in the aortic wall causing separation of its layers, typically presenting with abrupt severe chest pain that may radiate to the back. This is an important emergency differential diagnosis for this pain pattern.
symptoms_not_in_common: Repeated vomiting preceding the pain
Worsening nausea for 72 hours
Imaging evidence of cervical and mediastinal air
Imaging evidence of pleural air/fluid related to esophageal injury
Normal cardiac workup does not specifically support or exclude dissection

data.description: Myocardial ischemia or infarction due to reduced coronary blood flow, commonly causing pressure-like chest pain with diaphoresis, nausea, and autonomic symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain radiating to the back after repeated emesis
Imaging evidence of mediastinal and cervical air
Pleural fluid/possible hydropneumothorax
Normal cardiac workup

data.description: A mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction caused by forceful retching or vomiting, most often producing upper gastrointestinal bleeding rather than a full-thickness esophageal rupture.
symptoms_in_common: Chest or upper abdominal discomfort may occur after retching
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back
No hematemesis or other gastrointestinal bleeding
Imaging evidence of mediastinal and cervical air
Pleural fluid/possible hydropneumothorax
Diaphoresis and tachycardia are less typical without significant bleeding

data.description: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsive episodes: initial events involved shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs lasting 4–5 minutes, preceded by occipital pain radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, he had an episode during alcohol use with sudden body stiffening, fall backward, and shaking for 5–8 minutes with urinary incontinence. Despite levetiracetam, seizures continued about once weekly; one month before admission, he was found on the floor with shaking and clenching movements lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but nonverbal, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs. He had extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Past history included febrile seizure in childhood, several concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Family history was notable for maternal schizoaffective disorder and post-traumatic epilepsy. Laboratory studies were largely normal except for mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are not caused by abnormal epileptic cortical electrical activity. They are commonly associated with psychological trauma, PTSD, depression, anxiety, and other functional neurologic symptoms; ictal EEG often shows movement or muscle artifact without an evolving epileptiform seizure pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic PTSD, major depressive disorder, panic disorder, and agoraphobia
History of severe traumatic injury suggested by extensive burn scars
EEG appearance consistent with prominent movement/muscle artifact rather than a clear evolving ictal pattern
symptoms_not_in_common: Urinary incontinence during one event
Mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase
History of childhood febrile seizure
History of multiple concussions
Family history of post-traumatic epilepsy

data.description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures involve sudden tonic body stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking, often with loss of consciousness, falls, injuries, urinary incontinence, postictal confusion, elevated lactate, and elevated creatine kinase.
symptoms_in_common: Shaking of the trunk, arms, and legs
Episodes associated with mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase
History of febrile seizure in childhood
History of concussions, which can increase risk of post-traumatic epilepsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Episodes continue frequently despite levetiracetam
Events are often prolonged for 4–8 minutes
Intermittent nonrhythmic rather than clearly rhythmic movements
Awake and alert but nonverbal/stiff presentation
Strong psychiatric trauma-related comorbidity
EEG image does not show a clearly evolving generalized epileptiform ictal discharge

data.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
data.description: Focal seizures begin in a localized brain region and may progress to bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions. Auras can include visual symptoms, autonomic symptoms, nausea, cognitive changes, or focal pain, followed by impaired awareness and generalized convulsive activity.
symptoms_in_common: Possible prodrome/aura with occipital pain radiating to the neck
Progression to body stiffening and generalized shaking
History of repeated concussions, a possible epilepsy risk factor
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly described stereotyped focal neurologic onset such as unilateral motor activity, automatisms, or focal sensory symptoms
No documented postictal confusion or focal neurologic deficit
Persistently frequent convulsive events despite antiseizure therapy
Nonrhythmic tremor and stiff, nonverbal behavior between or around episodes
EEG image lacks a definite focal evolving ictal discharge

data.description: Transient cerebral hypoperfusion, often from vasovagal or cardiac causes, can produce loss of consciousness with brief tonic stiffening or myoclonic jerks. Palpitations and nausea may precede an episode, but convulsive movements are usually brief and recovery is relatively rapid.
symptoms_in_common: Brief shaking or clenching movements can occur with syncope
symptoms_not_in_common: Convulsions lasting 4–8 minutes are longer than typical convulsive syncope
Weekly recurrent episodes over two years without a described cardiovascular trigger
Urinary incontinence is less characteristic
Persistent stiff posture and nonrhythmic tremulous movements
Mild elevation of lactate and creatine kinase after episodes
Psychiatric and trauma history more strongly supports functional seizures

data.description: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

data.diagnosis: Incarcerated right obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
data.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through the obturator canal, typically occurring in thin, elderly multiparous women. Entrapment of bowel can cause mechanical small-bowel obstruction, and obturator nerve compression can cause medial thigh, hip, or knee pain (Howship-Romberg sign).
symptoms_in_common: Elderly woman with very low BMI
Sudden right knee pain without local knee swelling or tenderness
Right knee flexion for pain relief
Small right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal examination
CT appearance of bowel herniating through the right obturator canal
symptoms_not_in_common: No peritoneal irritation signs

data.description: An obturator hernia in which the trapped bowel has compromised blood supply, potentially progressing to ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. It often presents with bowel obstruction and may initially lack obvious abdominal wall findings.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden right knee pain due to obturator nerve irritation
Right pelvic extraluminal mass on rectal examination
CT evidence of a right obturator hernia
symptoms_not_in_common: No peritoneal irritation signs
No reported fever
No reported hemodynamic instability
No reported severe continuous abdominal pain or signs of bowel ischemia

data.description: A hernia through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, more common in older women and prone to incarceration and strangulation. It can produce bowel obstruction but is anatomically distinct from an obturator hernia.
symptoms_in_common: Possible right groin or pelvic mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Right knee pain relieved by flexion, which is more characteristic of obturator nerve compression
No described palpable groin mass below the inguinal ligament
Rectal examination finding of a deep right-sided pelvic mass
CT appearance localizing herniated bowel to the obturator canal rather than the femoral canal

data.description: Mechanical obstruction caused by fibrous intra-abdominal adhesions, most commonly after prior abdominal surgery or inflammation.
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of abdominal surgery
Sudden right knee pain without knee abnormalities
Pain relieved by flexing the right knee
Right-sided extraluminal pelvic mass on rectal examination
CT evidence of a bowel-containing obturator hernia

data.description: 23-year-old Korean female with 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache, worsening 1 month before presentation. She presented with 1 day of left-eye visual disturbance and visual field loss, followed 2 days later by sudden left-sided hearing loss. Three weeks after initial presentation, she developed right-eye visual field defect, and 2 days later was admitted with tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. Past history was negative for diabetes, hypertension, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, hematologic or cardiovascular disease, oral contraceptive use, and pregnancy. On exam, pupils were reactive without RAPD; corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, intraocular pressure was 18 mmHg bilaterally, and anterior segment exam was normal. Laboratory studies, including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, ESR, and CRP, were normal; cerebrospinal fluid showed mildly elevated protein (74.4 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands.

A rare autoimmune microangiopathy affecting small vessels of the brain, retina, and inner ear, classically causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss. Corpus callosum lesions on MRI are characteristic.
symptoms_in_common: Young woman with severe recurrent headache
Retinal arterial occlusive findings consistent with branch retinal artery occlusion
MRI lesion involving the corpus callosum/pericallosal region
Mildly elevated cerebrospinal-fluid protein without oligoclonal bands
Normal inflammatory markers and negative antiphospholipid antibody testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Preserved central visual acuity despite visual field loss is possible but not required
No overt confusion, cognitive decline, or encephalopathy was described

data.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause recurrent neurologic deficits, visual disturbances, sensory symptoms, and characteristic brain MRI lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent neurologic symptoms over several months
Visual disturbance and visual field defects
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus are uncommon presentations
Branch retinal artery occlusion is not typical of multiple sclerosis
Fluorescein angiographic retinal arterial occlusion is not typical
Cerebrospinal fluid lacked oligoclonal bands
The pattern of combined retinal, cochlear, and corpus callosum small-vessel disease is more typical of Susac syndrome

data.diagnosis: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system
data.description: An inflammatory vasculitis limited to the brain and spinal cord that may produce headache, multifocal ischemic lesions, focal neurologic deficits, and abnormal cerebrospinal fluid findings.
symptoms_in_common: Brain MRI lesion compatible with a small ischemic lesion
Normal systemic inflammatory markers can occur in isolated CNS vasculitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Branch retinal artery occlusion with visual field defects is less typical for vasculitis confined to the CNS
Sudden unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus are not typical
No systemic vasculitic symptoms were described
The characteristic corpus callosum lesion pattern and retinal-inner-ear involvement favor Susac syndrome

data.description: An autoimmune prothrombotic disorder that can cause arterial or venous thrombosis, including retinal vascular occlusion and cerebral ischemic events, often in young adults.
symptoms_in_common: Visual field loss associated with retinal arterial occlusion
Focal neurologic symptom of arm numbness
Brain lesion that could represent ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibody testing were normal
No history of thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity, oral contraceptive use, or systemic autoimmune disease
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus are less typical
Bilateral recurrent retinal, hearing, and corpus callosum involvement is more suggestive of Susac syndrome

data.description: 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of severe paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with slight stooping posture, then progressive gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor balance on tandem gait without limb ataxia, and MMSE 25/30. Labs showed elevated creatine kinase, normal blood and CSF lactate, low TSH, positive antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mildly positive ANA. EMG showed mild myopathic changes. Audiometry revealed sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss, and Holter monitoring showed frequent premature contractions.

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial myopathy due to an MT-TL1 m.3243A>G mutation (MELAS-spectrum mitochondrial disease)
data.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder with highly variable manifestations, including myopathy, exercise intolerance, sensorineural hearing loss, cardiac conduction abnormalities, cognitive impairment, seizures, and cerebellar involvement. Muscle biopsy may show ragged-red fibers and mosaic cytochrome-c oxidase deficiency.
symptoms_in_common: Late-onset progressive proximal and axial muscle weakness
Family history compatible with maternal inheritance and variable expression
Muscle pathology/imaging suggestive of mitochondrial dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported diabetes mellitus
No reported stroke-like episodes
Normal blood and cerebrospinal-fluid lactate
No reported migraine-like headaches, vomiting, or visual field deficits

data.diagnosis: MERRF syndrome due to an MT-TK m.8344A>G mutation
data.description: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers is a mitochondrial disorder that can cause myopathy, elevated CK, ataxia, hearing loss, cognitive decline, seizures, and cardiac abnormalities. Expression varies substantially among maternal relatives.
symptoms_in_common: Mitochondrial-type myopathy with paraspinal muscle wasting
Seizure reported in a family member
Muscle histology compatible with mitochondrial myopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: No myoclonus reported
No seizures reported in the patient herself
Disease began unusually late for classic MERRF
Normal lactate levels

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial recessive ataxia syndrome / POLG-related mitochondrial disease
data.description: POLG-related disorders are nuclear-gene mitochondrial diseases that may present with adult-onset ataxia, myopathy, seizures, neuropathy, hearing loss, cognitive changes, and mitochondrial abnormalities in muscle.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive myopathy with elevated creatine kinase
symptoms_not_in_common: The pedigree appears more suggestive of maternal than autosomal inheritance
No peripheral neuropathy described
No ophthalmoplegia or ptosis described
No liver dysfunction reported
No epilepsy reported in the patient

data.diagnosis: Myofibrillar myopathy, particularly myotilin-related or desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy
data.description: Myofibrillar myopathies are inherited muscle disorders characterized by progressive weakness, muscle atrophy, elevated CK, and abnormal protein aggregates in muscle. Desmin-related disease can additionally cause cardiomyopathy or arrhythmias.
symptoms_in_common: Premature cardiac contractions, particularly compatible with desminopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Cerebellar ataxia is not typical
Sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
Mild cognitive impairment is not typical
Seizures in relatives are not typical
Mitochondrial-type muscle biopsy changes would be less characteristic

data.description: SELENON-related myopathy is a congenital or slowly progressive muscle disorder marked by prominent axial weakness, spinal rigidity or scoliosis, neck weakness, and respiratory muscle involvement. CK can be mildly elevated.
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset at age 63 is much later than typical
Cerebellar ataxia is not typical
Sensorineural hearing loss is not typical
Cardiac premature contractions are not typical
Cognitive impairment and seizures are not typical
Maternal inheritance pattern and mitochondrial biopsy findings would not be expected
