data.description: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.

An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma of childhood, often involving extranodal sites and potentially disseminating to marrow and blood. Tumor cells typically express surface immunoglobulin and mature B-cell markers, and commonly have MYC rearrangement.
symptoms_in_common: Age 2 years, within the typical pediatric age range
Rapidly concerning soft-tissue mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle
Mature B-cell immunophenotype with strong CD45, CD19, CD20, HLA-DR, and surface IgG lambda expression
Absence of TdT and CD34, supporting a mature rather than precursor B-cell neoplasm
CD10 positivity in a subset of neoplastic cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Only partial/weak CD10 expression rather than the usual strong uniform expression
Aberrant CD13 and CD117 expression, which is unusual for classic Burkitt lymphoma
No reported abdominal mass, jaw lesion, or ileocecal involvement
Normal total white blood cell count despite atypical lymphocytes

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
data.description: A mature B-cell lymphoma composed of large malignant lymphoid cells. It can present as a nodal or extranodal soft-tissue mass and may occasionally involve peripheral blood or bone marrow.
symptoms_in_common: Extranodal mass-like lesion involving left anteromedial muscle
Hip pain related to local soft-tissue involvement
Mature clonal B-cell phenotype with CD19, CD20, CD45, HLA-DR, and surface IgG lambda positivity
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age, as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is less common in a 2-year-old child
Circulating atypical lymphocytes are less typical in localized diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
CD10 expression suggests germinal-center differentiation and may favor Burkitt lymphoma or another high-grade B-cell lymphoma
Aberrant CD13 and CD117 expression is not typical

data.diagnosis: High-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC rearrangement
data.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with high-grade morphology and genetic abnormalities involving MYC, sometimes with additional BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements. These tumors may resemble Burkitt lymphoma but can show atypical morphology or immunophenotype.
symptoms_in_common: Anemia and atypical lymphocytes in peripheral blood
Mature B-cell marker expression: CD19, CD20, CD45, and HLA-DR
Negative TdT and CD34, excluding typical precursor B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma
Partial CD10 positivity, compatible with germinal-center B-cell differentiation
symptoms_not_in_common: This category is much less common in very young children than Burkitt lymphoma
No explicit MYC, BCL2, or BCL6 molecular result is provided in the clinical description
No systemic B symptoms such as fever, drenching night sweats, or weight loss are reported

data.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors that commonly affects children and can involve marrow, blood, lymph nodes, bone, and soft tissue. It usually expresses precursor markers such as TdT and CD34 rather than surface immunoglobulin.
symptoms_in_common: Atypical lymphoid cells in peripheral blood
B-lineage marker expression including CD19 and CD10
symptoms_not_in_common: Strong surface IgG lambda expression indicates mature clonal B cells rather than lymphoblasts
CD20 is strongly expressed, whereas precursor B-lymphoblastic neoplasms are often CD20-negative or only weakly positive
TdT is negative
CD34 is negative
CD117 and CD13 expression is atypical and does not establish precursor B-cell disease

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

data.diagnosis: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni (periportal fibrosis/Symmers fibrosis)
data.description: Chronic hepatointestinal infection caused by Schistosoma mansoni eggs lodged in portal venules, producing granulomatous inflammation and characteristic periportal fibrosis that may lead to portal hypertension and splenomegaly.
symptoms_in_common: Schistosoma mansoni eggs detected in stool
Hepatic imaging abnormalities consistent with periportal fibrosis
symptoms_not_in_common: History of trauma
Persistent fever for two months

data.description: Intestinal disease caused by Schistosoma mansoni egg deposition in the colonic wall, resulting in granulomatous inflammation, abdominal symptoms, diarrhoea, and possible progression to hepatosplenic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Schistosoma mansoni eggs detected in stool
symptoms_not_in_common: Right upper-quadrant pain specifically suggesting liver involvement
Periportal hepatic fibrosis on imaging
Splenomegaly on CT imaging
History of trauma

data.description: A localized bacterial infection of the liver that can produce fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and a focal hepatic lesion, usually with imaging evidence of a fluid-containing collection.
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic diarrhoea as the dominant gastrointestinal symptom
Schistosoma mansoni eggs detected in stool
Diffuse periportal fibrosis rather than a typical focal fluid collection
Splenomegaly related to portal hypertension
History of trauma

data.diagnosis: Traumatic hepatic injury or resolving hepatic hematoma
data.description: Liver contusion, laceration, or hematoma following blunt abdominal trauma can cause right upper-quadrant pain and may appear as a focal low-attenuation hepatic abnormality on imaging.
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever evolving over two months
Chronic diarrhoea
Schistosoma mansoni eggs detected in stool
Periportal fibrosis pattern
Splenomegaly

data.description: 44-year-old man presented with severe substernal burning chest pain radiating to the left arm that awakened him from sleep 1 hour prior, with nausea and nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting. He reported similar but milder intermittent chest pain for the past month, lasting hours to days, not exertional and temporarily relieved by antacids and omeprazole. He denied dyspnea, edema, immobility, fever, cough, or trauma. Past medical history was unremarkable; he had not seen a physician for years. He denied tobacco, alcohol, and illicit drug use and had no family history of premature coronary artery disease. Exam showed considerable distress but was otherwise notable for afebrile status, regular cardiac rhythm, no JVD or edema, normal breath sounds, and a nontender chest and abdomen. Labs showed troponin 0.08 ng/mL, WBC 22,000/mm³ with neutrophilia and bandemia, platelets 771,000/mm³, hemoglobin 17.5 g/dL, and glucose 192 mg/dL. He recalled a prior platelet count of about 600,000/mm³ 12 years earlier and reported intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers, without bleeding, thrombosis, erythromelalgia, headache, dizziness, or other neurologic symptoms.
Acute myocardial infarction caused by coronary artery occlusion, with ECG findings consistent with anterior/anterolateral ST-segment elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating to the left arm
ST-segment elevation in anterior precordial ECG leads
symptoms_not_in_common: Month-long intermittent nonexertional chest pain lasting hours to days
Temporary relief with antacids and omeprazole
Marked chronic thrombocytosis
Intermittent pruritus after hot showers

data.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by increased red-cell production and often associated leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, aquagenic pruritus, and arterial or venous thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: History of platelet count around 600,000/mm³ years earlier
Possible arterial thrombosis presenting as myocardial infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe acute chest pain is not a direct constitutional symptom of polycythemia vera
Nausea and nonbloody vomiting
No reported headache, dizziness, visual symptoms, erythromelalgia, or splenomegaly

data.description: A myeloproliferative neoplasm with persistent high platelet counts that can cause arterial thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis and myocardial infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Acute myocardial infarction possibly due to arterial thrombosis
Leukocytosis can occur in this disorder
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated hemoglobin and aquagenic pruritus are more suggestive of polycythemia vera
No erythromelalgia
No headache, dizziness, or other microvascular neurologic symptoms
No bleeding symptoms

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary thrombosis secondary to a myeloproliferative neoplasm
data.description: Coronary artery thrombosis may occur in polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia because of increased blood viscosity, platelet activation, and abnormal blood-cell production.
symptoms_in_common: Acute severe chest pain with left arm radiation
symptoms_not_in_common: Chest pain temporarily relieved by antacids and omeprazole
No prior known thrombotic events
No conventional coronary risk factors reported, such as tobacco use or family history of premature coronary disease

data.description: Acid reflux or esophageal inflammation can cause burning substernal discomfort, sometimes with nausea or vomiting, and may improve with antacids or proton-pump inhibitors.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent chest pain over the prior month
Temporary symptom relief with antacids and omeprazole
symptoms_not_in_common: Radiation of severe pain to the left arm
Elevated troponin
Anterior ST-segment elevation on ECG
Marked thrombocytosis and leukocytosis
Acute severe distress consistent with myocardial ischemia

diagnoses.name: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction
diagnoses.title: Acute ST segment elevation myocardial infarction

data.description: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Mother was a 19-year-old gravida 1, para 1 with hepatitis C infection, treated Chlamydia trachomatis during pregnancy, and gestational hypertension. Prenatal ultrasounds showed right-sided urinary tract dilatation. At 40 weeks, after prolonged labor and cesarean delivery for nonreassuring fetal status with meconium-stained fluid, the infant was born in breech presentation with limp tone and no respiratory effort. Resuscitation for 16 minutes was required before return of spontaneous circulation. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU arrival, temperature was 34.9°C, heart rate 141 bpm, blood pressure 84/59 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97% on mechanical ventilation. Therapeutic hypothermia was started.

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary sequestration (likely intralobar sequestration of the left lower lobe)
data.description: A congenital nonfunctioning segment of lung that lacks normal bronchial communication and receives an anomalous systemic arterial supply, typically from the descending thoracic aorta. It may cause neonatal respiratory distress and can appear as an abnormal lower-lobe pulmonary opacity or hyperinflated region.
symptoms_in_common: Severe respiratory failure at birth requiring mechanical ventilation
Abnormal chest imaging involving a lower lung region
Imaging evidence of an anomalous systemic artery arising from the aorta and supplying abnormal lung tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Breech presentation
Prolonged labor
Profound perinatal asphyxia requiring 16 minutes of resuscitation
Prenatal right-sided urinary tract dilatation

data.diagnosis: Hybrid congenital pulmonary airway malformation and pulmonary sequestration
data.description: A hybrid congenital lung lesion combines features of congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM) with an anomalous systemic arterial supply characteristic of pulmonary sequestration. These lesions can produce cystic, hyperinflated, or consolidated lower-lobe abnormalities and respiratory compromise in newborns.
symptoms_in_common: Respiratory failure in the neonatal period
Possible hyperlucent or cystic-appearing lung abnormality on serial chest radiographs
Anomalous systemic arterial supply from the aorta on vascular imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Meconium-stained fluid
Breech delivery
Maternal hepatitis C infection
Maternal treated chlamydial infection
Prenatal urinary tract dilatation
Severe hypoxic-ischemic event from difficult delivery is not a typical direct manifestation of the lesion

data.description: CPAM is a developmental malformation of the lung characterized by abnormal bronchiolar and alveolar tissue, often producing cystic or hyperinflated lung areas. Large lesions can cause respiratory distress immediately after birth.
symptoms_in_common: Respiratory distress or respiratory failure at birth
Abnormal unilateral lower-lobe chest radiograph findings
Potential air-filled or hyperlucent abnormal lung region
symptoms_not_in_common: Anomalous systemic arterial supply from the descending aorta is not typical of isolated CPAM
Meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Breech presentation
Maternal infections
Prenatal right urinary tract dilatation
Cardiorespiratory arrest after prolonged labor is more suggestive of perinatal asphyxia than isolated CPAM

data.diagnosis: Neonatal pneumothorax or pulmonary air-leak syndrome
data.description: Air leakage into the pleural space or pulmonary interstitium can occur after vigorous resuscitation, positive-pressure ventilation, meconium aspiration, or underlying congenital lung disease. It may cause sudden respiratory decompensation and unilateral hyperlucency on radiographs.
symptoms_in_common: Severe respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation
Serial chest radiographs with hyperlucent peripheral lung regions suggestive of possible air leak
Potential association with meconium-stained fluid and positive-pressure ventilation
symptoms_not_in_common: A systemic arterial vessel arising from the aorta and supplying abnormal lung tissue
A persistent congenital lower-lobe lung abnormality on CT
Prenatal urinary tract dilatation
Breech presentation
Maternal hepatitis C infection

data.description: 54-year-old man with polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, hypertensive (172/110 mmHg), with distended neck veins and bibasilar crackles. Labs showed severe renal failure (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), anemia (hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL), proteinuria (urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 1.9), elevated LDH, rare schistocytes, reduced C3 with normal C4, and persistent C3 hypocomplementemia during hospitalization. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine metabolites. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Renal ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm. Family history was notable for a sister with renal failure requiring dialysis at age 45.

data.diagnosis: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, aHUS)
data.description: A complement dysregulation disorder causing endothelial injury, thrombotic microangiopathy, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and severe acute kidney injury. It may be triggered by cocaine use, hypertension, or infection and can be associated with inherited complement abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Severe renal failure with creatinine 16.0 mg/dL and BUN 99 mg/dL
Persistent low C3 with normal C4, suggesting alternative complement-pathway activation
Family history of early renal failure
Renal biopsy appearance consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy and chronic vascular injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked hypertension may be a trigger or consequence rather than a universal presenting feature
Cocaine-positive toxicology is not intrinsic to aHUS, although it can trigger it
Distended neck veins and bibasilar crackles reflect volume overload rather than the primary disease

data.description: Severe hypertension can cause acute endothelial damage in renal arterioles, producing thrombotic microangiopathy, fibrinoid vascular injury, onion-skin arteriolar thickening, hemolysis, and rapidly progressive kidney failure.
symptoms_in_common: Biopsy findings compatible with arteriolar thrombotic microangiopathy and concentric onion-skin vascular changes
Pulmonary congestion with bibasilar crackles and distended neck veins, consistent with hypertensive/uremic volume overload
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent isolated C3 hypocomplementemia is not typical of hypertension alone
Family history of dialysis-dependent renal failure at age 45 suggests an additional inherited renal or complement disorder
Cocaine exposure is a precipitating factor rather than a defining feature

data.diagnosis: Cocaine-associated thrombotic microangiopathy and hypertensive renal injury
data.description: Cocaine can cause intense vasoconstriction, severe hypertension, endothelial injury, platelet activation, and renal thrombotic microangiopathy. Levamisole-adulterated cocaine may also contribute to vascular and immune-mediated injury.
symptoms_in_common: Urine toxicology positive for cocaine metabolites
Renal vascular injury consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy
Altered mental status, which may result from uremia or hypertensive encephalopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent low C3 with normal C4 is not a typical isolated cocaine effect and suggests complement activation
Family history of early renal failure is not explained by cocaine use
Echogenic relatively small kidneys suggest pre-existing chronic kidney disease rather than solely an acute cocaine exposure

data.diagnosis: Hepatitis C-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (often cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis)
data.description: Chronic hepatitis C can cause immune-complex glomerulonephritis, particularly mixed cryoglobulinemic membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, leading to proteinuria, hematuria, renal dysfunction, and complement consumption.
symptoms_in_common: Low complement level, especially reduced C3
Hypertension can occur in advanced renal disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal C4 is less typical because cryoglobulinemic glomerulonephritis often causes prominent C4 consumption
Rare schistocytes and elevated LDH suggest thrombotic microangiopathy rather than isolated immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Biopsy vascular onion-skin/thrombotic microangiopathy changes are not the classic pattern of HCV-associated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
No reported purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy, or cryoglobulinemic systemic manifestations

data.diagnosis: Chronic kidney disease with superimposed acute kidney injury due to hypertensive nephrosclerosis
data.description: Long-standing hypertension causes progressive arteriolar sclerosis, glomerular ischemia, proteinuria, and small echogenic kidneys. A hypertensive emergency can precipitate acute deterioration and volume overload.
symptoms_in_common: Volume overload with distended neck veins and bibasilar crackles
Anemia compatible with advanced chronic kidney disease
Family history of renal failure may indicate susceptibility to chronic kidney disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent low C3 is not typical of uncomplicated hypertensive nephrosclerosis
Elevated LDH and schistocytes are not typical unless there is superimposed thrombotic microangiopathy
Abrupt profound renal dysfunction may be more severe than expected from uncomplicated chronic hypertensive nephrosclerosis

data.description: 44-year-old Chinese woman, previously healthy, with 7 weeks of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting and 13 kg weight loss, without abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea. She had no response to 3 weeks of treatment with antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, loss of pharyngeal reflex, decreased tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski sign. Prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal. Laboratory studies showed normal liver, kidney, thyroid, autoimmune, and glucose/HbA1c results; serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive.

data.diagnosis: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with area postrema syndrome
data.description: An autoimmune astrocytopathy associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies. Lesions in the dorsal medulla/area postrema can cause intractable nausea and vomiting, while additional brainstem or spinal cord involvement can produce neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Seven weeks of progressive intractable nausea and vomiting
Marked 13 kg weight loss due to persistent vomiting
No gastrointestinal structural cause on gastroscopy or abdominal CT
Poor response to anti-emetics and prokinetic therapy
Acute respiratory failure suggesting brainstem involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative serum AQP4-IgG, although CSF-only positivity can occur

data.description: A neurologic emergency caused by thiamine deficiency, often after prolonged vomiting or malnutrition. It classically causes encephalopathy, eye movement abnormalities, and gait ataxia.
symptoms_in_common: Severe weight loss and likely nutritional depletion
symptoms_not_in_common: Right-sided limb paralysis
Loss of pharyngeal reflex
Bilateral Babinski signs
Acute respiratory failure
Positive cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG
No reported confusion, memory impairment, or gait ataxia

data.description: Inflammation of the brainstem due to infectious, autoimmune, or paraneoplastic causes. It may produce cranial nerve dysfunction, eye movement abnormalities, long-tract signs, weakness, and respiratory compromise.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent vomiting that can occur with dorsal medullary involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG favors NMOSD rather than nonspecific brainstem encephalitis
No reported fever, altered mental status, headache, or infectious prodrome

data.diagnosis: Posterior circulation ischemic stroke involving the medulla/brainstem
data.description: An infarction in the vertebrobasilar circulation can affect the medulla or pons, causing vomiting, nystagmus, cranial nerve abnormalities, weakness, pyramidal signs, and potentially respiratory failure.
symptoms_in_common: Acute respiratory failure due to brainstem dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Seven weeks of gradually progressive vomiting rather than sudden symptom onset
Previously healthy 44-year-old woman without reported vascular risk factors
Positive cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG
Marked prolonged weight loss preceding the focal neurologic deficits

data.description:
47-year-old male with 2-month history of fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. History of inguinal hernia repair surgery 10 years ago and cardiac disease. On admission, body temperature was 37.3°C. A rare, subacute bacterial endocarditis caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, a gram-positive rod often associated with animal or animal-product exposure. It has characteristic intrinsic resistance to vancomycin and is usually susceptible to penicillin.
symptoms_in_common: Aortic diastolic murmur suggesting valvular insufficiency
Echocardiographic findings consistent with aortic-valve vegetation and regurgitation
symptoms_not_in_common: No skin lesion such as erysipeloid was reported
No reported occupational or animal exposure

data.description: Infection of a native heart valve causing persistent fever, systemic inflammatory symptoms, valve vegetation, and progressive valvular regurgitation. It may be caused by unusual gram-positive organisms including Erysipelothrix species.
symptoms_in_common: New or abnormal aortic diastolic murmur
Aortic regurgitation on color Doppler imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No embolic manifestations were reported
No peripheral stigmata such as petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, or Janeway lesions were reported

data.description: A culture-negative or difficult-to-culture subacute endocarditis caused by Coxiella burnetii, usually occurring in patients with pre-existing valvular disease and often involving the aortic valve.
symptoms_not_in_common: The antimicrobial susceptibility pattern with penicillin susceptibility and extreme vancomycin resistance is not typical for Coxiella burnetii
No reported exposure to livestock, parturient animals, or unpasteurized dairy products
Visible large valvular vegetation is less typical than in conventional bacterial endocarditis

data.description: A rare but severe complication of brucellosis in which Brucella species infect a heart valve, commonly producing a prolonged febrile systemic illness and destructive aortic-valve disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported livestock, animal, or unpasteurized dairy exposure
The reported beta-lactam and vancomycin susceptibility pattern is not characteristic of Brucella species
No hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or focal osteoarticular brucellosis was reported

data.description: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.
Entry of air into the venous circulation during an invasive procedure, potentially causing acute pulmonary vascular obstruction and hypoxaemia.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden gurgling sensation in the arm during venesection
Hypoxia with oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient left hemiplegia
Dysphasia
Right-to-left intracardiac shunt through a patent foramen ovale

data.diagnosis: Paradoxical air embolism through a patent foramen ovale
data.description: Venous air enters the right heart and crosses a patent foramen ovale into the systemic arterial circulation, allowing embolization to the cerebral and coronary arteries.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden onset during venesection with a gurgling arm sensation
Severe acute chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm
Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirming patent foramen ovale
symptoms_not_in_common: None; the combined acute neurologic, respiratory, and cardiac findings are highly compatible

data.diagnosis: Transient ischaemic attack or acute ischaemic stroke due to cerebral air embolism
data.description: Temporary or persistent focal neurological dysfunction caused by air embolization to cerebral arteries; rapid symptom resolution supports a transient ischaemic event.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt onset during an invasive procedure
Resolution of neurological deficits within 15 minutes
Patent foramen ovale permitting arterial embolization
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm
Raised troponin and inferior ECG T-wave inversion
Marked dyspnoea and hypoxia

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary air embolism
data.description: Myocardial ischaemia or infarction caused by air entering a coronary artery, in this case plausibly after paradoxical embolization through a patent foramen ovale.
symptoms_in_common: Radiation of pain to the jaw and left arm
Patent foramen ovale allowing systemic arterial air embolization
symptoms_not_in_common: Transient left hemiplegia
Dysphasia
Severe hypoxia and dyspnoea are not typical features of isolated coronary air embolism

data.description: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.

A rare, usually superficial astrocytic brain tumor that often arises in the temporal lobe and commonly presents with long-standing seizures in younger patients. Many PXAs harbor a BRAF V600E mutation and are WHO grade 2, although some may progress.
symptoms_in_common: History of biopsy/resection with pathology confirming PXA

data.description: Regrowth or persistence of a previously resected PXA. Recurrence may appear as a new or enlarging contrast-enhancing lesion with surrounding FLAIR/T2 signal abnormality at or near the prior tumor site.
symptoms_in_common: Enhancing intracranial lesion on MRI with adjacent signal abnormality
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly described new focal neurologic deficit
No documented progressive cognitive or language impairment

data.description: A higher-grade, more aggressive form of PXA characterized by increased mitotic activity and a greater tendency toward recurrence or progression. BRAF V600E mutations may still be present.
symptoms_not_in_common: No pathology findings of anaplasia or increased mitotic activity are provided
No rapid neurologic deterioration is described
No necrosis, marked mass effect, or other definitive high-grade imaging features are stated

data.description: A typically slow-growing glioneuronal tumor, often located in the temporal lobe and strongly associated with chronic focal seizures. Some gangliogliomas also carry BRAF V600E mutations and can resemble PXA radiologically and histologically.
symptoms_not_in_common: Resection pathology was reported as PXA rather than ganglioglioma
No specific glioneuronal histologic features are described

data.description: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous rash and progressive muscle pain and weakness. The rash began on the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and knees, later with heliotrope rash, periungual erythema/edema, and erythematous papules on the fingertips, fingers, elbows, and knees. One week after rash onset, he developed intense generalized myalgias and worsening weakness with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Exam showed bilateral weakness of the deltoids, triceps, hip flexors, hamstrings, quadriceps, grip, and foot dorsiflexion/plantar flexion, with normal muscle tone, reflexes, and sensation. On admission he was afebrile but tachycardic and tachypneic with hypoxemia, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, hypoactive bowel sounds, and pitting edema of the arms and legs. History includes prior meniscal repair; no smoking or illicit drug use.
An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by distinctive cutaneous findings and symmetric proximal muscle weakness due to muscle inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Heliotrope violaceous rash on the eyelids
Papules over metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints consistent with Gottron papules
Papules on the fingertips and fingers
Progressive symmetric muscle weakness involving shoulders, hips, thighs, and upper arms
Difficulty rising from a squat, walking, and climbing stairs
Normal sensation and reflexes despite weakness
Possible respiratory muscle or pulmonary involvement with hypoxemia and tachypnea
symptoms_not_in_common: Pitting edema of the arms and legs is not a classic feature, although it can occur in severe inflammatory disease
Hypoactive bowel sounds are not a typical primary manifestation

data.description: A dermatomyositis subtype often associated with painful ulcerative or inflammatory hand lesions, periungual changes, and potentially rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease; muscle weakness may be variable.
symptoms_in_common: Gottron-like papules over the finger joints, elbows, and knees
Papules on the fingertips and fingers
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, and diminished breath sounds that could suggest lung involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked generalized proximal and distal muscle weakness is less typical than in classic dermatomyositis because anti-MDA5 disease may be clinically amyopathic or mildly myopathic
Pitting peripheral edema is not a usual defining feature
No reported skin ulceration, palmar papules, arthritis, or fever

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy syndrome characterized by myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and sometimes mechanic's hands.
symptoms_in_common: Hypoxemia and tachypnea that may reflect interstitial lung disease
Possible bibasilar pulmonary abnormality suggested by diminished breath sounds
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash is more characteristic of dermatomyositis than antisynthetase syndrome
Gottron papules over the MCP and PIP joints are not typical of isolated antisynthetase syndrome
Periungual erythema and edema are less characteristic
No reported mechanic's hands
No reported inflammatory arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, or fever

data.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing subacute symmetric proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle inflammation, but without the characteristic skin findings of dermatomyositis.
symptoms_in_common: Weakness of the shoulder girdle and hip girdle muscles
Difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a squat
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope eyelid rash
Gottron papules over the MCP and PIP joints
Rash over elbows and knees
Periungual erythema and edema
Fingertip papules
Peripheral pitting edema is not typical

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory myositis overlap
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive rashes, inflammatory muscle disease, edema, pulmonary manifestations, and constitutional symptoms; overlap with dermatomyositis can occur.
symptoms_in_common: Myalgias and muscle weakness from inflammatory myositis
Hypoxemia and tachypnea, which can occur with lupus-related pulmonary disease
Peripheral edema, which may occur with renal or inflammatory involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash is more specific for dermatomyositis
Gottron papules over the knuckles, elbows, and knees strongly favor dermatomyositis
No reported photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, renal symptoms, or fever

data.description: 59-year-old woman with longstanding epilepsy with complex partial seizures treated with phenytoin for >20 years, presenting with a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness and generalized bone and muscle pain causing marked दैनिक activity limitation. Symptoms worsened with proximal muscle pain and weakness and increasing bone pain. Physical examination showed normal renal and liver function, and radiographs revealed bilateral Looser’s zones in the femoral neck.

Metabolic bone disease caused by long-term phenytoin use, often through increased vitamin D breakdown leading to impaired bone mineralization, hypocalcemia or hypophosphatemia, muscle weakness, bone pain, and insufficiency fractures.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral Looser’s zones in the femoral neck
Diffuse skeletal uptake pattern on bone scintigraphy consistent with metabolic bone disease

data.description: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization of mature bone, commonly caused by vitamin D deficiency. It produces diffuse bone pain, proximal myopathy, fragility or insufficiency fractures, and Looser’s zones.
symptoms_in_common: Bone scan findings suggestive of increased bone turnover and insufficiency fractures
symptoms_not_in_common: No stated history of poor dietary intake, malabsorption, or limited sunlight exposure
Long-term phenytoin exposure suggests a medication-induced cause rather than uncomplicated nutritional deficiency

data.description: Osteomalacia due to chronic low phosphate availability, which may result from renal phosphate wasting, medications, malabsorption, or tumor-induced osteomalacia. It causes bone pain, proximal weakness, and pseudofractures.
symptoms_in_common: Looser’s zones/pseudofractures in the femoral neck
Metabolic bone disease pattern on scintigraphic imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No phosphate level or evidence of renal phosphate wasting is provided
Normal renal function does not support chronic renal failure as the source
Long-term phenytoin use more strongly supports drug-related vitamin D metabolism disturbance

data.description: A rare paraneoplastic syndrome, usually caused by small phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors that produce excess FGF23, leading to renal phosphate wasting, osteomalacia, diffuse bone pain, weakness, and insufficiency fractures.
symptoms_in_common: Marked limitation in mobility and daily activity
Looser’s zones in the femoral neck
Diffuse skeletal abnormalities compatible with osteomalacia
symptoms_not_in_common: No identified tumor or soft-tissue mass is described
No laboratory evidence of phosphate wasting or elevated FGF23 is provided
Long-term phenytoin treatment provides a more direct explanation

data.description: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

data.diagnosis: Native mitral valve infective endocarditis caused by group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus
data.description: Infection of the native mitral valve endocardium with vegetation formation, caused here by bloodstream infection with group A Streptococcus. It can produce valvular destruction, emboli, fever, and systemic inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute dysarthria is not a primary cardiac symptom but is explained by embolic stroke
Respiratory distress is more suggestive of associated severe mitral regurgitation or heart failure than uncomplicated endocarditis

data.diagnosis: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke secondary to infective endocarditis
data.description: An acute cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected material from a cardiac valve vegetation. The brain image is consistent with a focal ischemic lesion in the left cerebral hemisphere, which can cause contralateral motor coordination deficits and dysarthria.
symptoms_in_common: Poor right-hand alternating movement test performance
Focal brain lesion on magnetic resonance imaging
Mitral valve vegetation as an embolic source
Fever and bacteremia supporting septic embolism from infective endocarditis
symptoms_not_in_common: Apical systolic murmur
Respiratory distress
Elevated NT-pro-BNP
Displaced apex beat
Marked inflammatory markers and positive blood culture are not typical of a noninfectious ischemic stroke

data.diagnosis: Acute severe mitral regurgitation due to infective mitral valve destruction
data.description: Severe backward flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium due to infection-related mitral leaflet or chordal damage. This can cause an apical pansystolic murmur, pulmonary congestion, respiratory distress, ventricular enlargement, and elevated natriuretic peptide levels.
symptoms_in_common: Grade 4/6 systolic murmur maximal at the apex
Displaced apex beat in the sixth intercostal space outside the midclavicular line
Color Doppler evidence of substantial mitral regurgitant flow
Mitral valve vegetation suggesting infective valvular injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute dysarthria
Right-hand coordination deficit
Positive blood culture and fever are due to the underlying infective endocarditis rather than mitral regurgitation alone
Focal cerebral infarction is not a direct manifestation of isolated mitral regurgitation

data.description: Ischemic injury of splenic tissue caused by embolization from infective endocarditis. Abdominal ultrasonography can show focal hypoechoic splenic lesions consistent with infarction or embolic involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Infective endocarditis with mitral valve vegetation
Systemic inflammatory response with fever, neutrophilia, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Abdominal ultrasound lesion compatible with splenic embolic infarction
Concurrent cerebral embolic infarction increases the likelihood of systemic embolization
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain or left upper-quadrant tenderness was reported
Dysarthria and right-hand incoordination are explained by cerebral rather than splenic embolism
Apical systolic murmur and respiratory distress are cardiac manifestations

data.description: 3.5-year-old male with proteinuria, hematuria, and glycosuria noted in the early neonatal period, followed by a UTI at 12 months and bronchopneumonia at 3 years with elevated creatinine. Ongoing laboratory findings showed constant proteinuria, glycosuria, hematuria, reduced eGFR, elevated serum creatinine, uric acid, urea, total cholesterol, and triglycerides. Renal ultrasound showed increased cortical echogenicity and decreased corticomedullary differentiation. Physical features included dolichocephaly, frontal bossing, full cheeks, broad nasal bridge, long/flat philtrum, narrow upper lip, everted lower lip, low-set/protruding ears, narrow chest, pectus excavatum, short ribs, rhizomelic limb shortening, short humeri, short fibulae, flattened epiphyses, brachydactyly, overlapping toes, joint laxity, fine sparse hair, small teeth, thin/short nails, and protuberant abdomen. Ophthalmologic findings included hyperopia, strabismus, and nystagmus. Family history was unremarkable; karyotype was normal (46,XY).

A rare autosomal-recessive ciliopathy characterized by craniofacial abnormalities, ectodermal defects involving hair, teeth and nails, skeletal dysplasia with narrow thorax and short limbs, and progressive tubulointerstitial kidney disease that may cause renal failure.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive renal dysfunction with reduced eGFR and elevated creatinine, urea and uric acid
Increased renal cortical echogenicity and poor corticomedullary differentiation
Full cheeks, broad nasal bridge, long flat philtrum, narrow upper lip and everted lower lip
Narrow chest, pectus excavatum and short ribs
Rhizomelic limb shortening, short humeri and short fibulae
Flattened epiphyses, brachydactyly, overlapping toes and joint laxity
Fine sparse hair, small teeth and thin short nails
symptoms_not_in_common: Urinary tract infection is not a defining feature
Bronchopneumonia is not a core diagnostic feature
Marked hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia are not classic primary findings

data.description: An autosomal-recessive skeletal ciliopathy causing a narrow thorax with short ribs, short limbs, brachydactyly, and variable renal disease including nephronophthisis and progressive chronic kidney disease.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive renal impairment with elevated creatinine and reduced eGFR
Abnormal renal ultrasound with increased cortical echogenicity
symptoms_not_in_common: Neonatal proteinuria, hematuria and glycosuria are less typical than later concentrating defects or nephronophthisis
Fine sparse hair
Small teeth
Thin short nails
Characteristic long philtrum, narrow upper lip and everted lower lip
Joint laxity
Hyperopia, strabismus and nystagmus are not typical core findings

data.description: A ciliopathy with skeletal dysplasia, particularly cone-shaped epiphyses and phalangeal abnormalities, progressive renal disease often resembling nephronophthisis, and possible retinal or ocular involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive chronic kidney disease with reduced eGFR and elevated creatinine
Proteinuria and abnormal renal ultrasound findings
Skeletal dysplasia with shortened long bones and flattened epiphyses
Ophthalmologic abnormalities including nystagmus and strabismus
symptoms_not_in_common: Fine sparse hair, small teeth and thin short nails are not typical major features
Characteristic craniofacial appearance with long flat philtrum and everted lower lip is less typical
Glycosuria and hematuria from the neonatal period are not classic presenting findings
Retinal dystrophy is more typical than hyperopia
Joint laxity is not a defining feature

data.description: A rare autosomal-recessive multisystem disorder caused by SMARCAL1 variants, characterized by progressive renal disease, skeletal dysplasia with short stature, facial dysmorphism, sparse hair, and susceptibility to infections due to immune dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive renal dysfunction with proteinuria and elevated creatinine
Hyperlipidemia associated with renal protein loss
Short stature phenotype with limb and epiphyseal skeletal abnormalities
Recurrent infections, including urinary infection and bronchopneumonia
symptoms_not_in_common: Glycosuria and hematuria beginning in the neonatal period are not typical
Narrow thorax with short ribs is not a classic feature
Small teeth and thin short nails are not typical
Brachydactyly and overlapping toes are less characteristic
Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia more commonly causes spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia rather than the described short-rib pattern
No immune deficiency, lymphopenia or opportunistic infection has been reported

data.description: A 58-year-old man presented with a six-week history of muscle weakness, dysphagia, and a symmetrical widespread rash on the face, torso, and limbs. Laboratory testing revealed elevated creatine kinase of 7070 u/L (reference range 30-175). An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed and showed abnormal findings, and a PET CT scan was arranged.

An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by proximal muscle inflammation and distinctive cutaneous findings, including Gottron papules over the knuckles. It may be associated with an underlying malignancy in adults.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia due to involvement of pharyngeal or oesophageal skeletal muscle
Papulosquamous erythematous lesions over the knuckles consistent with Gottron papules
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings are not caused directly by uncomplicated dermatomyositis
Focal oesophageal FDG uptake on PET-CT would suggest an associated process rather than dermatomyositis itself

data.description: Dermatomyositis occurring as a paraneoplastic syndrome, particularly in older adults. The inflammatory muscle and skin disease can precede or accompany discovery of a solid malignancy, including upper gastrointestinal cancers.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset of symmetric muscle weakness
PET-CT finding suspicious for an oesophageal lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: No constitutional cancer symptoms such as weight loss, anorexia, or night sweats were reported
No biopsy-confirmed malignancy was provided

data.description: A malignant tumour of the oesophagus that may cause dysphagia and can rarely trigger dermatomyositis as a paraneoplastic autoimmune syndrome. PET avidity in the oesophagus and abnormal endoscopy raise concern for this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Focal abnormal uptake in the oesophageal region on PET-CT
Potential paraneoplastic dermatomyositis manifestations, including weakness, elevated creatine kinase, and Gottron papules
symptoms_not_in_common: Muscle weakness is not usually caused directly by oesophageal carcinoma
Marked creatine kinase elevation is not typical of oesophageal carcinoma alone
Gottron papules and widespread inflammatory rash are not typical direct manifestations of oesophageal carcinoma

data.description: A severe autoimmune inflammatory myopathy causing prominent proximal weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase, sometimes associated with malignancy, medications such as statins, or autoantibodies.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia can occur in severe disease
Possible association with an underlying malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Gottron papules over the knuckles are not typical
A widespread characteristic dermatomyositis-like rash is not typical
Facial rash is less characteristic than in dermatomyositis

data.description: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head epiphysis in children, leading to femoral-head fragmentation, flattening, and possible lateral extrusion on radiographs.
symptoms_in_common: Radiographic femoral-head deformity/fragmentation consistent with Perthes disease

data.description: A self-limited inflammatory hip effusion, often following a viral illness, that commonly causes acute limp and hip pain in young children.
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent structural abnormality of the femoral head on radiographs
Marked restriction of internal rotation and abduction suggestive of chronic hip disease
No reported recent viral illness
Age 8 years is somewhat older than the typical peak age

data.description: Posteroinferior displacement of the femoral-head epiphysis relative to the femoral neck through the growth plate, usually occurring in adolescents during growth spurts.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced and painful internal rotation of the hip
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 8 years is younger than typical for SCFE
No obesity or endocrine disorder reported
Reduced abduction may occur but is less characteristic than obligatory external rotation
Radiographic appearance is more consistent with femoral-head avascular necrosis/fragmentation than physeal slipping

data.description: An acute bacterial infection of the hip joint that can rapidly damage cartilage and bone and usually requires urgent treatment.
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile
Otherwise healthy and well appearing
No acute systemic illness described
No severe acute pain or inability to bear weight reported
Radiographic femoral-head changes are more suggestive of chronic avascular necrosis than acute joint infection

data.description: A 62-year-old fit and well Romanian man presented with a two-week history of worsening acute localized pain in the upper abdomen and vomiting. His surgical history included an open appendectomy as a child and laparoscopic cholecystectomy 20 years ago. On presentation, he had fever (39°C) and tachycardia (104 beats/min), with blood pressure of 125/73 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness, worse in the right upper quadrant, with localized guarding in the right upper quadrant. Blood tests showed a raised white cell count of 16 × 10⁹/L (reference range 4-10 × 10⁹/L) and a C reactive protein concentration of 277 mg/L (reference value <9 mg/L). A frontal projection erect chest radiograph was initially reported as showing pneumoperitoneum, but showed a normal bowel gas pattern under the left hemidiaphragm.
A bacterial abscess within or immediately adjacent to the liver that contains gas, often causing severe systemic inflammation and right upper quadrant peritonism.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper quadrant tenderness and guarding
Gas-containing collection seen adjacent to the liver on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No specific atypical symptoms are described

data.description: A localized infected collection beneath the diaphragm, commonly occurring after upper abdominal surgery and potentially containing gas, which can mimic free intraperitoneal air on chest radiography.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent air beneath the right hemidiaphragm on erect chest radiograph
Right subdiaphragmatic gas-containing collection on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No shoulder-tip pain is reported
No cough, hiccups, or pleuritic chest pain is reported

data.diagnosis: Delayed abscess caused by dropped gallstones after laparoscopic cholecystectomy
data.description: A late complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy in which spilled or retained gallstones act as a nidus for infection, causing a perihepatic, subhepatic, or subphrenic abscess years after surgery.
symptoms_not_in_common: A retained or dropped gallstone is not explicitly visible in the provided imaging description
No prior history of documented gallbladder perforation or stone spillage is provided

data.description: A full-thickness gastric or duodenal ulcer perforation causing free intraperitoneal air and acute peritonitis.
symptoms_in_common: Initial radiographic concern for air beneath the right hemidiaphragm
symptoms_not_in_common: The illness evolved over two weeks rather than presenting as sudden severe pain
CT demonstrates a localized gas-containing collection rather than simple free intraperitoneal air
There is no reported history of dyspepsia, peptic ulcer disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, or NSAID use
Guarding is localized predominantly to the right upper quadrant rather than generalized rigid peritonitis

data.description: A 1-year and 4-month-old girl was admitted for evaluation of psychomotor retardation and an operation for exotropia. She was born at term (gestational age: 40 weeks) by cesarean delivery after an uneventful pregnancy, and was the first child of healthy, unrelated parents. The family history was unremarkable. On admission, she presented with a characteristic high-pitched cry and microcephaly. She showed delayed motor functions and crawling, was able to sit unassisted but unable to stand, with developmental characteristics lagging behind for normal chronologic age. On neurologic examination, she had left leg hypotonia, with normal tendon reflexes and normal cranial nerve signs. When she was 6 months old, ventricular septal defect was detected by echocardiography. Chromosome analysis revealed 46,XX,del (5) (p15.2) one month after delivery.

A chromosomal deletion disorder caused by loss of the short arm of chromosome 5, classically associated with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, facial/ocular abnormalities, and occasional congenital heart defects.
symptoms_in_common: Global psychomotor and motor developmental delay
Delayed crawling and inability to stand independently at 16 months
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly unilateral left-leg hypotonia with otherwise normal tendon reflexes

data.description: A congenital viral infection that can cause microcephaly, developmental delay, hypotonia, brain abnormalities, hearing loss, and growth restriction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Characteristic high-pitched cat-like cry
Confirmed chromosome 5p15.2 deletion
Exotropia as a prominent presenting feature
Ventricular septal defect
Uneventful pregnancy without reported congenital infection findings

data.description: An X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder, usually caused by MECP2 variants, characterized by initially apparently normal early development followed by developmental regression, loss of hand skills, impaired speech, microcephaly, gait abnormalities, and stereotyped hand movements.
symptoms_not_in_common: Characteristic high-pitched cat-like cry
Confirmed chromosome 5p15.2 deletion
No reported developmental regression
No reported loss of purposeful hand use
No reported stereotypic hand movements
Ventricular septal defect is not typical

data.description: A neurogenetic disorder involving loss of maternal UBE3A expression, causing severe developmental delay, absent or minimal speech, ataxia, seizures, a happy/excitable demeanor, and acquired microcephaly in many affected children.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to stand independently at the expected age
symptoms_not_in_common: Characteristic high-pitched cat-like cry
Confirmed chromosome 5p15.2 deletion
No reported seizures
No reported ataxic gait or frequent laughter/excitable behavior
Ventricular septal defect is not a typical feature
Exotropia is not a defining feature

data.description: 7-year-old girl with no past medical history, presented with intermittent abdominal pain for 1 month, not relieved by anti-inflammatory treatment. Abdominal CT showed peritoneal effusion and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Serum AFP was elevated at 1,210 ng/mL. Ultrasonography showed multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal hypoechoic lymph nodes; ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina were unremarkable. Surgery revealed a 4 cm full-thickness jejunal mass; sampled lymph nodes showed reactive hyperplasia.

data.diagnosis: Primary extragonadal yolk sac tumor of the jejunum
data.description: A rare malignant germ-cell tumor occurring outside the gonads. Yolk sac tumors commonly produce very high serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and may arise in the gastrointestinal tract, including the jejunum.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly elevated serum AFP level (1,210 ng/mL)
FDG-avid abdominal lesion on PET imaging
Normal ovaries and other female genital organs, supporting an extragonadal origin
symptoms_not_in_common: Reactive rather than metastatic lymph-node histology
Retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy may occur but is not necessarily present in localized jejunal disease

data.diagnosis: Hepatoblastoma with metastatic or ectopic abdominal disease
data.description: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary liver malignancy in young children and often causes major AFP elevation. Advanced disease can spread within the abdomen, although a primary jejunal mass would be unusual.
symptoms_not_in_common: No hepatic mass described on CT or ultrasound
A discrete full-thickness jejunal mass is not typical of hepatoblastoma
Age 7 years is older than the usual age at presentation, which is typically under 5 years
Normal pelvic organs do not specifically support or exclude this diagnosis

data.diagnosis: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the small bowel
data.description: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is a pediatric soft-tissue sarcoma that can rarely involve the gastrointestinal tract and present as an intestinal wall mass with abdominal pain.
symptoms_in_common: Possible peritoneal fluid in advanced intra-abdominal disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked AFP elevation is not typical
Yolk-sac-tumor-like histology and AFP-associated immunophenotype would not be expected
No description of rhabdomyoblasts or skeletal-muscle differentiation

data.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including Burkitt lymphoma, can involve the ileum or jejunum in children and cause bowel-wall masses, abdominal pain, ascites, and abdominal lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple enlarged abdominal and retroperitoneal lymph nodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked serum AFP elevation is not typical
Sampled lymph nodes showed reactive hyperplasia rather than lymphoma
Histology described as epithelial/glandular tumor rather than lymphoid proliferation
No constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss were reported

data.description: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumor of the intestinal lining that can form an infiltrative bowel-wall mass. It is very rare in children but may occasionally show AFP production in unusual AFP-producing variants.
symptoms_in_common: Possible FDG uptake on PET imaging
Epithelial/gland-forming histologic appearance may overlap with adenocarcinoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 7 years is highly atypical for conventional small-intestinal adenocarcinoma
Marked AFP elevation is uncommon except in rare AFP-producing tumors
Retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy with reactive sampled nodes is nonspecific
The clinical pattern strongly favors a germ-cell tumor over conventional adenocarcinoma

diagnoses.name: Primary yolk sac tumor of intestine
diagnoses.title: Yolk sac tumour, unspecified site, female

data.description: 6-month-old boy with 2 days of intermittent abdominal pain waking him from sleep, with crying, leg flexion, and episodes of abdominal rigidity, followed by progressive hematochezia culminating in a large bloody stool with clot. History of infantile colic and gastroesophageal reflux treated with ranitidine; recently started pureed foods and was on low-lactose cow milk-based formula. On exam he had diffuse abdominal tenderness, worse on the right, later pallor, tachycardia, and hypotension.

data.diagnosis: Bleeding Meckel diverticulum with ectopic gastric mucosa
data.description: A congenital ileal diverticulum that may contain acid-secreting gastric mucosa, causing adjacent ileal ulceration and potentially severe lower gastrointestinal bleeding. The scintigraphic appearance is consistent with a Meckel scan showing an abdominal focus of uptake appearing with gastric uptake.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive hematochezia with a large bloody stool and clot
Pallor, tachycardia, and hypotension consistent with significant gastrointestinal hemorrhage
Scintigraphic abdominal tracer uptake compatible with ectopic gastric mucosa
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with leg flexion is less typical of uncomplicated bleeding Meckel diverticulum
Episodes of abdominal rigidity suggest possible obstruction, inflammation, or intussusception in addition to bleeding

data.diagnosis: Intussusception, potentially with a Meckel diverticulum as a lead point
data.description: Telescoping of one segment of bowel into another, usually ileocolic in infants. It causes episodic severe colicky pain and may progress to bowel ischemia and bloody stool. A Meckel diverticulum can serve as a pathologic lead point.
symptoms_in_common: Six-month age, within the typical age range
Intermittent severe abdominal pain waking the child from sleep
Crying with flexion of the legs during painful episodes
Pallor, tachycardia, and hypotension in severe bowel ischemia or hemorrhage
symptoms_not_in_common: A large-volume bloody stool with clot is more suggestive of a major gastrointestinal bleeding source such as Meckel diverticulum than classic currant-jelly stool
The nuclear medicine uptake pattern indicating ectopic gastric mucosa is not typical of uncomplicated idiopathic intussusception

data.diagnosis: Enteric duplication cyst containing ectopic gastric mucosa
data.description: A congenital duplication of the gastrointestinal tract that can contain gastric mucosa, resulting in ulceration, bleeding, abdominal pain, obstruction, or intussusception. It can occasionally demonstrate uptake on a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan.
symptoms_in_common: Hematochezia from ulceration caused by ectopic gastric mucosa
Possible severe gastrointestinal bleeding with pallor and hypotension
Abdominal scintigraphic uptake that could reflect ectopic gastric mucosa
symptoms_not_in_common: Enteric duplication cysts are much less common than Meckel diverticulum
The scan appearance and right lower abdominal location more strongly favor Meckel diverticulum
The abrupt episodic colicky pattern is more typical of intussusception or intermittent obstruction

data.description: A non-IgE-mediated inflammatory reaction to dietary proteins, commonly cow's milk or soy protein, causing blood-streaked stools in otherwise well young infants.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dietary changes with introduction of pureed foods
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe intermittent abdominal pain with leg flexion
Abdominal rigidity and marked right-sided tenderness
Large bloody stool with clot
Pallor, tachycardia, and hypotension from major blood loss
Scintigraphic focal abdominal uptake consistent with ectopic gastric mucosa

data.description: A 69-year-old female non-smoker presented with a 6-month history of progressive breathlessness. She had no relevant past medical history or drug history. Spirometry showed FEV1 32% predicted and a flow-volume loop suggesting severe small airway disease. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal.

Abnormal direct communications between pulmonary arteries and veins, producing enhancing rounded vascular lesions with feeding and draining vessels. Multiple PAVMs may be idiopathic or associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple rounded pulmonary vascular lesions on CT with appearances of feeding/draining vessels
Normal transthoracic echocardiogram does not exclude PAVMs
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe small-airway obstructive pattern on spirometry (FEV1 32% predicted) is not a usual direct consequence of PAVMs
No reported cyanosis, platypnea, orthodeoxia, hemoptysis, migraine, or neurologic embolic events

data.diagnosis: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations
data.description: An autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, commonly involving the lungs, nose, gastrointestinal tract, liver, and brain. Multiple PAVMs strongly raise this possibility.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple pulmonary arteriovenous-malformation-like lesions on CT
Breathlessness, potentially due to right-to-left shunting from PAVMs
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of recurrent epistaxis
No reported mucocutaneous telangiectasias
No known family history of HHT
Severe small-airway obstruction is not typical of HHT itself

data.description: A small-airway disorder involving inflammatory and fibrotic narrowing of bronchioles, causing fixed severe airflow obstruction and progressive exertional dyspnea. CT may show mosaic attenuation and air trapping, particularly on expiratory imaging.
symptoms_in_common: Flow-volume loop suggesting severe small-airway disease
Non-smoker status, making smoking-related COPD less likely
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple discrete enhancing vascular pulmonary nodules with feeding/draining vessels are not typical of bronchiolitis obliterans
No reported prior severe respiratory infection, inhalational exposure, autoimmune disease, transplantation, or medication trigger

data.diagnosis: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease due to non-smoking-related small-airway disease
data.description: Chronic obstructive airflow limitation can occur in non-smokers because of asthma, environmental or occupational exposures, prior infections, or other bronchiolar disorders. It causes dyspnea and reduced FEV1 but would not usually produce vascular nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Flow-volume loop consistent with obstructive small-airway disease
symptoms_not_in_common: She is a non-smoker with no reported exposure history
Multiple rounded vascular-appearing lesions on CT are not a typical manifestation of COPD
No reported chronic cough, sputum production, wheeze, or emphysema

data.description: 27-year-old man, previously healthy, presented with a few days of cough, hemoptysis, and low-grade fever. He denied night sweats and weight loss. History notable for intermittent left supraclavicular lymph node enlargement since age 15. On exam, he was thin (168 cm, 48 kg), with low-grade fever (37.6°C), mild hypoxemia (SpO2 94% on room air), crackles in the left upper lung field, and a 2 cm left supraclavicular lymph node that was nontender, firm, nonfixed, circumscribed, and rubbery. Labs showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated ESR and CRP, and elevated soluble IL-2 receptor. Blood and sputum cultures, autoimmune serologies, HIV, and tumor markers were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation without identified pathogens.

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary sarcoidosis associated with unicentric Castleman disease
data.description: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disorder characterized by noncaseating granulomas, often involving the lungs and lymph nodes. The supraclavicular node histology is compatible with hyaline-vascular-type unicentric Castleman disease, a benign lymphoproliferative disorder that can coexist with sarcoid-like granulomatous lung disease.
symptoms_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation on transbronchial lung biopsy without identified pathogens
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemoptysis is relatively uncommon in typical sarcoidosis
Marked unilateral upper-lobe cavitary or bronchiectatic-appearing disease is atypical for usual pulmonary sarcoidosis
Neutrophilic leukocytosis is not a classic sarcoidosis finding
Absence of bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is less typical for classic sarcoidosis

data.description: Tuberculosis is a mycobacterial infection that commonly causes chronic cough, fever, hemoptysis, upper-lobe infiltrates or cavitation, and granulomatous inflammation. It must be excluded carefully despite initially negative sputum studies.
symptoms_in_common: Crackles in the left upper lung field
symptoms_not_in_common: No night sweats
No weight loss
Blood and sputum cultures were negative
No pathogen was identified in the lung biopsy
Long-standing intermittent lymph-node enlargement since age 15 is less typical of untreated active tuberculosis

data.description: Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, such as Mycobacterium avium complex or M. kansasii infection, can produce upper-lobe cavitary disease, nodules, bronchiectasis, chronic cough, hemoptysis, and granulomatous lung inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Upper-lobe-predominant pulmonary disease with cavitary or bronchiectatic features
Granulomatous inflammation without an organism initially identified
symptoms_not_in_common: Previously healthy young age is less typical than in patients with structural lung disease or immunosuppression
Only a few days of respiratory symptoms is less typical of the usually indolent course
Negative sputum cultures
Long-standing intermittent supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is not typical
Neutrophilic leukocytosis is not a defining feature

data.description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated vasculitis that can cause cough, hemoptysis, pulmonary nodules or cavitary infiltrates, systemic inflammation, and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in the respiratory tract.
symptoms_not_in_common: Autoimmune serologies were negative
No renal manifestations were reported
No sinus, nasal, ear, eye, skin, or neurologic manifestations were reported
Biopsy did not report vasculitis or necrotizing granulomas
Long-standing isolated supraclavicular lymph-node enlargement is not typical

data.description: Necrotizing sarcoid granulomatosis is a rare sarcoid-spectrum disorder characterized by pulmonary granulomas, variable granulomatous vasculitis, nodular or cavitary lung lesions, fever, cough, and occasionally hemoptysis.
symptoms_in_common: Upper-lobe pulmonary lesions with cavitary appearance
Granulomatous inflammation without identified infectious organisms
symptoms_not_in_common: The biopsy description does not mention necrosis or granulomatous vasculitis
Persistent supraclavicular lymph-node enlargement is less typical
Neutrophilic leukocytosis is not characteristic
The chronic intermittent lymph-node history suggests a separate lymphoproliferative process

After 40 days of fingolimod treatment, he developed seizures and visual field defects. Neurological examination revealed lateral nystagmus to the left, homonymous hemianopia, distal tremor and spasm of the upper limbs.
