data.diagnosis: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC polyomavirus
data.description: A severe opportunistic demyelinating infection of the brain caused by reactivation of JC polyomavirus, especially in patients receiving natalizumab or other immunosuppressive therapies.
symptoms_in_common: Recent natalizumab exposure with high anti-JCPyV antibody index
Switch to fingolimod, which can cause lymphocyte sequestration and immunosuppression
Subacute onset of visual field defects
Underlying multiple sclerosis, a population at risk when treated with natalizumab
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly reported cognitive decline, aphasia, personality change, or progressive weakness
No fever or systemic infectious symptoms reported

data.description: An acute or subacute episode of new inflammatory demyelination in the central nervous system causing new neurologic deficits in a patient with multiple sclerosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Seizures are less typical of a routine multiple sclerosis relapse
Severe leukopenia is not a typical manifestation of an MS relapse
High anti-JCPyV antibody index and extensive natalizumab exposure strongly suggest an alternative opportunistic infection risk
Abrupt concern for opportunistic CNS infection after immunomodulatory treatment is less typical for uncomplicated relapse

data.description: An inflammatory worsening of JC-virus brain infection that may occur after stopping natalizumab, removing immunosuppression, or changing disease-modifying therapy, as immune cells regain access to the CNS.
symptoms_in_common: Prior natalizumab treatment followed by treatment transition
High risk for natalizumab-associated JCPyV infection
New seizures and focal neurologic deficits
Visual field loss and homonymous hemianopia
Potential temporal association with discontinuation of natalizumab and initiation of fingolimod
symptoms_not_in_common: Leukopenia may reduce the likelihood of robust immune reconstitution at presentation
No reported MRI contrast enhancement, edema, mass effect, or inflammatory CSF findings
No documented clinical worsening after immune recovery or plasma exchange

data.description: A lymphoma confined to the brain, spinal cord, leptomeninges, or eyes; it is more likely in immunosuppressed patients and may cause focal deficits and seizures.
symptoms_not_in_common: The strong natalizumab/JCPyV risk profile is more characteristic of PML
No reported brain mass lesion, contrast-enhancing lesion, edema, or raised intracranial pressure
No constitutional symptoms or ocular symptoms reported
The short interval after fingolimod initiation is not specifically characteristic of CNS lymphoma

data.description: A 39-year-old Korean male presented with intermittent and atypical chest discomfort symptoms. His medical history included burning pain originating in the extremities and radiating inwards to the limbs since childhood, which was previously dismissed as 'growing pains'. He also experienced ringing in the ears, had angiokeratomas on his trunk, and cornea verticillata. Physical examination revealed proteinuria (P/C ratio 0.501) without hematuria and normal renal function. His plasma αGal-A activity was markedly lower than controls at 4.1 nmoL/hr/mg protein (normal cutoff >35 nmoL/hr/mg protein). Genetic testing identified a hemizygous mutation in exon 4 of GLA, c.617T>C (p.Leu206 Pro).

data.diagnosis: Classic Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency)
data.description: A lysosomal storage disorder caused by pathogenic GLA variants resulting in deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity and accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular, neural, renal, cardiac, and other cells. This case is strongly supported by markedly reduced alpha-Gal-A activity, a hemizygous GLA mutation, and characteristic clinical findings.
symptoms_in_common: Burning extremity pain since childhood consistent with acroparesthesias
Cardiac hypertrophy/repolarization abnormalities on ECG and echocardiographic imaging
Intracellular lamellar lipid inclusions on electron microscopy consistent with zebra bodies
Markedly reduced plasma alpha-galactosidase A activity

data.description: Cardiac involvement of Fabry disease caused by glycosphingolipid accumulation in cardiomyocytes, producing concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, chest pain, arrhythmias, conduction abnormalities, and progressive myocardial fibrosis.
symptoms_in_common: ECG features compatible with left ventricular hypertrophy and repolarization abnormalities
Echocardiographic evidence of ventricular wall hypertrophy
Electron-microscopy evidence of lysosomal lipid accumulation in cardiac tissue
Underlying alpha-galactosidase A deficiency and GLA mutation
symptoms_not_in_common: Angiokeratomas
Cornea verticillata
Childhood burning extremity pain
Tinnitus
Proteinuria

data.description: An inherited myocardial disorder, usually caused by sarcomeric gene variants, characterized by otherwise unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy that may cause chest discomfort, dyspnea, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death risk.
symptoms_in_common: Left ventricular hypertrophy on cardiac testing
ECG repolarization abnormalities that can occur with ventricular hypertrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Burning neuropathic extremity pain beginning in childhood
Angiokeratomas
Cornea verticillata
Tinnitus
Proteinuria
Markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity
Hemizygous GLA mutation
Lysosomal zebra-body inclusions on electron microscopy

data.description: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.
A pre-existing traumatic liver hematoma can become secondarily infected, producing a pyogenic abscess with systemic inflammatory signs.
symptoms_in_common: Ultrasound appearance of a complex intrahepatic collection

data.description: A localized bacterial infection within the liver that forms a pus-containing collection; it may occur after trauma, biliary infection, bacteremia, or infection of a hematoma.
symptoms_in_common: Critical illness and recent trauma as risk factors for infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain or right-upper-quadrant tenderness was reported
No jaundice was reported

data.description: A biloma is a collection of leaked bile caused by disruption of intrahepatic bile ducts, often after liver trauma. Infection of the collection can cause fever and sepsis.
symptoms_not_in_common: The initial lesion was described as a hematoma rather than a confirmed bile collection
No jaundice or bile leak was reported

data.description: A severe subtype of bacterial liver abscess in which gas-producing organisms, such as Klebsiella species or anaerobic bacteria, create gas within an infected hepatic collection.
symptoms_in_common: Complex hepatic lesion with possible internal echogenic foci or acoustic artifact on ultrasound
Traumatic hepatic hematoma that may serve as a nidus for infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No diabetes mellitus was reported, which is a common risk factor
No septic shock or severe hemodynamic instability was reported

data.description: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

A rare neutrophilic skin reaction caused by exposure to iodide-containing substances, including iodinated radiographic contrast. It can produce pustules, vesicles, bullae, and vegetating plaques, often with sterile cultures and neutrophilic histology.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt onset several hours after iodinated contrast exposure
Involvement of trunk, arms, and legs
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria preceding the skin eruption

data.description: A severe acute drug eruption characterized by rapid development of numerous sterile, nonfollicular pustules on erythematous skin, usually accompanied by neutrophilia. Iodinated contrast material is a recognized trigger.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset after medication/iodinated contrast exposure
Pustules involving the trunk and extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Large coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae are less typical
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis is not typical
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is not a characteristic histologic finding
Hematuria preceding the eruption

data.description: A severe mucocutaneous drug reaction with extensive keratinocyte death, epidermal necrosis, blistering, and skin detachment. Although iodinated contrast can rarely trigger it, pustules are not a usual dominant feature.
symptoms_in_common: Acute onset after exposure to a potential drug trigger
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominant pustular eruption
Diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate is less characteristic
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is not typical
No mucosal involvement is described
No skin detachment, targetoid lesions, or prominent systemic prodrome is described
Hematuria preceding the eruption

data.diagnosis: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), bullous variant
data.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory dermatosis that typically causes abrupt painful erythematous plaques or nodules and may rarely become vesiculobullous or pustular. It may be triggered by medications or systemic disease.
symptoms_in_common: Pustular and bullous skin lesions can occur in atypical variants
Mild eosinophilia may occasionally be present
symptoms_not_in_common: Clear temporal relationship to iodinated contrast favors iododerma or AGEP instead
Generalized coalescing pustules and pus-filled bullae are not the usual presentation
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis is not typical
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is not typical
Fever and painful tender plaques are not described
Hematuria preceding the eruption

data.description: 54-year-old female with hypertension and hyperlipidemia presented to cardiology clinic for follow-up 20 months since her most recent office visit. She was being evaluated for follow-up of cardiac risk factors and medication management. The patient was in her usual state of health and asymptomatic without changes in her exercise tolerance, weight, or energy levels. She did not have any gross hematuria or flank pain.

45-year-old man with acute nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting սկս starting the day before admission, after dog bites to the hands and forearms 3 days earlier. He also reported recent head trauma from a rusty nail and dental extractions 1–2 weeks earlier. Past history included asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse with intake up to 18 beers daily, stopped 3 days before admission. On examination he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and delayed capillary refill. He had multiple lacerations and scratch marks with necrotic edges on the hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm lesion with a 5–7 cm purplish surrounding border.

data.diagnosis: Capnocytophaga canimorsus fulminant sepsis with purpura fulminans
data.description: A rapidly progressive gram-negative zoonotic bloodstream infection transmitted by dog bites or saliva exposure. Severe disease is especially associated with heavy alcohol use, immunocompromise, and asplenia, and may cause septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpuric skin necrosis, and limb ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dog bites to the hands and forearms
Delayed capillary refill and shock-like appearance
Widespread purpuric/ecchymotic skin lesions shown in the images
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent rusty-nail head trauma
Recent dental extractions
Chronic back pain
Asthma and mild COPD

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing fasciitis due to dog-bite wound infection
data.description: A life-threatening deep soft-tissue infection involving fascia and subcutaneous tissue, often caused by polymicrobial infection or organisms introduced through traumatic wounds. It can rapidly produce necrosis, systemic toxicity, septic shock, and skin discoloration.
symptoms_in_common: Expanding purplish border around a forearm lesion
Systemic toxicity with hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, and poor perfusion
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported severe pain out of proportion to examination
No reported crepitus or soft-tissue gas on radiography
Diffuse purpura involving distant sites such as the legs is less typical of a localized necrotizing infection
Recent dental extractions
Recent rusty-nail head trauma

data.description: Pasteurella multocida is a gram-negative bacterium commonly found in dog and cat oral flora. It can cause rapidly developing cellulitis after bites and, less commonly, invasive bacteremia and septic shock in people with alcohol-related liver disease or other comorbidities.
symptoms_in_common: Lacerations and skin wounds on the hands and forearms
Local skin discoloration around bite wounds
Heavy alcohol use, a risk factor for invasive infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Extensive necrotic and purpuric skin lesions are less typical than cellulitis
Hypothermic shock with delayed capillary refill is uncommon in ordinary localized Pasteurella cellulitis
Diffuse purpura of the trunk and legs is not typical
Recent rusty-nail head trauma
Recent dental extractions

data.diagnosis: Vibrio vulnificus septicemia with hemorrhagic bullous/purpuric skin lesions
data.description: A severe gram-negative infection acquired from seawater exposure or raw seafood, particularly in people with heavy alcohol use or chronic liver disease. It can cause fulminant sepsis with painful purpuric lesions, hemorrhagic bullae, tissue necrosis, and shock.
symptoms_in_common: Heavy alcohol use, a major risk factor
Rapid onset of severe systemic illness
Delayed capillary refill and shock-like physiology
Widespread bruised/purpuric appearance in the images
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported seawater, marine wound, shellfish, or raw-seafood exposure
Dog bites provide a more direct alternative infectious source
Lesions began in areas of dog bites rather than after marine exposure
Recent dental extractions
Recent rusty-nail head trauma

data.description: A syndrome caused by abrupt cessation or reduction of heavy alcohol intake. Symptoms can begin within hours to a few days and include anxiety, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tremor, hypertension, agitation, seizures, or delirium tremens.
symptoms_in_common: History of intake up to 18 beers daily
Stopped alcohol consumption 3 days before admission
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypothermia is not typical
Delayed capillary refill and shock-like physiology are not typical
Necrotic dog-bite wounds are not caused by alcohol withdrawal
Purplish skin borders and widespread purpura/ecchymoses are not typical
No reported tremor, hallucinations, seizures, marked hypertension, or delirium

data.description: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 6, developed general muscle weakness and gait disturbance with decreased muscle tone/strength and atrophic muscle mass. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Current presentation at age 27 with left hemiplegia and aphasia. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). Negative for ASO antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-dsDNA, lupus anticoagulants, and anti-cytoplasmic antibody. DNA sequencing showed m.3303C>T mutation in mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene.

data.diagnosis: MELAS syndrome (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes) due to MT-TL1 m.3303C>T mutation
data.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic mitochondrial DNA variants, commonly involving the tRNA leucine gene. It causes impaired oxidative phosphorylation, myopathy, elevated lactate, neurologic deficits, and recurrent stroke-like episodes at a young age.
symptoms_in_common: Young-onset neurologic event with aphasia, dysarthria, and hemiplegia
Pathogenic m.3303C>T mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA leucine 1 gene
symptoms_not_in_common: A focal large-vessel arterial occlusion on MR angiography is less typical than the nonvascular-territory lesions usually seen in MELAS
Intracardiac thrombus suggested by echocardiography is not a primary defining feature of MELAS

data.description: A neuromuscular disorder caused by impaired mitochondrial energy production in skeletal muscle, resulting in exercise intolerance, weakness, hypotonia, muscle wasting, and lactic acidosis.
symptoms_in_common: Muscle biopsy showing mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute aphasia and dysarthria
Left hemiplegia
Acute ischemic stroke
Syncope
Possible intracardiac thrombus

data.diagnosis: Cardioembolic acute ischemic stroke involving the right middle cerebral artery territory
data.description: An ischemic stroke caused by embolic occlusion of a cerebral artery, often originating from a cardiac thrombus. The diffusion-weighted MRI lesion and MR angiographic arterial obstruction are compatible with an acute large-vessel ischemic infarction.
symptoms_in_common: Brain diffusion-weighted MRI showing an acute ischemic lesion
MR angiography showing focal intracranial arterial occlusion or markedly reduced flow
Echocardiographic appearance suggestive of a left ventricular intracardiac thrombus
symptoms_not_in_common: Longstanding childhood-onset generalized muscle weakness
Hypotonia and progressive muscle atrophy
Mitochondrial myopathy on biopsy
Elevated lactate due to systemic mitochondrial dysfunction
MT-TL1 m.3303C>T mitochondrial DNA mutation

data.diagnosis: Left ventricular thrombus associated with mitochondrial cardiomyopathy
data.description: Mitochondrial disease can involve cardiac muscle and cause cardiomyopathy, impaired ventricular contraction, and formation of mural thrombi. A left ventricular thrombus can embolize to the cerebral circulation and produce ischemic stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Echocardiographic intracavitary mass compatible with left ventricular thrombus
Mitochondrial DNA mutation capable of causing multisystem disease including cardiac involvement
Acute left hemiplegia, aphasia, and dysarthria consistent with embolic stroke
symptoms_not_in_common: Childhood-onset skeletal muscle weakness is not explained by left ventricular thrombus alone
Muscle biopsy showing mitochondrial myopathy
Elevated lactate
Gait disturbance, hypotonia, and muscle atrophy

data.description: 29-year-old woman with a 7-week history of progressive generalized pruritus, nausea, bloating, and watery mustard-colored diarrhea starting after eating sushi. Symptoms persisted despite treatment with methylprednisolone, hydroxyzine, and diphenoxylate-atropine. Three weeks later, she developed jaundice, right upper quadrant discomfort, decreased appetite, and amber urine. Four weeks before presentation, labs showed elevated ALT 327 U/L, AST 104 U/L, total bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, and CA 19-9 73 U/mL. Past history: anxiety and depression; no medications or drug allergies. On examination, she was thin, jaundiced with scleral icterus, and had diffuse excoriations from scratching; vitals were stable.

A malignant adenocarcinoma arising from the extrahepatic bile ducts that causes progressive biliary obstruction, often with ductal dilation, jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and elevated CA 19-9. The imaging and pathology are consistent with an obstructing pancreatobiliary-type adenocarcinoma.
symptoms_not_in_common: Watery mustard-colored diarrhea beginning after sushi consumption
Bloating as the initial dominant symptom
Young age of 29 years

data.diagnosis: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head
data.description: A pancreatic adenocarcinoma arising near the pancreatic head can obstruct the distal common bile duct, producing painless or minimally painful obstructive jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, anorexia, and elevated CA 19-9.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper quadrant or upper abdominal discomfort
Possible biliary duct obstruction on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 29 years, which is very atypical
Watery diarrhea starting after sushi consumption
No reported severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
No reported new-onset diabetes

data.description: Gallbladder cancer is usually an adenocarcinoma and may cause right upper quadrant discomfort, anorexia, jaundice, and biliary obstruction when it extends into or compresses the extrahepatic bile ducts.
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age of 29 years
Watery diarrhea after sushi
No known gallstones or chronic gallbladder disease
No fever or acute cholecystitis-like presentation

data.diagnosis: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with dominant biliary stricture
data.description: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disease of the bile ducts that can produce multifocal strictures, cholestatic liver injury, pruritus, jaundice, and recurrent biliary obstruction. It also substantially increases the risk of cholangiocarcinoma.
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated CA 19-9 is more concerning for associated malignancy than uncomplicated primary sclerosing cholangitis
Watery diarrhea after sushi is not typical
No known inflammatory bowel disease
Rapid progression over several weeks is less typical for uncomplicated chronic primary sclerosing cholangitis

data.description: A stone in the common bile duct can obstruct bile flow and cause jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, nausea, right upper quadrant pain, and elevation of bilirubin and liver enzymes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive symptoms over seven weeks without episodic biliary colic
Elevated CA 19-9, especially with malignant-appearing pathology/imaging
Watery persistent diarrhea after sushi
No reported gallstones, fever, or acute cholangitis
No severe colicky abdominal pain

data.description: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

data.diagnosis: Gallstone ileus with cholecystocolonic fistula and rectal gallstone impaction
data.description: A large gallstone enters the bowel through an abnormal fistula between the gallbladder and colon, travels distally, and may become impacted in the rectum, causing obstructed defecation (gallstone coleus).
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
Endoscopically identified gallstone in the rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: Known Crohn's disease is not required for this condition

data.description: Accumulation of hardened stool in the rectum that causes impaired evacuation, rectal pressure, and occasionally minor bleeding from mucosal irritation.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: A gallstone, rather than retained stool, was found in the rectum
Known Crohn's disease is not a typical direct cause

data.description: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect the colon, rectum, and anus, causing inflammation, ulcers, strictures, fistulas, bleeding, and altered bowel habits.
symptoms_not_in_common: Sensation of a discrete foreign body in the rectum is not typical
An endoscopically visualized gallstone in the rectum is not explained by Crohn's disease alone

data.diagnosis: Colorectal or rectal stricture due to Crohn's disease
data.description: Chronic intestinal inflammation from Crohn's disease can lead to fibrotic narrowing of the rectum or colon, producing obstructive defecatory symptoms and occasional bleeding.
symptoms_not_in_common: A foreign-body sensation due to a gallstone is not typical of a stricture alone
The rectal gallstone provides a more direct explanation for the acute symptoms

data.description: 15-year-old boy presented after injuring his left knee while carrying a tray of food at a fast food restaurant. He felt his knee 'wobble' and fell to the floor, unable to bear weight due to pain. Medical history included chronic fatigue syndrome. Had a Beighton score of 6 (indicating joint laxity) but no history of joint dislocations. On examination: laterally dislocated patella, moderate effusion, pain on palpation around medial patellofemoral ligament, range of movement reduced to extension-flexion of 0/10/60 degrees, ligamentous tests unremarkable. Two weeks later: complained of intermittent locking in left knee, had joint effusion and palpable loose body under patella.
Displacement of the patella out of the trochlear groove toward the lateral side of the knee, commonly occurring after twisting or minor trauma in adolescents with ligamentous laxity.
symptoms_in_common: Knee wobbling followed by a fall
Tenderness around the medial patellofemoral ligament
Generalized joint laxity with Beighton score of 6
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent locking two weeks after injury
Palpable loose body beneath the patella

data.diagnosis: Osteochondral fracture associated with patellar dislocation
data.description: A fracture involving articular cartilage and underlying bone, often occurring when the patella dislocates laterally and shears cartilage from the medial patella or lateral femoral condyle. The fragment may become a loose body in the joint.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable loose body under the patella
symptoms_not_in_common: Generalized joint laxity is not required for an osteochondral fracture
No clear direct blow to the knee was described

data.diagnosis: Intra-articular loose body of the knee
data.description: A free fragment of cartilage, bone, or osteochondral tissue within the knee joint, often resulting from an osteochondral injury after patellar dislocation. It can mechanically obstruct movement.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable loose body beneath the patella
Pain and restricted movement after knee trauma
Recent patellar dislocation that could produce an osteochondral fragment
symptoms_not_in_common: The initial visibly laterally dislocated patella is not caused by a loose body alone
Generalized hypermobility is not a typical consequence of a loose body

data.diagnosis: Patellofemoral instability related to generalized ligamentous laxity
data.description: A predisposition to recurrent or first-time patellar subluxation/dislocation due to laxity of stabilizing structures, sometimes accompanied by anatomical or connective-tissue-related risk factors.
symptoms_in_common: Beighton score of 6 indicating generalized joint hypermobility
Patella dislocated laterally after relatively low-energy activity
Sensation that the knee wobbled or gave way
Knee effusion and pain following patellar instability event
symptoms_not_in_common: Palpable intra-articular loose body is not explained by instability alone
Mechanical locking suggests an associated osteochondral fragment rather than uncomplicated instability

data.description: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring loss of axillary and pubic hair, and widespread follicular keratotic or spiny papules, often with intense itching.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic follicular papular spiny eruptions on the trunk and limbs
Scalp alopecia developing after the follicular eruption
Poor response to topical corticosteroids and oral antihistamines
Clinical and histologic appearance consistent with follicular lichenoid inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Family history of psoriasis in a sister is not a typical feature
Otherwise good general health is nonspecific

data.description: A lymphocyte-mediated inflammatory hair disorder that destroys hair follicles and produces scarring alopecia; follicular keratotic papules and perifollicular inflammation may occur, particularly in its Graham-Little variant.
symptoms_in_common: Follicular inflammatory findings on the scalp
symptoms_not_in_common: Extensive longstanding papular eruptions on the trunk and limbs are less typical in classic lichen planopilaris
Prominent pubic and axillary alopecia is more characteristic of the Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur variant
Family history of psoriasis is not typical

data.description: An uncommon follicular keratosis presenting with groups of rough, spiny keratotic papules that can produce a sandpaper-like texture, usually on the trunk and extremities.
symptoms_not_in_common: Scalp alopecia is not typical
Pubic alopecia is not typical
Axillary hair loss is not typical
Severe persistent pruritus is less typical
Follicular lichenoid inflammation and scarring alopecia would favor lichen planopilaris-spectrum disease rather than lichen spinulosus

data.description: 35-year-old woman with severe hypertension, edema, and renal failure. She had preeclampsia 12 months earlier during pregnancy, requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks, followed by persistent poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria >1 g/day. Six months before admission, she developed fatigue, headaches, worsening hypertension, and facial/pedal edema. She denied fever, neurologic symptoms, or preceding diarrheal illness. On exam she was pale with blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, proteinuria 4.9 g/24 h, hematuria, elevated reticulocytes and LDH, hyperbilirubinemia, low haptoglobin, schistocytes on smear, and a negative Coombs test. Liver enzymes, immunologic tests, viral screening, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal.

A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by uncontrolled alternative-complement activation, often triggered by pregnancy or the postpartum period. It causes microvascular thrombosis, severe kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, and sometimes cutaneous thrombotic lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, low haptoglobin, and reticulocytosis
Skin ulcerative/necrotic lesions consistent with thrombotic vasculopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: No major symptoms are strongly atypical; absence of neurologic symptoms is compatible with aHUS

data.description: A life-threatening thrombotic microangiopathy usually due to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with variable neurologic, renal, and systemic manifestations. Pregnancy can precipitate episodes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe progressive renal failure is more characteristic of aHUS than classic TTP
Marked proteinuria of 4.9 g/day is not typical of classic TTP
No neurologic deficits, confusion, seizures, or focal neurologic findings
No fever

data.description: Severe uncontrolled hypertension can damage small vessels, producing endothelial injury, ischemic renal disease, thrombocytopenia, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. It may overlap clinically with complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Cutaneous ischemic or ulcerative lesions may occur with severe small-vessel injury
symptoms_not_in_common: The postpartum onset after preeclampsia strongly suggests an underlying pregnancy-triggered thrombotic microangiopathy rather than hypertension alone
Severe thrombocytopenia may be more prominent than expected from hypertension alone
Persistent thrombotic microangiopathy despite the pregnancy ending is less typical for isolated preeclampsia-related hypertension

data.diagnosis: Pregnancy-associated hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets syndrome (HELLP syndrome) or persistent preeclampsia-related thrombotic microangiopathy
data.description: HELLP syndrome and severe preeclampsia are pregnancy-related endothelial disorders that can cause hypertension, proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, and kidney injury. They generally improve after delivery; persistence or worsening postpartum raises concern for aHUS.
symptoms_in_common: History of severe preeclampsia requiring premature Caesarean delivery
Hemolytic anemia with elevated LDH, bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and schistocytes
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal liver enzymes argue against HELLP syndrome
Progressive renal failure and hemolysis persisting for many months after delivery are not typical of resolved preeclampsia or HELLP syndrome
Cutaneous ulcerative thrombotic lesions are not a usual feature
Marked nephrotic-range proteinuria months postpartum is atypical

data.description: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune prothrombotic disorder that can cause pregnancy complications, renal vascular injury, hypertension, thrombocytopenia, and skin necrosis or ulcers. Catastrophic forms can produce multiorgan microvascular thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: Severe pregnancy complication with early delivery
Skin ulcerative or necrotic lesions that could reflect thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Antiphospholipid antibody testing was negative
No documented arterial or venous thrombosis
No recurrent pregnancy losses are reported
The pronounced Coombs-negative hemolysis with schistocytes is more suggestive of a primary thrombotic microangiopathy such as aHUS or TTP

data.description: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

A mesenchymal tumor arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells, commonly driven by activating KIT mutations. Ileal GISTs can present with occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding and anemia. The exon 11 KIT deletion strongly supports this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Severe anemia with hemoglobin of 6 g/dL
Syncope likely secondary to acute or severe blood-loss anemia
Contrast-enhancing mass arising from the ileal wall
Histologic appearance of a spindle-cell/epithelioid mesenchymal neoplasm
Immunohistochemical staining pattern consistent with KIT-positive tumor
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative colonoscopy, although this is expected when the bleeding source is in the ileum rather than the colon

data.description: A smooth-muscle tumor of the gastrointestinal tract. Benign leiomyomas are uncommon in the small bowel, while leiomyosarcomas are malignant smooth-muscle neoplasms that may form an enhancing bowel-wall mass and cause bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Possible absence of metastatic disease in a localized lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 deletion mutation, which strongly favors GIST rather than a smooth-muscle tumor
Immunohistochemical KIT-positive pattern, which is not typical of leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma
Relatively small 3.5 cm localized tumor without described smooth-muscle differentiation

data.description: A rare benign or low-grade peripheral nerve sheath tumor arising in the gastrointestinal wall. It may present as a submucosal small-bowel mass and can occasionally cause bleeding, but is much less common in the ileum than GIST.
symptoms_in_common: Mass arising from the ileal wall
Anemia from chronic or acute bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 activating deletion, which is characteristic of GIST and not typical of schwannoma
KIT-positive immunohistochemical staining pattern
Severe overt lower gastrointestinal bleeding is less typical for schwannoma
Syncope from profound blood-loss anemia is less typical

data.diagnosis: Small intestinal neuroendocrine tumor (ileal carcinoid tumor)
data.description: A neuroendocrine neoplasm commonly arising in the distal ileum. These tumors can cause abdominal pain, obstruction, mesenteric fibrosis, or metastatic disease; bleeding and anemia may occur but are less characteristic.
symptoms_in_common: May be localized without metastases when detected early
symptoms_not_in_common: KIT exon 11 deletion mutation, which is not typical of neuroendocrine tumors
Histologic mesenchymal/spindle-cell appearance rather than neuroendocrine nesting or trabecular architecture
KIT-positive immunohistochemical staining pattern rather than synaptophysin and chromogranin positivity
Severe bleeding with hemoglobin of 6 g/dL is less typical
No carcinoid syndrome symptoms such as flushing, diarrhea, or bronchospasm

diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

data.description: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

A rare malignant pancreatic epithelial tumor with acinar differentiation and characteristic squamoid corpuscles. Although predominantly a childhood tumor, it can rarely occur in older adults and often presents as a large, well-circumscribed pancreatic mass.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion consistent with pancreatic exocrine dysfunction
Older age is unusual but documented in rare adult cases
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal laboratory findings aside from elevated fasting glucose
Absence of abdominal pain or tenderness
Diabetes and hypertension are comorbidities rather than typical defining features

data.description: A rare malignant exocrine pancreatic tumor composed of cells showing acinar enzyme-producing differentiation. It commonly occurs in older adults and may form a large, relatively circumscribed mass.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion due to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
Painless or minimally symptomatic large pancreatic tumor
Imaging appearance of a large heterogeneous pancreatic mass
symptoms_not_in_common: No elevated serum lipase or lipase-hypersecretion syndrome
No panniculitis, polyarthritis, or eosinophilia
Normal laboratory findings other than hyperglycemia

data.description: A neoplasm arising from pancreatic endocrine cells. Nonfunctioning tumors may become large before detection and can present with mass effect, abdominal fullness, or digestive symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Diabetes or hyperglycemia can occur with pancreatic endocrine dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Maldigestion is less characteristic than in exocrine pancreatic tumors
No hormone-excess syndrome such as hypoglycemia, diarrhea, flushing, or peptic ulcer disease
No reported abnormal endocrine laboratory markers

data.description: The most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from pancreatic ductal epithelium. It typically causes obstructive symptoms, pain, weight loss, and jaundice, but may occasionally present as a pancreatic mass with digestive impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Maldigestion that may reflect pancreatic insufficiency
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal or back pain
No jaundice
No weight loss reported
No abnormal liver tests or other laboratory abnormalities
A large, well-demarcated mass is less typical than an infiltrative pancreatic lesion

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

diagnoses.name: Malignant gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Malignant GIST - [gastrointestinal stromal tumour] of large intestine

data.description: A 58-year-old overweight African American male presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash that worsened during summers, and blisters sometimes developed. Emollients were unhelpful. The patient was otherwise healthy, performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer, and had no significant sun exposure. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion. Further examination showed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.

An autosomal-dominant acantholytic skin disorder caused by impaired keratinocyte adhesion. It produces recurrent painful, pruritic, erosive and crusted plaques in flexural areas, often exacerbated by heat, sweating, and friction.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic recurrent rash in the axillae
Maceration, erosions, crusting, and malodor in an intertriginous site
Family history of a similar axillary rash in a sister
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple acrochordons are not a primary feature of Hailey-Hailey disease
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is not part of Hailey-Hailey disease
Hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation may occur secondarily but are not defining findings

data.description: An inherited disorder of keratinization characterized by greasy, crusted keratotic papules in seborrheic and flexural areas, frequently aggravated by heat and sweating. Histology typically shows acantholysis with dyskeratosis.
symptoms_in_common: Possible worsening with heat and sweating during summer
Occasional erosions and painful irritated skin
Acantholytic changes may be seen on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions limited predominantly to the axillae rather than widespread seborrheic areas
No characteristic nail abnormalities
No oral mucosal papules or cobblestoning
No typical widespread greasy keratotic papules
Family member has a similar isolated axillary eruption rather than classic generalized disease

data.description: A rare flexural variant of pemphigus vulgaris in which flaccid blisters evolve into erosive, vegetating, crusted plaques, often involving the axillae and groin.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erosive and crusted axillary plaques
Maceration and malodor in an intertriginous area
Vegetative or thickened appearance of lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Five-year familial pattern is not typical
Summer/friction-related flares are more characteristic of Hailey-Hailey disease
No oral or other mucosal involvement
Otherwise healthy status without evidence of autoimmune blistering disease
Histology described as acantholysis without the expected prominent eosinophilic inflammatory pattern

data.diagnosis: Intertrigo with secondary bacterial or fungal infection
data.description: Inflammation of opposing skin folds caused by moisture, friction, and heat, often complicated by Candida or bacterial overgrowth, producing maceration, odor, erosions, and crusting.
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent blistering is not typical of uncomplicated intertrigo
A similar rash in a sibling suggests an inherited disorder rather than simple intertrigo
Extensive acantholysis on histology is not expected
Marked irregular thickening with mixed hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation is not typical as the primary process
Failure of simple emollients and long-term recurrent course suggest an alternative underlying dermatosis

data.description: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

A rare aggressive cartilage-producing malignant bone tumor that often affects adolescents and young adults and may arise in the pelvis. Imaging commonly shows a destructive osseous mass with a large soft-tissue component and areas of chondroid mineralization/calcification.
symptoms_in_common: Destructive expansile lesion centered in the left iliac bone
Internal calcified or mineralized matrix on CT compatible with chondroid calcification
Increased uptake on nuclear medicine/PET imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No preceding trauma
Only short reported symptom duration of 1 month

data.description: A malignant cartilage-forming bone tumor that commonly occurs in the pelvis and can produce lobulated soft-tissue masses with rings-and-arcs, stippled, or peripheral calcification. It is more common in older adults but can occasionally occur in younger patients.
symptoms_in_common: Lobulated destructive bone lesion with soft-tissue extension
Calcified chondroid-appearing matrix within the mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 years is younger than typical for conventional chondrosarcoma
Rapidly noticed progression over only 1 month is less typical than a longer indolent course
No systemic symptoms, although these are usually absent

data.description: An aggressive small round cell malignancy of bone occurring mainly in children, adolescents, and young adults. Pelvic Ewing sarcoma may present as a painful enlarging mass with destructive bone changes and a large soft-tissue component.
symptoms_in_common: Age in the typical young-adult range
Increased metabolic activity on PET/nuclear imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent internal tumor calcification is uncommon for Ewing sarcoma
No fever or constitutional symptoms
No reported elevated inflammatory symptoms or signs

data.description: A malignant bone-forming tumor that can occur in young people and may arise in the iliac bone. Pelvic lesions often present late as large painful masses and may contain mineralized osteoid matrix.
symptoms_in_common: Destructive lesion involving the left ilium
symptoms_not_in_common: Pelvic osteosarcoma is less common than metaphyseal long-bone osteosarcoma
The mineralization pattern appears more compatible with cartilage-type calcification than dense cloud-like osteoid matrix
No reported periosteal reaction typical of some osteosarcomas

data.diagnosis: Giant cell tumor of bone with secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change
data.description: A locally aggressive benign bone tumor usually arising after skeletal maturity, often in women aged 20 to 40 years. It can affect the pelvis and cause an expansile lytic lesion with pain and a palpable mass; secondary aneurysmal bone cyst change can enlarge the lesion rapidly.
symptoms_in_common: Expansile destructive lesion involving pelvic bone
Possible relatively rapid increase in mass size
symptoms_not_in_common: Matrix calcification is not typical of a giant cell tumor
A large mineralized soft-tissue mass is less typical
Marked chondroid-appearing calcification favors a cartilage-producing malignancy instead

data.description: 36-year-old female with no past medical history who developed progressive lower-limb and paraspinal muscle spasms over 3 months, worsening over 6 months to wheelchair dependence. She became severely disabled, requiring regular IVIG (90 g every 12 days), diazepam 30 mg/day, and morphine up to 60 mg/day for pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus. The spasms were severe enough to compromise breathing, requiring intermittent oxygen.

A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder causing progressive axial and limb rigidity with painful stimulus-sensitive muscle spasms. Electromyography may show continuous motor-unit activity, and symptoms often improve with benzodiazepines and IVIG.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive paraspinal and lower-limb muscle stiffness and spasms
Progression to major disability and wheelchair dependence
Electrophysiologic findings compatible with continuous involuntary muscle activity and exaggerated reflex responses
Treatment requirement for diazepam and IVIG

data.diagnosis: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
data.description: A severe autoimmune stiff-person-spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, characterized by rigidity, painful spasms, exaggerated startle, myoclonus, brainstem involvement, autonomic dysfunction, and possible respiratory compromise.
symptoms_in_common: Severe progressive rigidity and lower-limb/paraspinal spasms
Possible exaggerated reflex/startle physiology on electrophysiologic testing
Potential responsiveness to IVIG and benzodiazepines
symptoms_not_in_common: No encephalopathy, confusion, or altered mental status reported
No myoclonus specifically reported
No brainstem symptoms such as eye-movement abnormalities, dysphagia, or dysarthria reported
No autonomic instability reported

data.description: A group of inherited disorders causing slowly progressive upper-motor-neuron dysfunction, predominantly affecting the legs, with spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and impaired gait.
symptoms_in_common: Wheelchair dependence due to progressive spasticity
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked painful paraspinal muscle spasms are less typical
Severe episodic spasms causing respiratory compromise are unusual
Need for high-dose diazepam, morphine, and frequent IVIG is not typical
Electrophysiologic continuous involuntary muscle activity is not typical
No family history or longstanding childhood/early-adult gait disorder reported

data.description: An immune-mediated central nervous system demyelinating disease that can cause upper-motor-neuron weakness, leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, sensory symptoms, visual symptoms, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent painful axial and paraspinal spasms are less characteristic as the dominant presentation
Continuous muscle activity/exaggerated reflex physiology is more suggestive of stiff-person-spectrum disease
No visual, sensory, bladder, bowel, or focal neurologic episodes reported
Respiratory compromise from spasms is unusual in typical multiple sclerosis
Regular IVIG treatment is not standard therapy for typical multiple sclerosis

data.description: A toxin-mediated neurologic illness caused by Clostridium tetani, producing generalized rigidity, painful stimulus-triggered spasms, hyperreflexia, autonomic instability, and possible respiratory failure.
symptoms_not_in_common: The course over months with progression over 6 months is not typical; tetanus is usually acute or subacute
No wound, infection, trismus, dysphagia, or risus sardonicus reported
Long-term dependence on IVIG and diazepam for a chronic disorder is not typical
Wheelchair dependence developing gradually over months is less typical

data.description: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

A chronic large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often occurring in younger women and causing stenosis or occlusion of carotid and subclavian arteries. Reduced scalp and cerebral perfusion can cause scalp ischemia, ulceration, syncope, and stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse consistent with cerebral hypoperfusion
History of ischemic right hemispheric stroke at a relatively young age
Prior carotid endarterectomy suggesting severe carotid arterial disease
Angiographic appearance of major cervical/aortic-arch branch arterial narrowing or occlusion
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported limb claudication
No reported pulse discrepancy or blood-pressure difference between arms
No reported constitutional symptoms such as fever, fatigue, weight loss, or night sweats

data.description: A granulomatous vasculitis involving medium and large arteries, especially cranial branches of the carotid artery. It can produce scalp tenderness, scalp necrosis, visual loss, and ischemic stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Scalp ulceration/necrosis compatible with ischemia of scalp arteries
Collapse could occur with severe vascular ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 46 years is substantially younger than the usual age of onset, which is generally over 50 years
No reported headache
No reported scalp tenderness before ulcer formation
No reported jaw claudication
No reported visual symptoms
Large-vessel carotid/subclavian occlusive disease at a young age is more suggestive of Takayasu arteritis than classic giant cell arteritis

data.diagnosis: Severe premature atherosclerotic carotid and arch-vessel disease
data.description: Atherosclerosis can cause progressive narrowing of carotid and subclavian arteries, resulting in transient cerebral hypoperfusion, ischemic stroke, and rarely tissue ischemia when collateral blood supply is poor.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse potentially due to cerebrovascular insufficiency
Imaging evidence of major arterial stenosis or occlusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe carotid disease requiring endarterectomy at approximately age 35 is unusually early for uncomplicated atherosclerosis
Scalp necrosis is uncommon in routine atherosclerotic carotid disease
Multifocal aortic-arch branch involvement may suggest inflammatory vasculitis rather than isolated atherosclerosis

data.description: An autoimmune thrombophilia that causes recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis, including ischemic stroke in younger adults. Arterial thrombosis could contribute to carotid occlusion and scalp ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Ischemic stroke at a young age
Scalp ischemia/necrosis could occur from arterial thrombosis
Frequent collapse may reflect recurrent cerebral ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported history of venous thrombosis
No reported recurrent miscarriage or pregnancy morbidity
No reported livedo reticularis, thrombocytopenia, or other autoimmune features
The vascular imaging pattern of large-vessel stenosis may be more typical of vasculitis than thrombosis alone

data.diagnosis: Scalp trauma with secondary skin necrosis related to recurrent falls
data.description: Repeated collapse can cause scalp injury; in a patient receiving dual antiplatelet therapy, trauma may lead to hematoma, skin breakdown, and delayed wound healing. This would not, however, explain the underlying major-vessel imaging abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse creating risk of repeated head/scalp trauma
Visible scalp wounds with crusting or necrotic appearance
Use of aspirin and clopidogrel, which can increase bruising and bleeding after trauma
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior young-onset ischemic stroke is not explained by scalp trauma
Carotid/arch-vessel stenosis or occlusion on imaging is not explained by trauma
The ischemic-looking scalp lesion may be disproportionate to uncomplicated minor trauma

data.description: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and adalimumab. Over 4 months, she developed pain and stiffness in the MCP and interphalangeal joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission, she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli. Labs then showed anemia, leukopenia with neutropenia, elevated rheumatoid factor, hypergammaglobulinemia, high-titer ANA, low C4, positive anti-dsDNA, and cryoglobulins; HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests were negative. On admission, she had fever and pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Blood film, cultures, chest/abdomen/pelvis CT, CMV PCR, and tuberculin skin test were negative. She had traveled to Athens 7 months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept dogs.

A systemic infection caused by Leishmania parasites, transmitted by sandflies. It commonly affects immunosuppressed individuals and can cause prolonged fever, pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and bone-marrow involvement. The image is consistent with Leishman-Donovan bodies (intracellular amastigotes) in macrophages.
symptoms_in_common: Positive rheumatoid factor and autoantibodies that may occur during chronic Leishmania infection
Travel to Greece, an area where Mediterranean visceral leishmaniasis occurs
Exposure to dogs, an important reservoir for Leishmania infantum
Bone-marrow image showing intracellular organisms compatible with Leishmania amastigotes
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of hepatosplenomegaly
Absence of lymphadenopathy
Prominent inflammatory polyarthritis
Livedo reticularis
Purpuric lesions around the malleoli

data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that may cause inflammatory arthritis, fever, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, positive ANA and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, and immune-complex vasculitic skin lesions.
symptoms_not_in_common: Travel-associated exposure to dogs in a visceral leishmaniasis-endemic region
Bone-marrow organisms compatible with Leishmania amastigotes
Marked hypergammaglobulinemia in the setting of chronic parasitic infection
Severe neutropenia with a demonstrable infectious cause

data.description: A complication of long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, usually with splenomegaly, and increased susceptibility to infections.
symptoms_in_common: Fever that could occur with infection in the setting of neutropenia
symptoms_not_in_common: No splenomegaly
Pancytopenia rather than predominantly neutropenia
High-titer ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies
Low C4 and cryoglobulins
Livedo reticularis and purpura
Bone-marrow organisms compatible with Leishmania amastigotes
Travel and dog exposure supporting visceral leishmaniasis

data.description: Visceral leishmaniasis occurring or reactivating in a patient receiving tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibition, such as adalimumab. TNF-alpha blockade impairs macrophage-mediated control of intracellular Leishmania parasites.
symptoms_in_common: Positive autoantibodies and cryoglobulins that can mimic autoimmune disease
Exposure in Greece with possible canine reservoir contact
Bone-marrow findings compatible with Leishmania infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No hepatosplenomegaly despite systemic disease
No lymphadenopathy
Prominent livedo reticularis and malleolar purpura
Pre-existing rheumatoid arthritis may independently explain some joint symptoms

data.description: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

A chronic granulomatous skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, typically causing slowly enlarging yellow-brown to reddish plaques on the shins with central atrophy, indentation, telangiectasia, and possible ulceration. Histology commonly shows layers of degenerated collagen (necrobiosis) with palisading granulomatous inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with elevated blood glucose
Initially reddish-brown macule that slowly enlarged over years
Hyperpigmented yellow-brown and erythematous plaque appearance
New tenderness, which can occur with inflammation or ulceration
Clinical appearance and biopsy pattern consistent with necrobiotic collagen and granulomatous inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age is less typical, as necrobiosis lipoidica more often affects adults aged 30 to 60 years

data.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis characterized by dermal palisading granulomas surrounding degenerated collagen. It commonly presents as firm annular papules or plaques, often on the hands, feet, elbows, or ankles; generalized forms may be associated with diabetes.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive lesion over several years
Possible histologic palisading granulomatous inflammation with collagen degeneration
May occur in patients with diabetes
symptoms_not_in_common: Shin location is less characteristic than acral sites
Central yellow-brown atrophy and indentation are not typical
Tenderness is uncommon because granuloma annulare is usually asymptomatic
The lesion does not have a classic annular ring of papules

data.description: A common diabetes-associated microvascular skin finding consisting of small, round or oval, brown, slightly atrophic macules on the shins, often called diabetic shin spots.
symptoms_not_in_common: Diabetic dermopathy lesions are usually small and do not progressively enlarge into a large plaque
Tenderness is not typical
Marked erythema, yellow-brown coloration, and scale are not typical
Histology would not typically show extensive necrobiosis with palisading granulomatous inflammation

data.description: A multisystem granulomatous disorder that can involve the skin, producing red-brown papules, plaques, nodules, or scars. Skin biopsy typically demonstrates noncaseating granulomas.
symptoms_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation can be seen on skin biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Diabetes-associated pretibial atrophic plaque is more characteristic of necrobiosis lipoidica than sarcoidosis
Central yellow-brown atrophy and indentation are less typical
Histology of sarcoidosis usually shows compact noncaseating granulomas rather than prominent necrobiotic collagen
No pulmonary, ocular, constitutional, or other systemic sarcoidosis features are reported

data.description: 14-year-old boy with acute fear of choking while swallowing սկսing 2 days before admission after choking on chicken. He subsequently avoided eating, vomited after trying ice cream, and markedly decreased oral intake to about 710 mL of water per day; on presentation he took only small sips and slept most of the day. Mother reported inspiratory stridor during sleep for several weeks. History includes infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, keratosis pilaris, eczema, incomplete immunizations after age 2.5 years, and childhood sensory-integration training. On exam he was alert but anxious, with persistent involuntary burping, drooling, dry oral mucosa, hypertonic leg muscles, and mildly positive left Chvostek sign; neurologic examination was otherwise normal. Initial labs showed severe hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia, elevated parathyroid hormone, and mildly elevated TSH with normal free T4.

data.diagnosis: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B due to paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q (GNAS methylation defect)
data.description: A disorder of parathyroid hormone resistance caused by abnormal imprinting/methylation at the GNAS locus, often due to paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 20q. It produces hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone despite adequate hormone production. The methylation pattern shown, with increased NESP methylation and reduced methylation at other GNAS differentially methylated regions, is consistent with this mechanism.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated parathyroid hormone indicating parathyroid hormone resistance
Mildly elevated TSH with normal free T4, consistent with possible TSH resistance
Inspiratory stridor, which can occur with hypocalcemia-related laryngospasm
Anxiety and fear during swallowing, potentially worsened by neuromuscular irritability from hypocalcemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset of choking fear immediately after choking on chicken
Avoidance of eating after the choking episode
Vomiting after ice cream
Persistent involuntary burping
Drooling
History of milk-protein allergy
Eczema and keratosis pilaris

data.description: A GNAS-related disorder causing resistance to parathyroid hormone and sometimes other hormones, including TSH. It is usually caused by an inactivating maternal GNAS mutation and is often associated with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy, including short stature, obesity, brachydactyly, and subcutaneous ossifications.
symptoms_in_common: Mildly elevated TSH with normal free T4
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal GNAS methylation pattern favoring pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B rather than type 1A
No reported short stature
No reported obesity
No reported brachydactyly
No reported subcutaneous ossifications
Acute choking-related food avoidance
Persistent burping and drooling

data.description: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability caused by low serum calcium. It may cause muscle stiffness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek sign, stridor, and laryngospasm. In this case, it is likely a manifestation of parathyroid hormone resistance rather than an isolated disease.
symptoms_in_common: Drooling and difficulty swallowing may occur if laryngeal or pharyngeal muscle irritability is present
Anxiety, which can accompany acute hypocalcemic symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperphosphatemia and elevated parathyroid hormone suggest an underlying parathyroid hormone resistance disorder rather than isolated tetany
Mild TSH elevation
Choking episode as the apparent trigger for food avoidance
Vomiting after ice cream
Persistent involuntary burping
History of atopy and sensory-integration training

data.diagnosis: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), choking-related subtype
data.description: An eating or feeding disorder characterized by restricted intake due to fear of aversive consequences of eating, such as choking or vomiting. It can lead to dehydration, weight loss, nutritional compromise, and marked anxiety around swallowing.
symptoms_in_common: Acute fear of choking after choking on chicken
Vomiting after attempting to eat ice cream
Sleeping most of the day, potentially related to poor intake and dehydration
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe hypocalcemia
Hyperphosphatemia
Elevated parathyroid hormone
Mildly elevated TSH
Positive Chvostek sign
Leg muscle hypertonia
Weeks of inspiratory stridor
Abnormal GNAS methylation testing

data.diagnosis: Vitamin D deficiency or nutritional hypocalcemia
data.description: Insufficient vitamin D intake, absorption, or sun exposure can reduce calcium absorption and produce hypocalcemia with secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone. It is a common cause of hypocalcemia in adolescents but usually produces low or normal phosphate because elevated parathyroid hormone increases renal phosphate excretion.
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperphosphatemia, which is atypical for straightforward vitamin D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Mildly elevated TSH with normal free T4 suggesting hormone resistance
Abnormal GNAS methylation pattern
Inspiratory stridor for several weeks
Acute choking-related fear of swallowing
Persistent burping and drooling

data.description: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months before admission, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; biopsy showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months before admission, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which showed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 nodes; BRAF V600E mutation was identified. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib, after which fever and nausea began within 1 day and improved when the drugs were temporarily stopped. Fever recurred 2 weeks before admission. On presentation, she had temperature 40.2°C, tachycardia, diaphoresis, ill appearance, and mild right upper-quadrant tenderness, without rash.

A common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition, characterized by recurrent high fever, chills or diaphoresis, fatigue, nausea, and occasionally hypotension or organ dysfunction. Symptoms often improve after treatment interruption and recur with rechallenge.
symptoms_in_common: Fever beginning within 1 day of starting dabrafenib and trametinib
Recurrent high fever to 40.2 degrees C
Improvement when dabrafenib and trametinib were temporarily stopped
symptoms_not_in_common: Right upper-quadrant tenderness
Hepatic, splenic, and pulmonary granulomatous-appearing imaging abnormalities

data.description: A drug-induced systemic inflammatory reaction that can resemble sarcoidosis, producing noncaseating granulomas and pulmonary, hepatic, splenic, lymph-node, or skin lesions during BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper-quadrant tenderness compatible with hepatic involvement
Multiple hepatic and splenic lesions on imaging
Temporal relationship to initiation of dabrafenib and trametinib
symptoms_not_in_common: Very abrupt fever onset within 1 day is more characteristic of BRAF/MEK inhibitor pyrexia syndrome
Absence of rash or other cutaneous sarcoid-like lesions

data.description: A multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, most often affecting the lungs and lymph nodes but also potentially involving the liver and spleen.
symptoms_in_common: Right upper-quadrant tenderness suggesting liver involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever onset immediately after starting dabrafenib and trametinib
Marked improvement after temporary interruption of the cancer drugs
Nausea is not a prominent typical manifestation
No rash, erythema nodosum, uveitis, or respiratory symptoms reported

data.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species that can produce fever, pulmonary disease, hepatosplenic involvement, granulomas, and yeast forms detectable with fungal stains in tissue.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported immunosuppressive therapy or epidemiologic exposure history
No cough, dyspnea, weight loss, or lymphadenopathy reported
Immediate onset after starting dabrafenib and trametinib with improvement after drug withdrawal favors a medication-related syndrome

data.description: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. In August 2011, presented to emergency room with abdominal pain. Lab tests showed elevated lipase (874 U/L), alkaline phosphatase (289 IU/L), and ALT (222 IU/L), with normal bilirubin. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Labs showed elevated alkaline phosphatase of 357 IU/L and normal serum lipase.

data.diagnosis: Gallbladder metastasis from prostate adenocarcinoma causing acute cholecystitis
data.description: Rare metastatic involvement of the gallbladder by prostate cancer, potentially causing cystic-duct obstruction, gallbladder distention, and an acute cholecystitis-like presentation.
symptoms_in_common: Known history of metastatic prostate cancer
Abdominal imaging and pathology showing a gallbladder lesion with malignant-appearing cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Initial markedly elevated lipase, which is more suggestive of pancreatitis
Normal bilirubin despite biliary-type symptoms

data.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually from cystic-duct obstruction by a gallstone, sludge, mass, or extrinsic compression; acalculous cholecystitis can occur without stones in severely ill or malignant patients.
symptoms_in_common: Normal bilirubin can occur when obstruction is limited to the cystic duct
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of fever
No reported leukocytosis
History and pathology suggesting a malignant gallbladder lesion rather than simple gallstone disease
Initial markedly elevated lipase

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the gallbladder that may obstruct the cystic duct or biliary tree and can present as cholecystitis, biliary pain, or cholestatic liver-enzyme elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated ALT during the initial presentation
Malignant-appearing gallbladder mass or abnormal tissue on imaging/pathology
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal bilirubin, whereas advanced biliary obstruction often produces jaundice
Positive Murphy's sign is more characteristic of acute cholecystitis than uncomplicated cancer
Known metastatic prostate cancer and immunopathologic appearance may favor metastatic disease over a new primary gallbladder tumor
Initial elevated lipase

data.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation caused by transient or persistent obstruction of the ampulla or common bile duct, most often from gallstones, sludge, or malignant biliary obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly elevated serum lipase during the first emergency presentation
symptoms_not_in_common: Later normal serum lipase
Pain localized to the right upper quadrant rather than typical severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
Positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder, which favor gallbladder inflammation
No reported jaundice or bilirubin elevation

data.description: 13-year-old Caucasian boy with Italian ancestry presenting with Addison’s disease, dysphagia, muscle weakness, fatigue, and recent gait ataxia. History of bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and hypospadias at birth; early normal development followed by global developmental delay and mild intellectual disability by age 9. Longstanding absence of tears since infancy. From age 2 he developed recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, and progressive hyperpigmentation; at age 4 had recurrent hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia leading to diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Severe progressive dysphagia began at age 11. Examination showed marked hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal arm weakness and wasting, milder pyramidal leg weakness, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Labs showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin, consistent with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.

An autosomal-recessive multisystem disorder caused by AAAS gene variants, classically characterized by alacrima, achalasia, and ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency; progressive neurologic dysfunction may produce the '4A' phenotype.
symptoms_in_common: Isolated glucocorticoid deficiency/Addison disease with markedly elevated ACTH
Recurrent hypoglycemia and hypothermia during childhood
Recurrent vomiting and failure to thrive
Progressive severe dysphagia, consistent with achalasia or esophageal dysmotility
Muscle weakness and distal arm wasting
Autonomic/ocular features including dilated poorly light-reactive pupils
Developmental delay and mild intellectual disability can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral cryptorchidism
Hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism
Hyperkeratosis

data.diagnosis: 4A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome with progressive neurologic dysfunction)
data.description: A neurologic form of Allgrove syndrome in which alacrima, achalasia, adrenal insufficiency, and progressive autonomic, central, and peripheral neurologic abnormalities coexist.
symptoms_in_common: Vomiting, hypoglycemia, and failure to thrive
Pyramidal signs including hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses
Nystagmus and abnormal saccadic eye movements
Dilated pupils with poor light response
symptoms_not_in_common: Cryptorchidism
Hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Marked facial dysmorphism
Hyperkeratosis

data.description: A group of inherited disorders causing adrenal glucocorticoid failure with high ACTH but generally preserved mineralocorticoid production, often presenting in childhood with hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation, and poor growth.
symptoms_not_in_common: Congenital absence of tears
Progressive severe dysphagia/achalasia
Nystagmus and abnormal eye movements
Dilated poorly reactive pupils
Optic atrophy
Progressive pyramidal signs and gait ataxia
Distal muscle wasting
Developmental delay and intellectual disability
Cryptorchidism and hypospadias

data.description: A peroxisomal disorder caused by ABCD1 variants that can cause primary adrenal insufficiency in boys and progressive inflammatory cerebral or spinal-cord neurologic disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of tears since infancy
Severe dysphagia beginning in childhood suggestive of achalasia
Normal mineralocorticoid function is less characteristic
Dilated pupils with poor light response
Recurrent early hypoglycemia as the predominant adrenal presentation
Cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and inguinal hernia
Typical brain white-matter abnormalities are not described

data.diagnosis: Syringomyelia due to cervical spinal cord syrinx
data.description: A fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord that may cause progressive weakness, muscle wasting, upper-motor-neuron signs, and gait disturbance. The cervical MRI appearance is compatible with a central intramedullary fluid signal/syrinx.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cervical cord cavity/syrinx on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Alacrima
ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency
Hyperpigmentation
Hypoglycemia and hypothermia
Vomiting and failure to thrive
Progressive dysphagia due to esophageal dysmotility
Dilated pupils with poor light response
Optic atrophy
Developmental delay
Cryptorchidism and hypospadias

data.description: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of invasive ductal breast cancer, stage IV with metastases to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy, multiple systemic therapies, and stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier. She had been on anastrozole for 3 months and paracetamol for pain. She developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found on the floor, disoriented, with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions. Exam showed she was awake but unresponsive and uncooperative, without initial focal neurologic deficits; vital signs were notable for mild tachycardia and no fever. Baseline brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

Neurologic injury caused by fat emboli entering the cerebral circulation, usually after trauma or orthopedic procedures but occasionally associated with extensive bone metastases. MRI commonly shows multifocal punctate diffusion-restricted lesions ('starfield' pattern), edema, and microhemorrhages.
symptoms_in_common: Acute multifocal bilateral brain lesions with diffusion restriction
Known extensive bone metastases, a potential source of marrow fat embolization
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported recent long-bone fracture or orthopedic surgery
No reported respiratory distress or hypoxemia
No reported petechial rash
No fever
