data.diagnosis: Cancer-associated multifocal embolic ischemic stroke (malignancy-related hypercoagulability/Trousseau syndrome)
data.description: Advanced malignancy can cause a hypercoagulable state, nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, or tumor-associated thrombosis, resulting in multiple acute embolic cerebral infarcts in different vascular territories.
symptoms_in_common: Multifocal bilateral diffusion-restricted lesions consistent with acute ischemic injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear focal neurologic deficit was initially documented
No known atrial fibrillation, valvular disease, or documented arterial thrombus
Microhemorrhagic MRI findings are less typical than in cerebral fat embolism
The diffuse encephalopathy is more prominent than a typical territorial embolic stroke presentation

data.description: A clinicoradiologic syndrome of vasogenic edema, commonly related to severe hypertension, renal dysfunction, cytotoxic therapy, or endothelial injury. It causes altered mental status, seizures, headache, and visual symptoms, usually with posterior-predominant MRI abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Acute encephalopathy with confusion and unresponsiveness
History of malignancy and prior systemic anticancer treatments
symptoms_not_in_common: No severe hypertension was reported
No seizures, headache, or visual disturbance were reported
Diffusion restriction suggesting multifocal infarction is less typical than vasogenic edema
The MRI pattern includes widespread punctate lesions rather than classic parieto-occipital vasogenic edema

data.diagnosis: Brain metastases from breast cancer with hemorrhagic or ischemic complications
data.description: Breast cancer can metastasize to the brain and cause focal deficits, seizures, headache, cognitive changes, edema, and occasionally hemorrhage. Metastases usually appear as enhancing mass lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema.
symptoms_in_common: Long history of stage IV invasive ductal breast cancer
Progressive confusion and altered mental status
Multifocal intracranial abnormalities including possible hemorrhagic foci
symptoms_not_in_common: Brain MRI was normal 2 weeks earlier
No discrete mass lesions or mass effect are described
Rapid progression over days to coma is less typical without major edema, hemorrhage, or leptomeningeal involvement
No initial focal neurologic deficits were identified

data.diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy due to liver metastases or hepatic failure
data.description: Hepatic dysfunction can lead to accumulation of neurotoxins, particularly ammonia, causing fluctuating confusion, impaired attention, altered consciousness, and coma.
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute multifocal diffusion-restricted and microhemorrhagic brain lesions are not typical of uncomplicated hepatic encephalopathy
No jaundice, ascites, asterixis, or documented liver failure was reported
Lower-leg weakness and focal-appearing MRI lesions are not typical primary manifestations
No laboratory evidence of hyperammonemia or hepatic synthetic dysfunction was provided

data.description: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive weakness in all four extremities and sensory changes, followed by urinary difficulty. Examination showed hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski signs, bilateral Hoffmann and Tromner signs, and motor weakness (MRC 2 on the right, MRC 4 on the left). Sensory loss included decreased pinprick and temperature below the C4 level, worse on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, worse on the right. Serologic autoimmune studies were normal, cerebrospinal fluid studies were normal, and systemic imaging/nerve conduction studies showed no other organ involvement.

Granulomatous inflammation of the spinal cord due to sarcoidosis, which may occur without pulmonary or other systemic involvement. MRI often shows an enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion, and biopsy demonstrates noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.
symptoms_in_common: Upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski signs, Hoffmann signs, and Tromner signs
Dissociated sensory deficits involving pain/temperature and proprioception/vibration
Urinary difficulty from spinal cord involvement
Intramedullary cervical spinal cord lesion on MRI
No systemic organ involvement can occur in isolated neurosarcoidosis
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly atypical clinical symptoms; the presentation is compatible with cervical cord neurosarcoidosis

data.diagnosis: Cervical spinal cord tumor (intramedullary astrocytoma or ependymoma)
data.description: Primary intramedullary tumors can expand and compress cervical spinal cord pathways, producing progressive myelopathy, sensory changes, weakness, and bladder dysfunction. However, granulomatous histology argues against a neoplasm.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive weakness in all four extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: One-month progression is relatively rapid for many intramedullary tumors
Histology showing granulomatous inflammation and giant cells is not typical of astrocytoma or ependymoma
Marked inflammatory-appearing MRI enhancement is less typical for some low-grade spinal cord tumors

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder that commonly causes acute or subacute transverse myelitis, often involving long segments of the spinal cord and causing weakness, sensory loss, and sphincter dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Quadriparesis due to cervical spinal cord involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No optic neuritis or visual symptoms were reported
The lesion appears focal rather than a typical longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis lesion
Normal autoimmune and cerebrospinal fluid studies do not support an inflammatory demyelinating disorder
Granulomatous biopsy findings are not typical of NMOSD

data.diagnosis: Spinal cord tuberculosis (intramedullary tuberculoma or granulomatous myelitis)
data.description: Tuberculosis can cause granulomatous inflammation or a tuberculoma within the spinal cord, resulting in progressive myelopathy. Histology may show granulomas and giant cells, usually with caseous necrosis or microbiologic evidence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
symptoms_in_common: Sensory level and sensory tract dysfunction
Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells on tissue examination
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, weight loss, pulmonary symptoms, or known tuberculosis exposure was reported
No systemic organ involvement was identified
Normal cerebrospinal fluid studies are less typical for central nervous system tuberculosis
Noncaseating granulomas without reported acid-fast organisms favor sarcoidosis over tuberculosis

data.description: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and small amounts of yellow-white sputum शुरू after a cold. No hemoptysis, fever, chills, chest pain, or dyspnea initially. Treated at a local clinic with intravenous therapy without improvement. Cough worsened 7 days before admission, especially at night causing sleep difficulty, sometimes with right-sided chest pain. Previously healthy; smoked about 10 cigarettes/day for over 10 years, no alcohol use. Exam: T 36.2℃, pulse 112/min, RR 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg. Chest exam showed symmetric thorax and respiratory movement, normal percussion, coarse breath sounds bilaterally, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung; no dry rales or pleural friction rub.

A rare chronic granulomatous inflammatory disorder caused by impaired macrophage bacterial killing, most often associated with gram-negative infection. It can form a mass-like pulmonary consolidation and may show foamy histiocytes with characteristic Michaelis-Gutmann bodies on pathology.
symptoms_in_common: Worsening cough despite prior intravenous treatment
CT appearance of a focal right lower-lobe consolidative/cavitary lesion
Histology suggesting abundant macrophage-rich inflammatory infiltrate
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or chills
No known immunosuppression or major chronic illness
No hemoptysis

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia with lung abscess
data.description: A severe bacterial infection causing pulmonary consolidation, tissue necrosis, and formation of one or more cavities or abscesses, commonly involving dependent portions of the lower lobes.
symptoms_in_common: Wet rales over the right lung
Right lower-lobe consolidation with cavitary or necrotic-appearing areas on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No chills
No dyspnea
Only a small amount of sputum
No clear systemic toxic appearance described

data.description: A chronic suppurative infection caused by Actinomyces species that can produce mass-like consolidation, abscesses, cavitation, and extension toward the pleura or chest wall. Diagnosis is usually made by pathology or microbiologic identification of sulfur granules.
symptoms_in_common: Failure to improve after nonspecific initial intravenous therapy
Mass-like right lower-lobe consolidation with cavitary change on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or constitutional symptoms
No reported poor dentition, aspiration risk, or recent dental disease
No hemoptysis

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the lung, which may cause prolonged cough, sputum production, cavitary lesions, and focal consolidation; lower-lobe involvement can occur but is less classic than upper-lobe disease in reactivation tuberculosis.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms not improving with routine treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Short symptom duration of about 20 days
No fever
No night sweats
No weight loss
No hemoptysis
Predominantly right lower-lobe rather than classic upper-lobe involvement

data.diagnosis: Post-obstructive pneumonia due to an endobronchial lesion
data.description: Infection and collapse/consolidation distal to obstruction of a bronchus by a tumor, foreign body, mucus plug, or inflammatory lesion. Obstruction can lead to persistent localized pneumonia, bronchiectatic change, or abscess formation.
symptoms_in_common: Localized right lower-lobe abnormality on CT
Possible cavitary or bronchiectatic changes within consolidated right lower-lobe lung
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age makes bronchogenic carcinoma less likely
No hemoptysis
No weight loss or other systemic cancer symptoms
Acute onset after a cold favors an infectious process

data.description: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

data.diagnosis: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
data.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually involving dogs as reservoir hosts. In humans it commonly presents as a solitary painless subcutaneous nodule; histology may demonstrate a thick-cuticled nematode.
symptoms_in_common: Migrating nodules in the brachial/upper-arm region
Normal blood count and inflammatory markers
Outdoor exposure in forested and island areas where mosquito vectors may occur

data.description: A tissue helminth infection caused by Gnathostoma larvae, classically producing intermittent migratory subcutaneous swellings after ingestion of undercooked freshwater fish, eels, frogs, or other intermediate hosts in endemic regions.
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel outside Croatia or known exposure in a typical endemic region
Nodule was painless rather than painful, pruritic, or inflammatory
Normal blood count without reported eosinophilia
No reported history of eating raw or undercooked freshwater animals

data.description: Infection by migrating larval Spirometra tapeworms, usually acquired through ingestion of contaminated water or raw amphibian/reptile meat. It can cause a slowly migrating subcutaneous mass.
symptoms_in_common: Possible migratory character of the lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel to areas where sparganosis is more commonly reported
No reported ingestion of untreated water, raw frog, snake, or other relevant exposures
Normal laboratory findings without reported eosinophilia
No local pain, inflammation, or pruritus

data.description: Tissue infection with larval Taenia solium cysts that can form painless subcutaneous or intramuscular nodules, often in association with exposure to fecal contamination or undercooked pork in endemic settings.
symptoms_not_in_common: Nodules were described as migrating, which is not typical for cysticercosis
Cysticercosis serology was negative
No travel outside Croatia or reported exposure in a typical endemic setting
No neurologic symptoms or multiple fixed nodules

data.description: 66-year-old man with progressive gait imbalance and recurrent falls beginning around 2000, later developing blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening unsteadiness. He had bilateral cataract surgery with lens implantation in 2000 without improvement. By 2003 he had irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes, slow and limited voluntary vertical eye movements, slow horizontal pursuit with bilateral adduction paresis, and impaired rapid alternating distal movements with backward falls. Over time he developed frequent falls requiring a cane, retrocollis, slurred speech, inability to look down, and dysphagia. On admission in March 2007 for dysphagia with repeated aspiration, he had absent vertical and medial eye movements, impaired lateral gaze, no convergence, no Bell’s phenomenon or optokinetic nystagmus, absent caloric and doll’s eye responses, severe nuchal rigidity, axial rigidity, inability to sit independently, and recurrent backward falls. Reflexes were symmetric and mildly brisk with bilateral flexor plantar responses.
A progressive tauopathy causing early postural instability and falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and midbrain atrophy.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive gait imbalance with early recurrent backward falls
Severe axial rigidity and nuchal rigidity with retrocollis
Slow, limited, then absent vertical eye movements, especially downgaze
Impaired horizontal pursuit and impaired voluntary lateral gaze
Absent convergence, optokinetic nystagmus, Bell's phenomenon, caloric responses, and doll's eye responses
Bradykinetic impaired rapid alternating distal movements
Mildly brisk symmetric reflexes with flexor plantar responses
MRI appearance compatible with midbrain-predominant atrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Blurred vision and photophobia as prominent early complaints
Irregular pupils with sluggish light reflexes
History of cataract surgery without visual improvement

data.description: A synucleinopathy characterized by parkinsonism, autonomic failure, cerebellar dysfunction, dysarthria, dysphagia, and sometimes abnormal eye movements.
symptoms_in_common: Impaired smooth pursuit and abnormal eye movements
symptoms_not_in_common: Early recurrent backward falls as the dominant presentation
Severe vertical supranuclear gaze palsy progressing to near-complete ophthalmoplegia
Retrocollis and marked nuchal rigidity
No reported autonomic failure such as orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention, erectile dysfunction, or anhidrosis
No reported cerebellar ataxia, limb dysmetria, or characteristic pontocerebellar MRI findings

data.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy that usually causes asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, dystonia, myoclonus, and sometimes supranuclear gaze palsy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are not described as markedly asymmetric
No limb apraxia
No cortical sensory loss
No alien-limb phenomenon
No focal dystonia or myoclonus
Early severe backward falls and vertical gaze palsy are more characteristic of PSP

data.diagnosis: Dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson disease with dementia
data.description: Synucleinopathies causing parkinsonism with cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, fluctuating attention, REM sleep behavior disorder, and autonomic dysfunction; eye movement abnormalities can occur later.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive parkinsonian features including rigidity and impaired rapid alternating movements
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported cognitive fluctuations, dementia, visual hallucinations, or REM sleep behavior disorder
No reported resting tremor
Very early and profound backward falls
Severe vertical gaze palsy and loss of convergence are unusual
Prominent retrocollis and early axial rigidity are more typical of PSP

data.diagnosis: Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset neurologic form
data.description: A lysosomal cholesterol-trafficking disorder that can present in adults with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and psychiatric or cognitive symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with inability to look down
Progressive abnormal eye movements including impaired pursuit and convergence
symptoms_not_in_common: Late onset at approximately 60 years of age is less typical
Marked axial rigidity, retrocollis, and early backward falls favor PSP
No reported hepatosplenomegaly or systemic visceral disease
No reported psychiatric illness, cognitive decline, cataplexy, or childhood neurologic symptoms

data.description: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

Opportunistic fungal meningitis caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeast, classically occurring in advanced HIV/AIDS. The images are consistent with encapsulated budding yeasts demonstrated by India ink staining.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced HIV infection with CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL
symptoms_not_in_common: No major atypical symptoms are described; the presentation is highly characteristic

data.description: A subacute meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated opening pressure, and neurologic impairment. It is more likely in people with advanced HIV infection.
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF glucose is not markedly low
Microscopy images show encapsulated yeasts rather than acid-fast bacilli
No pulmonary tuberculosis symptoms, weight loss, or night sweats are reported

data.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as herpesviruses or enteroviruses. CSF typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with relatively preserved glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated opening pressure is less typical
Very advanced HIV-related immunosuppression strongly favors opportunistic infection
CSF protein is substantially elevated
Microscopy images show encapsulated budding yeasts, which are not consistent with viral infection

data.description: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute ischemic infarction of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) causing left internuclear ophthalmoplegia
data.description: A small acute brainstem ischemic stroke affecting the left MLF, the pathway coordinating conjugate horizontal eye movements. This produces impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye. The diffusion-weighted MRI appearance is consistent with an acute small brainstem infarct.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
Nystagmus of the right eye during attempted leftward gaze
Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation, increasing embolic stroke risk

data.description: An acute ischemic stroke caused by embolization from the heart, particularly in atrial fibrillation. Small emboli can occlude perforating brainstem vessels and cause an isolated ocular-motor syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: MRI evidence of an acute brainstem ischemic lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: No limb weakness, sensory loss, dysarthria, or ataxia

data.description: Multiple sclerosis can produce demyelinating lesions of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and is a classic cause of internuclear ophthalmoplegia, often with diplopia and abducting nystagmus.
symptoms_in_common: Impaired adduction of the left eye
Nystagmus of the contralateral eye during attempted horizontal gaze
symptoms_not_in_common: Very advanced age at presentation
Sudden onset over hours rather than a typical demyelinating relapse pattern
Atrial fibrillation with substantial vascular stroke risk
MRI appearance more consistent with a small acute infarct than disseminated demyelinating lesions

data.description: An autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disorder that may cause fluctuating diplopia and ophthalmoparesis, usually without pupillary abnormalities or other focal neurological deficits.
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden fixed onset rather than fluctuating fatigable symptoms
Specific left adduction deficit with contralateral abducting nystagmus, which localizes to the MLF
MRI evidence of an acute brainstem lesion
No reported ptosis or fatigability

data.description: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and feeding breast milk and formula. He was well 2 days before admission, then developed fussiness, pallor, warmth, vomiting, fever, tachycardia, mottled skin, and respiratory distress over 1 day. On presentation he was pale, listless, fussy, with temperature 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, oxygen saturation 97% on 1 L nasal cannula, a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, and spleen palpable 2–3 cm below the costal margin; arms and legs were mottled and slightly cool. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH and AST, elevated D-dimer, and blood smear with parasitemia; CSF was clear with no organisms on Gram stain and intraerythrocytic ring forms on Wright stain.

Malaria acquired transplacentally or during delivery, with symptomatic infection appearing in the first weeks of life. P. falciparum commonly causes high parasitemia, severe hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and life-threatening systemic illness.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH and AST consistent with hemolysis
Dark red urine with blood and granular casts, compatible with hemoglobinuria
Intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood and CSF Wright stains
Multiple ring forms within erythrocytes, consistent with P. falciparum
symptoms_not_in_common: No major atypical symptoms; the presentation is highly consistent with severe congenital falciparum malaria

data.diagnosis: Severe falciparum malaria with hemolysis and shock
data.description: Severe Plasmodium falciparum infection can cause massive red-cell destruction, hemoglobinuria, thrombocytopenia, metabolic stress, circulatory compromise, and respiratory distress. In a young infant, this may resemble bacterial sepsis.
symptoms_in_common: Mottled cool extremities suggesting poor perfusion
Altered behavior including listlessness and irritability
symptoms_not_in_common: No coma or seizures were reported
Oxygen saturation remained relatively preserved on low-flow oxygen
No documented severe hypoglycemia, acidosis, or renal failure

data.description: Babesiosis is an intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that can produce fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH, and hemoglobinuria. On blood smear it may resemble malaria, although Babesia classically may show tetrads forming a Maltese-cross pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Dark red urine compatible with hemoglobinuria
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple delicate ring forms within erythrocytes are more characteristic of Plasmodium falciparum
No Maltese-cross tetrads were described
Congenital babesiosis is uncommon compared with congenital malaria
The very high fever and severe acute neonatal presentation are more strongly suggestive of falciparum malaria

data.diagnosis: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
data.description: Neonatal sepsis can cause fever, lethargy, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, thrombocytopenia, coagulation abnormalities, and multiorgan dysfunction. It is an important clinical mimic of severe malaria in young infants.
symptoms_not_in_common: Intraerythrocytic ring forms and documented parasitemia are not typical of bacterial sepsis
Marked hemolytic anemia with dark red urine is more characteristic of malaria-associated hemolysis
Splenomegaly is less typical in acute bacterial sepsis
CSF showed ring forms rather than bacteria on Gram stain

data.description: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

data.diagnosis: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal involvement
data.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with locally recurrent pelvic disease involving or compressing the rectum and distant metastases to the lungs and liver.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic disease
Liver lesion consistent with metastatic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No urinary obstructive symptoms, hematuria, or bone pain are reported

data.diagnosis: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with liver and lung metastases
data.description: Cancer arising from the rectum that may cause local rectal pain and tenesmus, with hematogenous spread commonly involving the liver and lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple lung nodules compatible with metastatic spread
symptoms_not_in_common: No rectal bleeding is reported
No altered stool caliber, constipation, diarrhea, or bowel obstruction is reported
Prior high-grade prostate cancer makes recurrent prostate malignancy an important competing explanation

data.diagnosis: Rectal involvement by metastatic prostate cancer presenting as a rectal tumor
data.description: A specific manifestation of recurrent prostate cancer in which tumor extends into or infiltrates the rectal wall, potentially mimicking a primary rectal cancer and producing severe anorectal symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Prior radical prostatectomy for aggressive prostate cancer
Long interval followed by possible late recurrence
Pelvic lesion adjacent to or involving the rectum
Evidence of distant metastatic disease in lung and liver
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported elevation in prostate-specific antigen
No reported urinary symptoms or perineal pain

data.diagnosis: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or urinary tract
data.description: Urothelial cancer can invade pelvic structures and metastasize to lymph nodes, liver, and lungs, although the clinical history more strongly favors recurrent prostate cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Liver lesion and pulmonary nodules that could represent metastases
symptoms_not_in_common: No hematuria is reported
No dysuria, urinary frequency, or other lower urinary tract symptoms are reported
Severe tenesmus and rectal pain are less typical as presenting symptoms
No known history of urothelial carcinoma

data.description: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive proximal leg myalgias followed by acute inability to lift his legs, stand, or move in bed, with associated arm weakness. For several months আগে presentation, he had insomnia, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremors. He started an herbal stress-reducing supplement 4 days before presentation. On exam: bilateral conjunctival injection, generalized weakness (upper extremities 4/5, lower extremities 3/5), hyperreflexia, and fine hand tremor. Labs showed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis and elevated alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin, mildly elevated CK and aldolase, and venous pH 7.29.

data.diagnosis: Graves disease causing thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis
data.description: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism due to thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, often associated with diffuse thyroid enlargement and marked hypervascularity. In susceptible patients, thyrotoxicosis can cause intracellular potassium shifting and acute flaccid weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Acute proximal-predominant leg weakness progressing to paralysis
Diffuse hypervascular thyroid appearance on Doppler ultrasound
Thyroid histology compatible with hyperplastic/autoimmune thyroid disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival injection without clearly described proptosis or ophthalmopathy
Venous acidemia (pH 7.29), which is not a classic feature of thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Mild CK and aldolase elevation, which may occur from muscle injury but is not central to Graves disease

data.description: An acute neuromuscular complication of thyrotoxicosis in which thyroid hormone excess increases cellular potassium uptake, producing profound hypokalemia and sudden reversible muscle weakness or paralysis.
symptoms_in_common: Proximal leg weakness more severe than arm weakness
Inability to stand, lift the legs, or move in bed
Preceding symptoms of hyperthyroidism including weight loss, diarrhea, tremor, and insomnia
Possible trigger from recent herbal supplement use
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive myalgias for 3 days, as classic attacks are often painless
Conjunctival injection
Mild cholestatic liver-enzyme abnormalities
Acidemia, whereas thyrotoxic periodic paralysis more often involves transcellular potassium shift without substantial metabolic acidosis

data.diagnosis: Herbal supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm spectrum
data.description: Thyrotoxicosis may be precipitated or worsened by supplements containing thyroid hormone, iodine, stimulants, or adulterants; it can exacerbate underlying Graves disease and trigger hypokalemic paralysis.
symptoms_in_common: Recent initiation of an herbal stress-reducing supplement
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis were present for several months before supplement initiation, suggesting an underlying chronic thyroid disorder rather than purely supplement-induced disease
No reported fever
No reported marked tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, agitation, delirium, or heart failure that would strongly support thyroid storm
No reported goiter-related neck symptoms

data.diagnosis: Distal renal tubular acidosis with hypokalemic paralysis
data.description: A renal acidification disorder that causes non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, renal potassium wasting, and potentially severe hypokalemic muscle weakness; autoimmune thyroid disease can coexist with autoimmune renal tubular disorders.
symptoms_in_common: Mild CK elevation potentially related to hypokalemic muscle injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Weight loss, tremor, insomnia, loose stools, and hyperreflexia strongly suggest thyrotoxicosis rather than isolated renal tubular acidosis
The thyroid ultrasound and histologic findings support thyroid disease
No reported urine potassium, urine pH, bicarbonate level, nephrolithiasis, or other evidence of renal tubular acidosis
The acute episode followed a likely thyrotoxic trigger

data.description: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.
A benign, non-neoplastic bony exostosis arising from the midline of the hard palate. It is often lobulated, slowly enlarges over time, and is usually asymptomatic.
symptoms_in_common: Midline hard-palate mass with a lobulated appearance
Mass reportedly present since birth/for many years
Difficulty cleaning around the lesion due to food entrapment

data.description: A benign localized overgrowth of mature bone on the palate. Torus palatinus is the most characteristic type of palatal exostosis.
symptoms_in_common: Appearance consistent with a smooth, broad-based bony prominence
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported presence since birth is less typical for an acquired exostosis

data.description: A benign reactive gingival growth containing fibrous tissue and mineralized material, usually arising from the interdental gingiva rather than the palate.
symptoms_in_common: May interfere with oral hygiene if sufficiently large
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesion is located in the midline hard palate rather than the gingiva
Mass has reportedly been present since birth
Lobulated broad palatal bony appearance
Halitosis from food trapped around a palatal prominence is not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Pleomorphic adenoma of a minor salivary gland
data.description: A benign salivary-gland tumor that may occur on the palate, usually presenting as a slow-growing, painless, firm submucosal mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: Mass reportedly present since birth
Midline lobulated appearance consistent with a bony prominence
Difficulty cleaning around a fixed palatal exostosis
Halitosis from food entrapment is not a typical feature

data.diagnosis: Palatal malignant salivary-gland neoplasm (such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma)
data.description: A malignant tumor of minor salivary glands that can present as a palatal swelling, sometimes initially painless, but often with progressive enlargement, ulceration, pain, or tissue destruction.
symptoms_in_common: May occasionally be painless early in its course
symptoms_not_in_common: Congenital or lifelong presence
Minimal symptoms over many decades
No reported pain, ulceration, bleeding, rapid enlargement, or sensory change
Lobulated midline bony appearance
Food entrapment-related halitosis is not typical

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of lower back pain radiating into her left leg with associated leg weakness. She had a history of chronic back pain. Neurological examination revealed reduced power in her left leg (3/5), but was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Lumbar intervertebral disc herniation with L4-L5 nerve-root compression
data.description: Displacement of degenerative disc material into the spinal canal or neural foramen, causing compression of a lumbar nerve root and radiculopathy. The MRI appearance is most consistent with a prominent lower-lumbar disc protrusion/extrusion, particularly at L4-L5.
symptoms_in_common: Pain radiating into the left leg
Middle age with degenerative spinal disease risk

data.diagnosis: Lumbar spinal canal stenosis due to degenerative disc disease
data.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal from disc bulging, facet-joint degeneration, and ligament thickening, potentially compressing the cauda equina or individual nerve roots.
symptoms_in_common: Leg pain consistent with lumbar radiculopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Very acute two-day onset of symptoms is less typical than gradual or exertional symptoms
No reported neurogenic claudication or walking-related symptom worsening

data.description: A fluid-containing cyst arising from a degenerative lumbar facet joint that can extend into the spinal canal and compress a nerve root, most commonly at L4-L5.
symptoms_in_common: Focal left-leg weakness due to nerve-root compression
Age compatible with degenerative facet-joint disease
Possible focal posterior epidural compressive lesion at a lower-lumbar level
symptoms_not_in_common: No known history of significant facet arthropathy or spondylolisthesis was provided
Abrupt onset over two days is less typical unless there is acute cyst enlargement or hemorrhage

data.diagnosis: Lumbar epidural venous varix or thrombosed epidural varix
data.description: Dilated or thrombosed epidural veins can form a mass-like lesion in the lumbar canal and mimic a disc herniation, producing acute radicular pain and neurological deficit.
symptoms_in_common: Acute lower back pain with unilateral leg radiation
Potential mass-like lower-lumbar epidural finding on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic mechanical back pain is not specifically characteristic
No known venous disease, increased intra-abdominal pressure, or provoking vascular factor was reported

diagnoses.name: Intervertebral disc prolapse
diagnoses.title: Intervertebral disc degeneration without prolapsed disc with determinant

data.description: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

data.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) with multisystem thromboembolic/vasculitic involvement
data.description: A disorder characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia causing eosinophil-mediated injury to organs, particularly the heart, nervous system, lungs, skin, and blood vessels. Cardiac involvement can produce embolic cerebral infarctions.
symptoms_in_common: No identified secondary cause of eosinophilia such as parasite, allergy, malignancy, or vasculitis
Acute multifocal cerebral ischemic lesions on diffusion-weighted MRI
Cognitive dysfunction including disorientation, attention deficit, and immediate-memory disturbance
Bilateral upper-extremity weakness, hyperreflexia, and right hemiparetic gait
Elevated troponin-I and creatine kinase-MB suggesting cardiac involvement
Angiographic abnormalities compatible with cerebral vascular involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: None strongly inconsistent; the presentation is highly compatible with HES

data.diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss syndrome)
data.description: A necrotizing small- to medium-vessel vasculitis associated with eosinophilia, asthma, chronic sinus disease, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, and possible cardiac or central nervous system involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Neurologic deficits and multifocal cerebral infarctions that can occur from vasculitis or cardiac embolism
Cardiac enzyme elevation and regional ventricular wall-motion abnormality
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of asthma
No sinusitis or chronic rhinosinusitis
No reported allergic rhinitis
No reported peripheral neuropathy, purpura, renal disease, or gastrointestinal vasculitic symptoms

data.diagnosis: Eosinophilic myocarditis with cardioembolic multifocal ischemic stroke
data.description: Eosinophil-mediated inflammation of the myocardium, often associated with hypereosinophilic disorders, that can lead to myocardial injury, mural thrombus formation, embolic stroke, and heart failure.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple acute ischemic brain lesions in different vascular territories, compatible with embolic events
Acute focal neurologic deficits including dysarthria and hemiparetic gait
Cognitive impairment from multifocal cerebral infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported chest pain
No reported palpitations, dyspnea, edema, or overt heart failure
No documented intracardiac thrombus in the provided echocardiographic findings

data.diagnosis: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
data.description: An uncommon inflammatory vasculitis limited to the brain and spinal cord that causes multifocal ischemic infarctions, hemorrhage, encephalopathy, and angiographic segmental stenoses or beading.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute cognitive decline with disorientation, impaired attention, and memory disturbance
Focal neurologic deficits including dysarthria, upper-extremity weakness, hyperreflexia, and hemiparetic gait
Cerebral angiographic vascular irregularities suggestive of vasculopathy
Possible small hemorrhagic lesion on susceptibility-sensitive MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked hypereosinophilia is not typical of isolated PACNS
Elevated cardiac enzymes and ventricular wall-motion abnormality suggest systemic cardiac involvement
Pulmonary nodular lesion is not expected in disease confined to the central nervous system

data.diagnosis: Polyarteritis nodosa or another systemic medium-vessel vasculitis
data.description: A systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized arteries that can cause cerebral ischemia, cardiac ischemia, pulmonary or systemic vascular abnormalities, and constitutional symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Multifocal cerebral ischemic lesions with focal neurologic deficits
Possible angiographic arterial irregularity or stenosis
Cardiac injury markers and regional ventricular hypokinesia
Possible pulmonary vascular or nodular abnormality
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe eosinophilia is not a typical feature of classic polyarteritis nodosa
No reported fever, weight loss, skin nodules, livedo reticularis, renal hypertension, abdominal pain, or peripheral neuropathy
Pulmonary involvement is uncommon in classic polyarteritis nodosa

data.description: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.
A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly involving bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and the lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with intense FDG uptake
Negative tuberculosis skin test and tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior stage IIIA triple-negative breast cancer
History of breast radiation therapy
Mild anemia

data.diagnosis: Breast cancer recurrence with mediastinal and hilar lymph-node metastases
data.description: Recurrent breast carcinoma can spread to intrathoracic lymph nodes, lungs, bone, liver, or other organs and may produce FDG-avid lesions on PET imaging.
symptoms_in_common: History of node-positive stage IIIA breast cancer
FDG-avid mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas rather than malignant breast carcinoma cells
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level
Symmetric bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, which is more characteristic of sarcoidosis
Negative evidence of tumor on the described biopsy

data.description: Tuberculosis is a granulomatous infection that can cause thoracic lymph-node enlargement and pulmonary abnormalities; granulomas are often caseating but may occasionally be noncaseating.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative purified protein derivative skin test
Negative tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma result from the biopsy sample
Noncaseating rather than typical caseating granulomas
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level
No reported tuberculosis exposure, fever, night sweats, chronic cough, or weight loss

data.description: Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas may cause FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy and constitutional or hematologic abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: History of prior chemotherapy, which can increase risk of therapy-related hematologic malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy demonstrating noncaseating granulomas rather than lymphoma cells
Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level
No reported fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, or peripheral lymphadenopathy
Symmetric hilar adenopathy and pulmonary findings more suggestive of sarcoidosis

data.description: 78-year-old woman referred for anemia and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue. Past history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination showed no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy, with normal cardiac, respiratory, and neurologic findings; ECOG performance status 1. Initial tests revealed hemoglobin 99 g/L, normal white cell and platelet counts, ESR 120 mm/h, mildly elevated creatinine 110 mmol/L, calcium 2.81 mmol/L, and mildly elevated LDH 333 U/L. Further studies showed IgG kappa paraprotein 32 g/L, β2-microglobulin 6.3 mg/L, free kappa light chains 1,400 mg/L, kappa/lambda ratio 280, and urinary Bence-Jones protein (kappa) detected; 24-hour urine protein excretion was normal. Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase were normal.

data.diagnosis: IgG kappa multiple myeloma with osteosclerotic bone involvement
data.description: A malignant plasma-cell disorder producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin, associated with marrow infiltration, anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, and bone disease. Rarely, myeloma may produce osteosclerotic rather than classic lytic skeletal lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Very high serum free kappa light chains
Mild renal impairment with elevated creatinine
Bone marrow appearance consistent with plasma-cell infiltration
Abnormal skeletal imaging compatible with osteosclerotic bone involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No organomegaly
No lymphadenopathy
No reported bone pain
Normal white blood cell and platelet counts

data.diagnosis: POEMS syndrome associated with osteosclerotic plasma-cell neoplasm
data.description: A rare plasma-cell disorder characterized by polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal protein, skin changes, and usually osteosclerotic bone lesions. The monoclonal protein is more often lambda restricted.
symptoms_not_in_common: No peripheral neuropathy or neurologic abnormalities
No organomegaly
No lymphadenopathy
No reported endocrinopathy
No skin changes reported
Kappa rather than the more typical lambda light-chain restriction
Hypercalcemia is not typical
Significant Bence-Jones proteinuria is less typical

data.description: An asymptomatic precursor plasma-cell neoplasm with a substantial monoclonal protein and/or marrow plasma-cell burden but without myeloma-defining organ damage or biomarkers requiring treatment.
symptoms_not_in_common: Anemia compatible with myeloma-related marrow disease
Hypercalcemia
Renal impairment
Marked free light-chain ratio of 280, which is a myeloma-defining biomarker when involved light chain is sufficiently elevated
Skeletal abnormalities suggesting active bone involvement
Lethargy and fatigue likely related to symptomatic anemia

data.description: A common premalignant condition in older adults characterized by a small monoclonal protein without end-organ injury, substantial marrow plasma-cell infiltration, or myeloma-defining features.
symptoms_in_common: Presence of an IgG kappa monoclonal protein
symptoms_not_in_common: Paraprotein concentration of 32 g/L
Severe elevation of free kappa light chains
Kappa/lambda ratio of 280
Urinary Bence-Jones protein
Anemia
Hypercalcemia
Renal impairment
Skeletal and bone-marrow abnormalities
Fatigue and lethargy attributable to plasma-cell disease

data.description:
20-year-old male with 3-year history of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. He also had 4 years of prior polydipsia and polyuria that had recently improved, blurred vision corrected with glasses, occasional post-exertional headaches, and reduced facial hair growth. Past history included generalized nocturnal tonic-clonic and focal right leg seizures in childhood treated with carbamazepine until age 14. He reported recent constipation and a chronic pilonidal cyst. 

On examination, he appeared young with minimal facial hair, small testes, bilateral breast enlargement without retraction, masses, or discharge, and a small posterior anal fissure with a coccygeal lump. Initial labs showed marked hypernatremia and hyperosmolality, elevated prolactin, very low LH, FSH, and testosterone, low IGF-1, low free thyroxine, and low cortisol; CSF showed elevated red cells and protein but no malignant cells.

data.diagnosis: Multifocal intracranial germinoma with suprasellar involvement
data.description: A malignant germ-cell tumor of the central nervous system that commonly involves the suprasellar/hypothalamic-pituitary region and may be multifocal, including basal ganglia or pineal-region lesions. It can cause diabetes insipidus, visual symptoms, hyperprolactinemia from stalk disruption, and panhypopituitarism.
symptoms_in_common: Previous polydipsia and polyuria consistent with central diabetes insipidus
Blurred vision and abnormal visual-field testing
Elevated prolactin compatible with pituitary stalk effect
Very low LH, FSH, and testosterone causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Reduced facial hair and small testes
Low free thyroxine, cortisol, and IGF-1 indicating panhypopituitarism
Suprasellar/pituitary stalk lesion with additional enhancing intracranial lesions on MRI
History of seizures, which can occur with multifocal or basal-ganglia involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic pilonidal cyst
Posterior anal fissure
Constipation

data.diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis involving the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
data.description: A histiocytic inflammatory/neoplastic disorder that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, most often producing central diabetes insipidus and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. CNS lesions can occur but multifocal enhancing brain lesions are less typical than in germinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Polydipsia and polyuria suggestive of central diabetes insipidus
Pituitary hormone deficiencies including low gonadotropins, testosterone, thyroid hormone, cortisol, and IGF-1
Small testes, reduced facial hair, and gynecomastia from central hypogonadism
Elevated prolactin due to hypothalamic-pituitary stalk dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple intracranial enhancing lesions are less characteristic
No reported lytic bone lesions
No reported skin rash, scalp lesions, ear disease, or pulmonary involvement
Blurred vision/visual-field abnormalities are less typical as a presenting feature
Chronic pilonidal cyst and anal fissure are not typical

data.description: A benign but locally aggressive epithelial tumor arising near the pituitary stalk and suprasellar region. It commonly causes visual impairment, headaches, hyperprolactinemia, diabetes insipidus, and multiple anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.
symptoms_in_common: Prior polydipsia and polyuria compatible with diabetes insipidus
Panhypopituitarism with low cortisol, free thyroxine, IGF-1, LH, FSH, and testosterone
Delayed/poor androgenization, minimal facial hair, small testes, and gynecomastia
symptoms_not_in_common: Multifocal enhancing lesions elsewhere in the brain are not typical
Seizure history is not a usual manifestation of an isolated craniopharyngioma
Imaging appearance suggesting multiple germinoma-like lesions is atypical
Chronic pilonidal cyst and anal fissure are unrelated

data.diagnosis: Primary hypothalamic-pituitary lymphoma or secondary CNS lymphoma
data.description: Lymphomatous infiltration of the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, or suprasellar region can cause diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, visual symptoms, and panhypopituitarism. Multifocal enhancing CNS lesions may occur, although this is uncommon in an otherwise healthy young adult.
symptoms_in_common: Suprasellar/pituitary stalk lesion with multifocal intracranial enhancement
Polydipsia and polyuria with hypernatremia, suggesting central diabetes insipidus
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age is less typical for primary CNS lymphoma
No reported systemic lymphoma symptoms such as fever, night sweats, weight loss, or lymphadenopathy
CSF cytology showed no malignant cells
Gynecomastia is secondary to endocrine failure rather than a usual direct lymphoma presentation
Pilonidal cyst and anal fissure are unrelated

data.description: Granulomatous inflammation from sarcoidosis can infiltrate the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, and meninges, leading to central diabetes insipidus, hyperprolactinemia, visual symptoms, and anterior pituitary failure. It can also produce enhancing CNS lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Polydipsia and polyuria compatible with central diabetes insipidus
Low gonadotropins, testosterone, cortisol, thyroid hormone, and IGF-1
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported pulmonary, skin, eye, lymph-node, or systemic sarcoidosis manifestations
Age 20 is possible but less typical than in adult systemic sarcoidosis
The imaging pattern of discrete multifocal lesions is more suggestive of germinoma
Gynecomastia and reduced facial hair are indirect consequences of hypopituitarism rather than typical primary sarcoidosis symptoms
Pilonidal cyst and anal fissure are not typical

data.description: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic anemia and leukocytosis, with blood cultures growing methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

data.diagnosis: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus native aortic-valve infective endocarditis
data.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, caused here by MRSA. Intravenous drug use, persistent fever, positive blood cultures, peripheral embolic signs, and echocardiographic valve lesions strongly support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Five days of swinging fever and rigors
New early diastolic decrescendo murmur consistent with aortic regurgitation
Digital infarct of the left third toe
Recent discitis and psoas abscess, which may represent metastatic Staphylococcus aureus infection
Echocardiographic appearance consistent with aortic-valve vegetation
symptoms_not_in_common: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is not a typical manifestation of infective endocarditis
Left arm upper motor neuron weakness is a complication from cerebral embolism rather than a primary symptom of valve infection

data.diagnosis: Aortic root/perivalvular abscess complicating infective endocarditis
data.description: A localized collection of infection adjacent to the aortic valve annulus or aortic root, usually caused by invasive infective endocarditis. It can damage the conduction system and cause new PR prolongation or atrioventricular block.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent fever despite a serious invasive infection
Early diastolic murmur suggesting aortic-valve destruction or regurgitation
ECG findings concerning for PR-interval prolongation/conduction delay
Echocardiographic findings suggestive of a peri-aortic or aortic-root collection
Systemic embolic signs including splinter hemorrhages and toe infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Left arm weakness is more directly explained by an embolic cerebral infarct
Headache is nonspecific and not a characteristic isolated feature of an aortic root abscess
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is not specifically typical of aortic root abscess

data.diagnosis: Septic embolic ischemic stroke due to infective endocarditis
data.description: Cerebral infarction caused by embolization of infected valvular material from infective endocarditis into the cerebral circulation. It may produce focal neurological deficits, altered consciousness, and headache.
symptoms_in_common: Reduced level of consciousness at presentation
Left arm weakness with an upper motor neuron pattern
Infective endocarditis with likely valvular vegetation
Peripheral embolic phenomena, including a digital infarct
symptoms_not_in_common: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur is due to underlying aortic-valve disease rather than stroke
PR-interval/conduction abnormality is more suggestive of peri-annular extension of endocarditis than cerebral embolism
Recent discitis and psoas abscess are not typical manifestations of ischemic stroke

data.diagnosis: Acute or worsening aortic regurgitation secondary to infective endocarditis
data.description: Failure of the aortic valve to close properly because of infective destruction, perforation, or annular involvement. It produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur and may occur with aortic-valve endocarditis or peri-annular abscess.
symptoms_in_common: Soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border
MRSA bacteremia and infective endocarditis, which can damage the aortic valve
symptoms_not_in_common: Splinter hemorrhages are manifestations of infective endocarditis rather than isolated aortic regurgitation
Digital infarct is an embolic complication rather than a usual feature of aortic regurgitation
Fever, rigors, leukocytosis, and anemia indicate infection rather than isolated valve regurgitation
Left arm upper motor neuron weakness is more consistent with embolic stroke

data.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

data.diagnosis: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
data.description: An autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, resulting in glycogen accumulation predominantly in cardiac and skeletal muscle. Classic infantile-onset disease commonly causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, elevated muscle enzymes, hypotonia, and progressive respiratory muscle weakness.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly deficient confirmatory lymphocyte GAA activity
Two pathogenic GAA variants in trans: c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T
Elevated ALT, which can occur with muscle and/or cardiac involvement
Subtle decreased facial folds, which may represent early facial hypotonia
symptoms_not_in_common: No poor feeding
No poor activity
No weak cry
Normal muscle power
Normal reflexes
No macroglossia
No overt generalized hypotonia at 7 days of age

data.diagnosis: Infantile-onset Pompe disease with early hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
data.description: A cardiac-predominant presentation of infantile Pompe disease in which profound GAA deficiency causes glycogen deposition in the myocardium, producing cardiomegaly and often hypertrophic cardiomyopathy before major skeletal-muscle weakness becomes evident.
symptoms_in_common: Biallelic GAA variants consistent with Pompe disease
Enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest radiograph
Lack of advanced skeletal-muscle symptoms can occur early in the disease course
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented echocardiographic evidence of ventricular hypertrophy or outflow obstruction
No tachypnea or respiratory distress reported
No feeding difficulty or failure to thrive reported
No signs of overt heart failure reported
Normal muscle strength and reflexes

data.description: A benign genetic state in which certain GAA variants reduce activity in dried-blood-spot screening assays without causing clinically significant Pompe disease. It is an important cause of false-positive newborn screening results.
symptoms_in_common: Low GAA activity on newborn screening
Absence of obvious feeding difficulty, weak cry, or marked hypotonia at 7 days of age
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly deficient lymphocyte GAA activity rather than only mildly reduced screening activity
Two GAA variants in trans consistent with pathogenic disease
Cardiomegaly on chest radiograph
Markedly elevated pro-BNP
Elevated CK
Elevated ALT
Subtle decreased facial folds suggesting possible early muscle involvement

data.description: A 6-year-old girl with a 1-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain developed rib pain, right knee pain with limping, and left flank pain radiating to the left leg. Six days before admission, she developed back pain, worsening limp, and intermittent fever up to 39.8°C. The day before admission, she had periorbital swelling, abdominal distention, and periumbilical discoloration. On examination, she was febrile, had bilateral periorbital discoloration, a soft nontender abdomen, slight limping, and pain with external rotation of the right hip. Past history included infant gastroesophageal reflux and pollen allergy with allergic rhinitis. Family history included rheumatoid arthritis and breast cancer in the paternal grandmother, without other childhood arthritis or autoimmune disease.

A malignant proliferation of immature B-lymphoblasts in the bone marrow, often causing bone pain, fever, cytopenias, and extramedullary infiltration. The marrow morphology and flow cytometry showing blast cells expressing B-cell markers such as CD19 and CD10 support this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: One-year history of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain
Hip pain with painful external rotation
Periorbital swelling and bilateral periorbital discoloration
Imaging evidence of multifocal soft-tissue and/or organ involvement
Bone marrow findings consistent with lymphoblast proliferation
symptoms_not_in_common: Soft nontender abdomen despite abdominal distention
History of allergic rhinitis and pollen allergy
Infant gastroesophageal reflux

data.description: A childhood embryonal tumor of sympathetic nervous-system tissue, commonly arising in the adrenal gland or paraspinal region. It can metastasize to bone and bone marrow and may cause periorbital ecchymoses, bone pain, limp, fever, and abdominal distention.
symptoms_in_common: Back and flank pain radiating to the leg
Periorbital swelling and discoloration resembling 'raccoon eyes'
Possible multifocal skeletal and soft-tissue disease on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Longstanding migratory joint pain is less characteristic than persistent pain from metastatic disease
Pain with external rotation of the hip is nonspecific
Bone marrow flow cytometry with a CD19/CD10-positive B-lymphoblast population would not be typical
No clear adrenal or dominant abdominal primary mass is described

data.diagnosis: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including myeloid sarcoma
data.description: A hematologic malignancy caused by proliferation of myeloid blasts in marrow and blood. AML can cause fever, bone pain, marrow failure, and extramedullary myeloid sarcomas involving bone, soft tissues, skin, or the orbit.
symptoms_in_common: Bone pain involving ribs, knee, hip, and back
Limping due to painful bone or joint involvement
Periorbital swelling and discoloration, which can occur with orbital myeloid sarcoma
Abdominal distention from possible organ infiltration
symptoms_not_in_common: A year of intermittent migratory bone and joint pain is less typical of acute AML presentation
Flow cytometry showing CD19 and CD10 expression favors B-lymphoblastic leukemia rather than AML
No characteristic myeloid marker profile is provided
No reported gingival hypertrophy, skin leukemia lesions, or prominent bleeding manifestations

data.description: An aggressive small round cell sarcoma of bone and soft tissue, usually affecting children and adolescents. It often causes localized bone pain, fever, limp, and can metastasize to lung, bone marrow, and other bones.
symptoms_in_common: Knee, hip, back, and flank pain
Potential multifocal skeletal or soft-tissue abnormalities on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Migratory pain involving multiple joints over one year is less typical than pain centered at a primary bone lesion
Periorbital discoloration and swelling are not typical presenting features
Abdominal distention and periumbilical discoloration are not typical
Bone marrow flow cytometry showing a B-lymphoblast immunophenotype would not support Ewing sarcoma
No dominant destructive bone mass is described

data.description: 54-year-old woman without comorbidities presented to emergency department with 12-hour history of redness and painful swelling in left gluteal region. Denied trauma. At admission: afebrile (36.2°C), normal blood pressure (109/65 mmHg), heart rate 89 bpm, mild peripheral oxygen desaturation (92% on room air) without respiratory distress. Rest of physical exam normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute bacterial cellulitis of the gluteal region
data.description: A diffuse bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, commonly caused by streptococci or staphylococci. Ultrasound may show subcutaneous edema with a cobblestoned appearance and no drainable abscess.
symptoms_in_common: Acute onset of painful left gluteal swelling
Diffuse erythema of the left buttock
Ultrasound appearance compatible with subcutaneous tissue edema
No history of trauma is required
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Mild oxygen desaturation without respiratory symptoms

data.description: A superficial form of bacterial cellulitis involving the upper dermis and lymphatic vessels, usually caused by beta-hemolytic streptococci. It produces rapidly developing painful red skin swelling, often with relatively defined borders.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or systemic constitutional symptoms
The described erythema appears relatively diffuse rather than sharply demarcated
Mild peripheral oxygen desaturation is not typical

data.diagnosis: Superficial thrombophlebitis of a gluteal superficial vein
data.description: Inflammation and thrombosis of a superficial vein, causing localized pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. Ultrasound can demonstrate a noncompressible superficial venous structure with surrounding inflammatory change.
symptoms_in_common: Possible superficial vascular abnormality on ultrasound
Absence of trauma does not exclude spontaneous superficial venous thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: No described palpable tender venous cord
Broad diffuse buttock erythema is more suggestive of cellulitis
Mild oxygen desaturation is not typical unless there is associated pulmonary embolism

data.description: A rapidly progressive, potentially life-threatening infection of skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, or muscle. Early findings can resemble cellulitis, but pain is often severe and progression may be rapid; ultrasound may show edema, fascial fluid, or gas.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset of painful erythematous swelling
Gluteal location can be involved in necrotizing soft-tissue infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is not described as disproportionate to examination
No fever, hypotension, tachycardia, or toxic appearance
No skin necrosis, bullae, crepitus, or gas described on imaging
Normal overall physical examination apart from the gluteal lesion

data.description: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

A late immune-mediated complication of allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation in which donor immune cells attack recipient tissues. Skin involvement may be lichenoid, poikilodermatous, or sclerotic and can cause fascial tightening and joint contractures.
symptoms_in_common: History of allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation 2 years earlier
Diffuse nonpruritic rash involving the face, trunk, and extremities
Skin changes on the face, chest, and hands
Impaired wrist dorsiflexion with the prayer sign, suggesting skin/fascial sclerosis
Mild elevation of AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase, which can occur with hepatic cGVHD
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent fever is not a defining feature and should prompt evaluation for infection or inflammatory overlap disease
Abrupt onset immediately after a sailing trip is less typical than a more gradual cGVHD presentation

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive cutaneous eruptions; it may occur as an autoimmune syndrome after transplantation or overlap with chronic GVHD.
symptoms_in_common: Rash on the upper chest and extremities
Mild AST and ALT elevation, which may reflect muscle inflammation
Possible violaceous or erythematous lesions over the dorsal hands
symptoms_not_in_common: The prayer sign and reduced wrist mobility suggest fascial or sclerotic disease rather than classic dermatomyositis
No clearly described heliotrope rash
No clearly described Gottron papules over the knuckles
No documented symmetric proximal muscle weakness or elevated creatine kinase
History of allogeneic transplant more strongly supports chronic GVHD

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
data.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive rash, fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, and positive antinuclear antibodies. Lupus-like syndromes can rarely develop after stem-cell transplantation.
symptoms_in_common: Positive ANA at high titer with speckled pattern
Mild liver-enzyme abnormalities can occur in systemic autoimmune inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Male sex makes classic SLE less common
The prayer sign with restricted wrist extension is not a typical lupus finding
No reported inflammatory arthritis, oral ulcers, alopecia, nephritis, serositis, cytopenias, or neurologic manifestations
Post-transplant timing and skin sclerosis favor chronic GVHD over primary SLE

data.description: An inflammatory fibrosing disorder of the fascia that causes painful swelling followed by skin induration, restricted joint movement, and contractures. It may resemble scleroderma and can occur in association with immune dysregulation or chronic GVHD.
symptoms_in_common: Restricted wrist dorsiflexion and positive prayer sign
Possible skin thickening or induration of the hands and extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Photosensitive facial and truncal rash is not typical
Intermittent fever is less characteristic
No reported peripheral eosinophilia
No described symmetric painful limb edema, peau d'orange appearance, or groove sign
The prior allogeneic transplant more strongly suggests sclerodermatous chronic GVHD

data.description: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.
A rare form of eruptive keratoacanthoma characterized by the progressive appearance of numerous crateriform, keratin-filled papules and nodules, often on sun-exposed skin, with substantial pruritus.
symptoms_in_common: Numerous progressive papules and nodules on sun-exposed extremities
Crateriform and hyperkeratotic lesions clinically visible on the hands and forearms
No evidence of metastatic disease on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Terminal kidney disease requiring long-term hemodialysis
Prior kidney transplantation with graft rejection
Factor V Leiden mutation
Coexisting verruca vulgaris lesions

data.diagnosis: Multiple keratoacanthomas associated with chronic renal failure and dialysis
data.description: Multiple keratoacanthomas may occur in patients with chronic renal failure, dialysis, prior transplantation, or altered immune function. They present as rapidly developing keratinizing crateriform papules or nodules and can resemble well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Long-term peritoneal dialysis followed by ongoing hemodialysis
History of kidney transplantation and immunologic graft complications
Multiple keratotic papules and nodules on the extremities
Progressive course with recurrent or newly developing lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked localization to sun-exposed skin
Severe generalized pruritus and sleep disturbance
Coexisting verruca vulgaris
No prior habitual ultraviolet-light exposure

data.description: Keratoacanthoma-type squamous cell carcinoma is a keratinocyte malignancy that can appear as a rapidly growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug. Multiple lesions may occur in patients with immunologic dysfunction or prior immunosuppression.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple crateriform, ulcerated, hyperkeratotic papules and nodules
Lesions on chronically sun-exposed hands and forearms
Prior kidney transplantation, a risk factor for keratinocyte tumors
Progressive lesions requiring excision and topical field-directed treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe itch as the principal complaint
Large number of lesions developing over a short period
No habitual ultraviolet exposure
Absence of metastases or lymphadenopathy despite numerous lesions
Histology also showing benign verruca vulgaris lesions

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis of renal failure
data.description: An intensely pruritic skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes and chronic kidney disease/dialysis, characterized by excoriated hyperkeratotic papules or nodules, usually on the extensor surfaces of the limbs.
symptoms_in_common: Excoriated crusted papules and nodules on the extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Histology demonstrating keratoacanthomas rather than transepidermal elimination of collagen or elastin
Crateriform keratin-filled tumors
Predominant occurrence on sun-exposed areas
Histologically confirmed verruca vulgaris in some lesions
Treatment response to imiquimod and 5-fluorouracil, which is more consistent with keratinocytic neoplasia

data.description: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst initially presented with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute low back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission, she had mild left-sided weakness and proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, with no fever, no meningism, and GCS 15. Labs showed mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria and urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF examination and electromyography were normal. PCR detected high concentrations of Zika virus in serum, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid; other viral, bacterial, and autoimmune tests were negative.

An inflammatory spinal cord syndrome caused by neuroinvasive Zika virus infection, producing motor weakness, sensory level, pain, and autonomic dysfunction. MRI may show focal or longitudinal intramedullary T2 hyperintensity.
symptoms_in_common: Acute/subacute left-sided weakness progressing to hemiparesis
Left arm and leg pain worsened by movement
Loss of temperature sensation below thoracic sensory levels
Bilateral Hoffman signs suggesting corticospinal tract involvement
MRI spinal cord signal abnormalities compatible with myelitis
High concentrations of Zika virus detected by PCR in serum, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of fever or rash, although Zika infection can be afebrile and neurologic disease may occur without classic systemic symptoms
Normal cerebrospinal fluid examination, which is possible but less typical in inflammatory myelitis
