Laboratory tests showed anemia with hematocrit 31.8% and hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 3.92 × 10³/μL, elevated liver enzymes with AST 78 IU/L and ALT 71 IU/L, and markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase 1,591 IU/L. Serum cortisol level was 17.47 μg/dL at 8 AM and ACTH level was 12.1 pg/mL (normal range: 10-90). Ten days after admission, the patient developed pancytopenia with WBC 2.88 × 10³/μL, Hb 10.7 g/dL, and platelets 129 × 10³/μL. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for specific hematologic or malignant disorder.

A rare aggressive extranodal B-cell lymphoma in which malignant lymphoid cells proliferate mainly within small blood vessels. It often presents with fever, markedly elevated LDH, cytopenias, and no detectable lymphadenopathy; adrenal, liver, lung, skin, neurologic, and bone marrow involvement can occur.
symptoms_in_common: Pulmonary infiltrative abnormalities on chest imaging
Nonspecific hepatic lesions or infiltration on abdominal imaging
Negative or nondiagnostic initial bone marrow biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Lumbar pain is not a classic presenting symptom, although it may occur with adrenal or retroperitoneal involvement
Young age of 29 years is less typical because the disease usually affects older adults

data.diagnosis: Primary adrenal lymphoma with systemic dissemination
data.description: An aggressive lymphoma, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, involving one or both adrenal glands. It may cause fever, constitutional symptoms, elevated LDH, cytopenias, and adrenal insufficiency when both glands are affected.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral adrenal enlargement/infiltrative appearance on imaging
Possible hepatic and pulmonary extranodal involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal morning cortisol and ACTH without overt adrenal insufficiency
No hepatosplenomegaly on examination
Young age is unusual because primary adrenal lymphoma is generally seen in older adults

data.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species. Disseminated disease can involve the reticuloendothelial system, liver, bone marrow, lungs, and adrenal glands, causing fever, cytopenias, transaminitis, and adrenal enlargement.
symptoms_in_common: Possible multifocal hepatic lesions or hepatic infiltration
Nondiagnostic bone marrow biopsy can occur early
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported immunosuppression, travel exposure, cave exposure, bird or bat exposure, or endemic-area history
No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, which are common in disseminated infection
Lumbar pain is less characteristic unless related to enlarged adrenal glands

data.description: Systemic Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can involve the lungs, liver, bone marrow, and adrenal glands. Adrenal tuberculosis may produce bilateral enlargement and eventually adrenal insufficiency.
symptoms_in_common: Anemia and leukopenia progressing to pancytopenia
Bilateral adrenal enlargement or infiltrative adrenal lesions
Lumbar pain may occur with retroperitoneal or adrenal inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Very high LDH is more suggestive of aggressive lymphoma than tuberculosis
No cough, weight loss, night sweats, or known tuberculosis exposure reported
Normal cortisol and ACTH do not suggest established adrenal destruction or Addison disease
No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly reported

data.diagnosis: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis secondary to occult lymphoma or infection
data.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterized by persistent fever, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, high LDH, and often very high ferritin. It can be triggered by lymphoma, viral infection, fungal infection, or tuberculosis.
symptoms_in_common: Systemic illness without a clear diagnosis on initial bone marrow biopsy
Potential underlying hepatic, pulmonary, adrenal, or lymphomatous disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No ferritin, triglyceride, fibrinogen, soluble IL-2 receptor, or hemophagocytosis results are provided
No hepatosplenomegaly, which is frequently present
Adrenal masses/enlargement are not a direct hallmark of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

diagnoses.name: Non-Hodgkin T-cell lymphoma, natural killer (NK)/T-cell, nasal type
diagnoses.title: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type

data.description: A 23-year-old female presented with a complaint of intermittent dyspnea (New York Heart Association NYHA grade, II), which aggravates on exertion and mild chest pain. No past significant medical and surgical history was given by the patient. On clinical examination, bruit was heard on auscultation in the left mid-zone.

A congenital persistent communication between the descending thoracic aorta and the pulmonary artery, causing a left-to-right shunt, pulmonary arterial enlargement, and a characteristic continuous murmur or bruit.
symptoms_in_common: Bruit heard over the left mid-chest region
Young adult presentation with no prior major medical history
Imaging appearance of a prominent vascular communication between the aorta and left pulmonary artery
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical symptoms are clearly inconsistent; fever, productive cough, and acute pleuritic pain are not reported

data.diagnosis: Ductus arteriosus aneurysm associated with patent ductus arteriosus
data.description: An aneurysmal dilation of the ductus arteriosus or its aortic/pulmonary arterial connection. In adults it may cause chest discomfort, dyspnea, compression of adjacent structures, or turbulent flow producing a bruit.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging suggestion of a markedly enlarged abnormal vascular structure near the aortic arch and left pulmonary artery
symptoms_not_in_common: Hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve compression is not reported
Cough, dysphagia, hemoptysis, or signs of rupture are not reported

data.description: A rare congenital defect consisting of an abnormal direct communication between the ascending aorta and pulmonary artery, resulting in a left-to-right shunt and possible pulmonary overcirculation or pulmonary hypertension.
symptoms_in_common: Thoracic bruit due to turbulent high-flow shunting
Abnormal communication involving the aorta and pulmonary arterial circulation on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: This condition usually presents in infancy or childhood rather than at 23 years of age
No reported signs of severe heart failure, failure to thrive, cyanosis, or recurrent respiratory infections

data.description: An abnormal direct connection between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein that bypasses the capillary bed. Larger lesions can produce dyspnea, chest bruit, hypoxemia, and paradoxical embolic complications.
symptoms_in_common: Exertional worsening of shortness of breath
Abnormal prominent pulmonary vascular structures on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No cyanosis or documented hypoxemia
No hemoptysis
No neurologic complications such as stroke, transient ischemic attack, or brain abscess
The imaging pattern appears more consistent with a central aortopulmonary connection than a peripheral pulmonary artery-to-vein fistula

data.description: A 65-year-old man presented with bilateral leg swelling that had worsened over six weeks. He reported vague abdominal discomfort and tiredness. Physical examination revealed bilateral pitting edema up to the groin, without erythema, tenderness, or warmth. The patient was systemically well with normal heart sounds and clear chest examination. No palpable masses or lymphadenopathy were found in the abdomen. Laboratory testing showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 95 g/L; normal range 130-180), elevated C-reactive protein of 33.0 mg/L (normal range 0-5.0), and raised IgG4 level (3.55 g/L; normal range 0.08-1.4). Doppler ultrasound showed no deep vein thrombosis.

An immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder in which IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration causes a retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass, often encasing major vessels and ureters. Venous compression can cause marked bilateral leg edema.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive bilateral pitting leg edema extending to the groin
CT appearance of retroperitoneal soft-tissue/fibrotic tissue around major abdominal vessels
No deep vein thrombosis on Doppler ultrasound
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical symptoms are strongly discordant; urinary obstruction, flank pain, or hydronephrosis are common in some cases but were not reported

data.description: A fibroinflammatory condition characterized by plaque-like retroperitoneal tissue, commonly surrounding the aorta, iliac vessels, and ureters. It may obstruct venous or lymphatic drainage and produce lower-limb edema.
symptoms_in_common: Pitting edema without signs of cellulitis
Retroperitoneal infiltrative soft tissue on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Raised IgG4 level is more suggestive of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis than purely idiopathic disease
No reported ureteric obstruction, hydronephrosis, flank pain, or renal impairment

data.description: Lymphoma can present as retroperitoneal nodal or infiltrative soft-tissue disease that compresses the inferior vena cava, iliac veins, or lymphatic channels, resulting in bilateral lower-extremity edema.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral progressive leg edema due to possible venous or lymphatic obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable lymphadenopathy
No reported fever, drenching night sweats, or weight loss
Raised IgG4 level favors IgG4-related disease rather than lymphoma
No discrete bulky lymph-node masses were described

data.diagnosis: Malignant retroperitoneal mass causing inferior vena cava or iliac venous compression
data.description: Primary retroperitoneal tumors or metastatic malignancy may produce an infiltrative or mass-like retroperitoneal lesion that obstructs venous return from both legs, causing severe bilateral edema.
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable abdominal mass
No weight loss or other constitutional cancer symptoms reported
Elevated IgG4 level and fibroinflammatory imaging pattern are more consistent with IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis
No described invasive mass, organ metastases, or lymphadenopathy

data.description: A 19-year-old man with no previous medical problems presented with a six-day history of breathlessness and left-sided chest pain that had started acutely. On examination, his respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute with oxygen saturations of 95% on room air. The patient had no significant past medical history and no other baseline characteristics were reported.

Air in the pleural space causing partial or near-complete collapse of the lung, occurring without trauma or known underlying lung disease; it is most common in young men. The radiograph shows a large left pneumothorax with absent peripheral lung markings and a collapsed left lung medially.
symptoms_in_common: Mild tachypnea with respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute
Chest radiograph consistent with a large left pneumothorax
symptoms_not_in_common: Six-day duration of symptoms is longer than the very sudden presentation often described, although persistent symptoms can occur
Oxygen saturation of 95% on room air is relatively preserved despite the large radiographic pneumothorax

data.description: A large collection of air in the left pleural cavity causing substantial collapse of the left lung. This is a radiographic diagnosis and may be primary spontaneous, secondary spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic depending on the clinical cause.
symptoms_in_common: Chest radiograph showing marked left-sided hyperlucency with loss of peripheral vascular markings and a medially collapsed lung
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hypoxemia
No reported reduced blood pressure, cyanosis, or severe respiratory distress

data.description: A life-threatening form of pneumothorax in which pleural air accumulates under pressure, potentially shifting mediastinal structures and impairing venous return and cardiac output. It is primarily a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment when suspected.
symptoms_in_common: Large left pneumothorax on chest radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: Oxygen saturation is relatively preserved at 95% on room air
No reported hypotension
No reported tachycardia
No reported marked mediastinal shift or tracheal deviation
No reported signs of shock or severe hemodynamic compromise

data.description: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries, usually by thrombus, which can cause acute pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, and hypoxemia. However, it would not explain the visible large pleural air collection on this radiograph.
symptoms_not_in_common: Chest radiograph demonstrates a large left pneumothorax, which is not typical of pulmonary embolism
No reported risk factors for venous thromboembolism
No reported hypoxemia
Young age and absence of baseline medical problems make pulmonary embolism less likely

data.description: 28-year-old woman with no significant known medical history presented with fatigue and migratory joint pain/swelling. She first developed pain and swelling in the right foot and ankle causing difficulty walking, lasting several days and resolving, followed by pain in the knees and hips and swelling/pain in the right elbow. She reported intermittent low-grade fevers. On initial exam, she had fever to 38.3°C, diffuse joint tenderness without visible swelling or erythema, normal range of motion, and tachycardia. Five days later she returned with progressive dyspnea worse when supine, with persistent right knee pain and stiffness. Repeat exam showed tachycardia, elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral crackles, a holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, and a warm left knee with limited range of motion and severe pain on flexion. She was born in Brazil and later recalled childhood exertional dyspnea.

data.diagnosis: Acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic carditis and mitral regurgitation
data.description: An immune-mediated complication of group A streptococcal streptococcal infection, characterized by migratory polyarthritis, fever, and carditis. Valvulitis commonly affects the mitral valve and can cause severe mitral regurgitation and heart failure.
symptoms_in_common: Migratory joint pain and swelling involving ankle, knees, hips, elbow, and knee
New holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla, consistent with mitral regurgitation
Bilateral crackles consistent with pulmonary edema/heart failure
Young age and origin from a region where rheumatic fever remains more prevalent
Childhood exertional dyspnea suggesting possible prior rheumatic cardiac involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No recent sore throat or documented preceding streptococcal pharyngitis was reported
No erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, or chorea were described

data.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis with mitral valve regurgitation
data.description: Infection of the endocardial surface, usually involving a heart valve, that can produce fever, a new or worsening regurgitant murmur, systemic inflammation, embolic phenomena, and heart failure.
symptoms_in_common: Holosystolic murmur consistent with mitral valve regurgitation
Progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, and crackles consistent with heart failure
Arthralgias and joint pain can occur with subacute infective endocarditis
symptoms_not_in_common: The clearly migratory pattern of acute large-joint arthritis is more characteristic of acute rheumatic fever
No persistent high fever, chills, weight loss, embolic lesions, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, or Osler nodes were reported
No known intravenous drug use, prosthetic valve, or other stated endocarditis risk factor
No visible evidence of valvular vegetation was described

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory arthritis and possible valvular involvement
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that commonly affects young women and may cause fatigue, fever, inflammatory polyarthritis, serositis, and occasionally nonbacterial valvular disease such as Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
symptoms_in_common: Migratory or episodic joint pain and swelling
Possible cardiac valvular disease and heart failure symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: No malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, alopecia, Raynaud phenomenon, renal symptoms, cytopenias, or neurologic manifestations were described
Acute severe mitral regurgitation with classic migratory large-joint arthritis is more suggestive of rheumatic fever
No typical small-joint symmetric inflammatory arthritis pattern was reported

data.diagnosis: Disseminated gonococcal infection with gonococcal arthritis
data.description: Hematogenous spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae can cause fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and septic monoarthritis, most often affecting young sexually active adults.
symptoms_in_common: A warm, severely painful knee with limited range of motion, which could represent septic arthritis
symptoms_not_in_common: No rash, pustular skin lesions, tenosynovitis, genital symptoms, or sexual history suggesting gonococcal infection were reported
Mitral regurgitation murmur and signs of congestive heart failure are not typical features
Progressive orthopnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, and pulmonary crackles are not explained by uncomplicated gonococcal arthritis

data.description: A 56-year-old female patient presented with low-back and hip pain radiating down to her left leg for 12 months. She did not respond to initial management with conservative therapy of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

data.diagnosis: Lumbar facet joint synovial cyst (juxtafacet cyst) causing radiculopathy
data.description: A fluid-containing degenerative cyst arising near a lumbar facet joint that can extend into the spinal canal or neural foramen and compress a nerve root. The MRI appearance of a focal posterior-lateral epidural cystic lesion adjacent to a degenerated facet joint is most consistent with this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral pain radiating down the left leg
Symptoms compatible with lumbar nerve-root compression
Persistent symptoms despite conservative NSAID treatment
Age in the typical degenerative age range

data.diagnosis: Lumbar spinal stenosis due to degenerative facet arthropathy and ligamentous hypertrophy
data.description: Degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal or lateral recess caused by facet-joint osteoarthritis, disc degeneration, and thickening of supporting ligaments. It may produce nerve-root compression and radicular leg pain.
symptoms_in_common: Lack of adequate response to NSAIDs
symptoms_not_in_common: No exertional neurogenic claudication or relief with flexion is described
No bilateral leg symptoms are described

data.diagnosis: Lumbar disc herniation or degenerative disc disease with left-sided radiculopathy
data.description: Degeneration or protrusion of a lumbar intervertebral disc may narrow the lateral recess or neural foramen and irritate or compress a lumbar nerve root, producing sciatica-like pain.
symptoms_not_in_common: The imaging appearance favors a posterior facet-adjacent cystic lesion rather than an isolated disc herniation
No acute onset after lifting or trauma is reported
No neurologic weakness, sensory loss, or reflex changes are reported

data.description: A benign nerve-sheath tumor arising from a spinal nerve root that can produce a focal epidural mass and slowly progressive radicular pain. It is a differential consideration for an enhancing epidural lesion, although the apparent facet-adjacent cystic morphology is less typical.
symptoms_not_in_common: No progressive neurologic deficit is reported
No sensory disturbance, weakness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction is described
Imaging appearance is more suggestive of a juxtafacet cyst than a solid nerve-sheath tumor

data.description: A 57-year-old male patient presented with a three-month history of fatigue, recurrent sore throats, and a persistent 'cold sore.' The patient had no relevant medical history, drank little alcohol, and was a non-smoker.
HIV infection can impair cellular immunity, causing persistent or unusually severe herpes simplex lesions, recurrent infections, fatigue, and generalized or cervical lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent crusted ulcerative cold sore at the lip
Possible cervical or submandibular lymph node enlargement shown in the image
symptoms_not_in_common: No other systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss, night sweats, or diarrhea were reported

data.diagnosis: Chronic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection with possible immunosuppression
data.description: HSV-1 commonly causes recurrent painful vesicles and crusted ulcers at the lip margin. Persistence for months or unusually large ulceration raises concern for underlying immune dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent lesion described as a cold sore
Crusted ulcerative lesion at the lip commissure
Recurrent sore throats may accompany recurrent oral HSV infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Fatigue is not usually caused by uncomplicated recurrent herpes labialis
Possible neck lymph node enlargement is less typical for a simple chronic cold sore
Persistence for three months is atypical in an immunocompetent person

data.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip/oral cavity
data.description: Squamous cell carcinoma can present as a persistent nonhealing ulcer or crusted lesion on the lip and may spread to submandibular or cervical lymph nodes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent sore throats are not a typical primary feature
Fatigue is nonspecific and is not usually an early isolated symptom
The patient is a non-smoker and drinks little alcohol, reducing but not eliminating risk

data.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma may cause fatigue, recurrent infections from immune dysfunction, and painless cervical lymphadenopathy; immunosuppression can also predispose to persistent HSV lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cervical or submandibular lymph node enlargement
Persistent herpes-like lesion may occur in the setting of immune dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: A localized lip ulcer is not a typical direct manifestation of lymphoma
No reported fever, drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or widespread lymph node enlargement

data.diagnosis: Hematologic malignancy causing immunosuppression, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia
data.description: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and related blood cancers can present with fatigue, recurrent upper-respiratory infections, lymphadenopathy, and prolonged mucocutaneous herpesvirus infections.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent cold sore suggesting impaired immune control of HSV
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported easy bruising, bleeding, pallor, recurrent severe bacterial infections, or abdominal fullness
A lip ulcer is not usually a direct manifestation of leukemia

diagnoses.name: Perioral lesion with plasma cell rich infiltrate
diagnoses.title: Plasma cell neoplasms

data.description: 28-year-old male patient admitted on November 27, 2013, complaining of diarrhea (loose stool, three to five times per day) for over 10 years and hematochezia for about 1 month. Had been diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia 5 months after birth, with hemoglobin level remaining 70-80 g/L (normal range 110-150 g/L) for most of the time. On admission, albumin level was 26 g/L (normal range 35-52 g/L). Liver and renal function were otherwise normal. Patient reported recurrent arthralgia in the knee and ankle joints.

A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, commonly causing transmural bowel inflammation, ulceration, strictures, anemia, malnutrition, and extraintestinal joint manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic diarrhea for more than 10 years
Imaging/endoscopic findings suggestive of bowel wall inflammation, ulceration, and possible narrowing
symptoms_not_in_common: Iron deficiency anemia diagnosed at 5 months of age is unusually early for typical Crohn disease

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease limited primarily to the colon and rectum, producing continuous mucosal inflammation, bloody diarrhea, anemia, protein loss, and sometimes peripheral arthritis.
symptoms_in_common: Endoscopic evidence of colonic mucosal inflammation and ulceration
symptoms_not_in_common: Possible small-bowel involvement on imaging is less typical
Iron deficiency anemia beginning in infancy is unusual
Long-standing diarrhea without earlier prominent rectal bleeding is less typical

data.description: An inherited hamartomatous polyposis syndrome characterized by gastrointestinal polyps, recurrent bleeding and anemia, abdominal symptoms, and a risk of bowel intussusception and malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: Possible bowel obstruction or intussusception-related changes on abdominal imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent knee and ankle arthralgia is not typical
Marked hypoalbuminemia is less typical unless there is severe protein-losing enteropathy
No mucocutaneous pigmentation is described

data.description: A hereditary hamartomatous polyposis disorder causing multiple gastrointestinal juvenile polyps, rectal bleeding, chronic anemia, diarrhea, and occasionally protein-losing enteropathy.
symptoms_in_common: Iron deficiency anemia beginning early in life
Hypoalbuminemia consistent with intestinal protein loss
Endoscopic appearance potentially compatible with multiple gastrointestinal polyps
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent knee and ankle arthralgia is not a typical manifestation
Inflammatory-appearing bowel ulceration or transmural bowel disease would be less typical

data.diagnosis: Common variable immunodeficiency or another primary immunodeficiency with nodular lymphoid hyperplasia
data.description: Primary immune disorders can cause chronic infectious or inflammatory diarrhea, nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the bowel, malabsorption, protein loss, anemia, and occasionally inflammatory bowel disease-like colitis.
symptoms_in_common: Very early onset iron deficiency anemia
Possible nodular or polypoid intestinal lesions
Hematochezia can occur with inflammatory colitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent knee and ankle arthralgia is less characteristic
No recurrent respiratory infections, unusual infections, or other immunodeficiency features are reported

data.description: A 65-year-old male retired farmer presented with an inability to fully straighten the ring finger and little finger of his right hand, which had progressed over the past two years. He had recently noticed a 'rope like' swelling in his palm with no history of trauma. His medical history was unremarkable except for smoking cessation 10 years earlier with a 90 pack-year history. His father had a similar deformity. On examination, he had palpable cords to his middle, ring, and little fingers with palpable nodules on the volar aspect of all proximal phalanges, causing flexion contractures of the proximal interphalangeal joints. The cord and nodules in the ring finger were adherent to the overlying skin.
A benign fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia that produces nodules and cords, progressively causing flexion contractures, most often involving the ring and little fingers.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive inability to fully straighten the ring and little fingers over two years
Palpable rope-like cords in the palm
Flexion contractures of the proximal interphalangeal joints
Predominant involvement of the middle, ring, and little fingers
Nodules and cords adherent to the overlying skin
Positive family history in his father

data.description: A condition in which thickening of the flexor tendon or A1 pulley causes painful catching, locking, or difficulty extending an affected finger.
symptoms_in_common: Palmar thickening or nodule near the flexor tendon region
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple palpable cords extending to the middle, ring, and little fingers
Fixed progressive proximal interphalangeal flexion contractures
Skin-adherent palmar cords and nodules
No reported painful clicking, catching, or locking
Strong familial history of a similar hand deformity

data.diagnosis: Flexor tendon contracture or post-traumatic scar contracture
data.description: Shortening or scarring of flexor tendons and surrounding soft tissues can produce persistent finger flexion deformities, usually after trauma, surgery, infection, or immobilization.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to fully extend the fingers
Flexion contractures affecting proximal interphalangeal joints
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of hand trauma, surgery, infection, or prolonged immobilization
Palpable rope-like palmar fascial cords
Multiple volar nodules on the proximal phalanges
Skin adherence of the ring-finger cord and nodules
Family history of a similar deformity
Characteristic ring and little finger distribution

data.description: A congenital or developmental condition characterized by flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal joint, commonly affecting the little finger.
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset at age 63 with progressive symptoms over two years
Palmar rope-like cords
Palpable nodules in the palm and volar proximal phalanges
Involvement of the middle and ring fingers in addition to the little finger
Skin-adherent cord
Family history specifically resembling an acquired palmar fibromatosis deformity

data.description: 57-year-old man with 8 years of HIV infection and a 10-year history of bilateral inguinal hernias presented with 3 weeks of worsening left inguinal pain and enlargement of the hernia. He had 3 months of increasing pain with hernia bulging, and over the prior 3 weeks developed intermittent subjective fevers, night sweats, and hard, tender lumps adjacent to the hernia; his temperature reached 38.1°C the night before presentation. He had well-controlled HIV on antiretroviral therapy (CD4 count 250/mm³, undetectable viral load). Past history included Kaposi sarcoma, molluscum contagiosum, anal dysplasia, pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection, pneumocystis pneumonia, thrush, preseptal cellulitis, and cryptosporidium-related diarrhea. On examination, he was afebrile with easily reducible bilateral inguinal hernias and bulky, slightly tender left inguinal lymphadenopathy with three large nodes up to 3 cm.

Lymph-node involvement by Treponema pallidum, often occurring in secondary syphilis. It can cause prominent inguinal lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms, follicular hyperplasia, plasmacytosis, and demonstrable spirochetes on immunohistochemical staining.
symptoms_in_common: HIV infection, which increases risk of syphilis coinfection
Subacute course over several weeks to months
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked tenderness of the lymph nodes, since syphilitic nodes are often painless or only mildly tender
Painful enlarging inguinal hernia, which is unrelated to syphilitic lymphadenitis
Bilateral long-standing inguinal hernias

data.description: A sexually transmitted Chlamydia trachomatis infection, usually caused by serovars L1-L3, that can produce painful unilateral inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: HIV infection as a risk factor for sexually transmitted infections
symptoms_not_in_common: Three months of pain attributed to hernia bulging
Easily reducible bilateral inguinal hernias
No reported genital ulcer, proctitis, rectal pain, or purulent nodal drainage
Pathology demonstrating spirochetes would not be expected

data.description: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, can occur in people with HIV and may present with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes and constitutional symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Tender lymph nodes, as lymphoma nodes are often painless
Painful reducible inguinal hernia, which does not result from lymphoma
Histologic evidence of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia and spirochetes rather than a clonal malignant lymphoid proliferation

data.description: Disseminated or localized MAC infection can cause fever, night sweats, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with advanced HIV-related immunosuppression.
symptoms_in_common: Prior pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Well-controlled HIV infection with an undetectable viral load and CD4 count of 250 cells/mm3, which makes disseminated MAC less typical
Localized unilateral bulky inguinal adenopathy without reported disseminated systemic illness
Painful enlarging reducible hernia
Spirochetes on lymph-node staining would not be expected

diagnoses.name: Necrotizing lymphadenitis
diagnoses.title: Histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis of Kikuchi and Fujimoto

data.description: A 16-year-old girl presented with acute left shoulder pain, left-sided chest pain, and shortness of breath. She had a 4-month history of intermittent left shoulder and left-sided chest pain following a dance recital, which had been treated with analgesia and physiotherapy. She denied fever, cough, orthopnea, weight loss, and appetite change. Physical examination revealed tenderness at the location of the left fifth rib and reduced left chest expansion.

data.diagnosis: Solitary osseous Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma) of the rib
data.description: A localized form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects bone in children and adolescents. Rib lesions can cause focal pain, lytic bone destruction, chest-wall inflammation, and reactive pleural effusion.
symptoms_in_common: Several months of localized left chest and shoulder pain
Focal tenderness over the left fifth rib
Acute worsening with shortness of breath
Imaging appearance consistent with a rib/chest-wall lesion and associated left pleural fluid
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain beginning after a dance recital is not a typical causal trigger
Acute dyspnea is less common in a small isolated bone lesion unless there is a significant pleural reaction or effusion

data.diagnosis: Ewing sarcoma of the rib (chest-wall Ewing sarcoma/Askin tumor)
data.description: An aggressive malignant small round cell tumor of bone and soft tissue that often occurs in adolescents. Rib involvement may produce chest pain, a chest-wall mass, pleural effusion, and respiratory symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent localized chest and shoulder pain
Shortness of breath and reduced left chest expansion
Possible pleural effusion or chest-wall involvement on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No weight loss
No appetite change
No reported palpable chest-wall mass

data.description: Infection of a rib, usually bacterial and less commonly tuberculous, which can cause focal bone pain, tenderness, adjacent soft-tissue inflammation, and reactive pleural effusion.
symptoms_in_common: Localized pain over the left fifth rib
Reduced chest expansion and shortness of breath if pleural inflammation or effusion is present
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No cough
No reported preceding infection
No constitutional symptoms such as weight loss or appetite change

data.diagnosis: Rib stress fracture or occult traumatic rib fracture with reactive pleural effusion
data.description: Repetitive mechanical loading, such as intense dance activity, can cause a stress fracture of a rib. Rib fractures produce focal pain and tenderness and may rarely be associated with pleural irritation, hemothorax, or effusion.
symptoms_in_common: Pain began after a dance recital
Localized tenderness at the fifth rib
Shoulder pain can be referred from chest-wall injury
Shortness of breath and reduced chest expansion can occur when pain limits deep inspiration or when pleural fluid is present
symptoms_not_in_common: Four months of persistent intermittent symptoms is longer than expected for an uncomplicated fracture
A substantial pleural effusion or destructive rib lesion would be unusual for a simple stress fracture
No clear direct chest trauma was reported

data.diagnosis: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) / chronic nonbacterial osteitis involving a rib
data.description: A sterile autoinflammatory bone disorder affecting children and adolescents, particularly girls. It can involve the clavicle, spine, and ribs, causing recurrent focal bone pain and tenderness.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic intermittent focal bone and chest-wall pain
Absence of fever and other infectious symptoms
Absence of weight loss or appetite change
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute shortness of breath is not typical
Pleural effusion and reduced chest expansion are uncommon
Only one symptomatic bone site is described, whereas CRMO often involves multiple sites

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

data.description: A 66-year-old man presented with a 4 to 5-month history of fever, chills, drenching night sweats, and unintentional 35-kg weight loss. He had previously undergone work-up for fever of unknown origin including evaluation for infectious causes such as tuberculosis, typhoid, and brucellosis, but these were not revealing. On physical examination, his spleen was palpable but no adenopathy was detected. Blood tests revealed anemia with hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL (normal 13.0-18.0 g/dL), microcytosis with mean corpuscular volume of 75 fl (normal 80.0-94.0 fl), normal platelet count of 354,000/μL, and elevated international normalized ratio of 1.30 (normal 0.85-1.20). His serum ferritin level was significantly elevated at 1,796.0 ng/mL (normal 25-310 ng/mL).

A rare extranodal presentation of classical Hodgkin lymphoma confined predominantly to the spleen, characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells that are typically CD30-positive and associated with systemic inflammatory symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Splenomegaly with a splenic mass on imaging
Elevated ferritin as an inflammatory marker
Cytology showing large atypical cells compatible with Reed-Sternberg-type cells
Immunostaining pattern suggestive of CD30-positive atypical large cells
Absence of peripheral adenopathy can occur in primary splenic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Microcytic anemia is not specifically characteristic of Hodgkin lymphoma
Normal platelet count despite splenomegaly is less suggestive of advanced hypersplenism
Mildly elevated INR is not a typical defining feature

data.description: A mature T-cell lymphoma composed of large pleomorphic CD30-positive malignant cells. ALK-negative disease more often affects older adults and may present with systemic symptoms and extranodal involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Fever, chills, and drenching night sweats
Strong CD30-type immunostaining of atypical cells
symptoms_not_in_common: No lymphadenopathy is less typical because many patients have nodal disease
Isolated splenic presentation is uncommon
Microcytosis is not a usual lymphoma-specific finding
Elevated INR is not a typical presentation

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the spleen
data.description: An aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma that can arise primarily in the spleen or involve it secondarily, often causing a splenic mass, constitutional symptoms, and anemia.
symptoms_in_common: Constitutional B symptoms including fever, night sweats, and major weight loss
Elevated ferritin due to inflammation or tumor burden
Large atypical lymphoid cells may be seen on cytology
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent CD30-positive/Reed-Sternberg-like morphology is more characteristic of classical Hodgkin lymphoma or anaplastic large cell lymphoma
No adenopathy is less common in disseminated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Microcytic anemia is not a typical defining feature
Mild INR elevation is not typical

data.description: Tuberculosis can rarely involve the spleen, causing fever of unknown origin, weight loss, splenomegaly, focal splenic lesions, and elevated inflammatory markers; it is more common in immunocompromised patients or disseminated infection.
symptoms_in_common: Presentation as fever of unknown origin
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior tuberculosis evaluation was unrevealing
Large atypical CD30-positive cells on cytology are not typical of tuberculosis
No reported granulomas or acid-fast organisms
No pulmonary or lymph-node findings were described

data.description: A systemic protozoal infection that can cause prolonged fever, weight loss, marked splenomegaly, anemia, and hyperferritinemia. Diagnosis is usually made by finding intracellular amastigotes in splenic or bone marrow samples.
symptoms_in_common: Fever of unknown origin after common infectious investigations
symptoms_not_in_common: A discrete splenic mass is less typical than diffuse splenomegaly
Normal platelet count is less typical because thrombocytopenia is common
Cytology showing large atypical CD30-positive cells is not consistent with leishmaniasis
No pancytopenia was reported

diagnoses.name: Splenic involvement
diagnoses.title: Fibrosis of spleen[Schistosomiasis involving the skin]

data.description: 52-year-old man presented with acute palpitations and chest pressure. Two days earlier, he developed epigastric burning, fatigue, weakness, and vomiting, with partial relief from antacids. He denied fever, chills, or other localizing symptoms. Past history included hypertension, benign prostatic hypertrophy with obstructive nephropathy, chronic renal insufficiency requiring dialysis until a living-related renal transplant 1 year earlier, and hyperparathyroidism with bilateral cataract surgery. On presentation, heart rate was 200 bpm with atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response; after cardioversion, pulse was 53 bpm. Exam showed a diffuse, laterally displaced apical impulse, prominent second heart sound, and audible fourth heart sound, without murmurs or jugular venous distention. Labs showed creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, troponin T 1.04 ng/mL, urinalysis with 2+ proteinuria, and markedly reduced leukocyte α-galactosidase activity.

An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficient alpha-galactosidase A activity, resulting in globotriaosylceramide accumulation. It commonly causes progressive renal disease, proteinuria, concentric left-ventricular hypertrophy, conduction abnormalities, atrial arrhythmias, and myocardial fibrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic renal insufficiency progressing to dialysis and renal transplantation
Left-ventricular hypertrophy suggested by displaced apical impulse and ECG voltage abnormalities
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Chest pressure with elevated troponin, compatible with Fabry-related microvascular ischemia or myocardial injury
Gastrointestinal symptoms including epigastric burning and vomiting
History of bilateral cataract surgery, which can occur with Fabry-related ocular involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset palpitations at 200 bpm is a complication rather than a classic initial symptom
No reported angiokeratomas
No reported neuropathic burning pain in the hands or feet
No reported hypohidrosis or heat intolerance

data.description: Cardiac manifestation of Fabry disease characterized by glycosphingolipid deposition in cardiomyocytes and conduction tissue, producing concentric ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, atrial enlargement, arrhythmias, and myocardial ischemia or fibrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse and laterally displaced apical impulse, suggesting cardiac enlargement or hypertrophy
Fourth heart sound, consistent with a stiff hypertrophied ventricle and diastolic dysfunction
ECG features compatible with left-ventricular hypertrophy and repolarization abnormalities
Bradycardia after cardioversion, suggesting conduction-system disease
Echocardiographic appearance consistent with ventricular hypertrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Proteinuria and prior renal failure are systemic Fabry manifestations rather than isolated cardiac disease
Vomiting and epigastric burning are not primary manifestations of cardiomyopathy
No overt congestive-heart-failure findings such as jugular venous distention or pulmonary edema

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
data.description: Acute myocardial injury due to ischemia, usually from coronary atherosclerotic plaque rupture or supply-demand mismatch. It can present with chest pressure, gastrointestinal symptoms, arrhythmia, and elevated cardiac troponin.
symptoms_in_common: Epigastric burning that may represent an anginal equivalent
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, which can accompany or precipitate myocardial ischemia
Hypertension as a cardiovascular risk factor
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly reduced leukocyte alpha-galactosidase activity is not explained by acute coronary syndrome
Longstanding renal failure with proteinuria and renal transplantation suggests an underlying systemic disorder
Marked ventricular hypertrophy and conduction abnormalities are more suggestive of infiltrative/storage cardiomyopathy
No clear ischemic ECG pattern or focal wall-motion abnormality is provided
No fever or infectious symptoms, though these are not required for acute coronary syndrome

data.diagnosis: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or severe hypertensive left-ventricular hypertrophy
data.description: A condition with abnormal thickening of the left ventricular wall, caused either by genetic sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or chronic pressure overload from hypertension. It may produce diastolic dysfunction, an S4, chest pain, and atrial arrhythmias.
symptoms_in_common: ECG findings suggestive of left-ventricular hypertrophy with repolarization changes
Elevated troponin can occur with hypertrophy-related demand ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase activity strongly favors Fabry disease rather than primary hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or hypertension alone
Severe renal disease with proteinuria and prior renal transplantation is not typical of isolated hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Gastrointestinal symptoms and cataracts are not typical manifestations
No murmur suggestive of dynamic left-ventricular outflow obstruction is described

data.description: Male infant, 22 hours old, admitted for repeated right-sided limb clonic seizures for 16 hours. Born at 40+6 weeks by cesarean section after fetal heart monitoring showed frequent variable decelerations; amniotic fluid was reduced and grade I turbid. Apgar scores were 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes; birth weight 3380 g. Seizures began 6 hours after birth, occurred 4 times, were not associated with consciousness disturbance or cyanosis, and resolved spontaneously. On admission, the infant was alert with good response; temperature 36.7°C, pulse 125/min, respiration 46/min, BP 74/47 mmHg, weight 3290 g, head circumference 36 cm. Exam showed normal skin color, flat anterior fontanelle, equal reactive pupils, coarse breath sounds without rales, normal heart sounds, soft abdomen without masses, normal limb tone and movement, and normal primitive reflexes.

data.diagnosis: Neonatal arterial ischemic stroke (left middle cerebral artery territory infarction)
data.description: An acute focal cerebral infarction caused by arterial occlusion, most commonly involving the middle cerebral artery in term neonates. MRI diffusion restriction in a unilateral cortical-subcortical distribution supports this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Focal clonic seizures involving the right limbs
Seizure onset within the first day of life
Term infant with otherwise relatively normal initial examination
No cyanosis or major cardiorespiratory instability during seizures
Imaging appearance consistent with an acute unilateral cerebral ischemic lesion
Perinatal fetal heart rate decelerations, which may be associated with perinatal vascular risk
symptoms_not_in_common: No persistent focal weakness or abnormal tone was identified on the initial examination
No altered consciousness was reported
Apgar scores were normal and there was no obvious severe birth depression

data.description: Brain injury from impaired oxygen delivery and/or cerebral perfusion around birth. HIE commonly produces encephalopathy, seizures, and bilateral or watershed-pattern brain abnormalities rather than a single focal arterial-territory lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Neonatal seizures beginning shortly after birth
Frequent variable fetal heart rate decelerations before delivery
Reduced amniotic fluid and turbid amniotic fluid, suggesting possible perinatal stress
Possible ischemic signal abnormality on brain MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal Apgar scores at 1, 5, and 10 minutes
Alert mental status and good responsiveness
Normal tone, primitive reflexes, and limb movement
No respiratory depression, cyanosis, or need for resuscitation described
Seizures were focal to the right side rather than generalized or multifocal
Imaging appears focal and unilateral rather than the more typical diffuse or bilateral HIE pattern

data.description: Bleeding within the brain or intracranial spaces can provoke seizures in newborns. Causes include birth trauma, coagulation disorders, vascular malformations, or hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Seizures during the first day of life
Focal right-sided clonic movements can occur with a unilateral cerebral lesion
Cesarean delivery following fetal distress may be associated with complicated perinatal events
symptoms_not_in_common: No bulging fontanelle or rapidly increasing head circumference
No lethargy, coma, apnea, pallor, or hemodynamic instability
No anemia, bleeding tendency, or traumatic delivery findings reported
The described MRI diffusion-restriction pattern is more suggestive of acute ischemic infarction than primary hemorrhage

data.description: 19-year-old woman with 3 weeks of right shoulder and right flank pain, followed 2 weeks later by exertional dyspnea and nonproductive cough that progressively worsened over 8 days, causing severe dyspnea with walking and wheelchair dependence. On presentation she had respiratory failure with ill appearance, increased work of breathing, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and a cardiac murmur. She also reported intermittent back pain for 6 months, visible chest pulsations and labored breathing during sleep for 2 weeks, and two episodes of diarrhea during the cruise. History included anxiety, anemia, asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection 2 months earlier, and dental cleaning 5 weeks earlier.

data.diagnosis: Infective aortic-valve endocarditis complicated by aortic root abscess and aorto-left atrial fistula
data.description: Infection of the aortic valve can destroy valve tissue and extend into the aortic root, forming an abscess or pseudoaneurysm that may rupture into an adjacent cardiac chamber. Severe aortic regurgitation and abnormal aorta-to-left-atrium flow can cause acute heart failure and respiratory failure.
symptoms_in_common: Visible chest pulsations and labored breathing during sleep
Right shoulder and back pain, which may be referred pain from aortic or cardiac inflammation
Recent dental cleaning, a potential source of transient bacteremia
Echocardiographic appearance of abnormal aortic-valve/aortic-root tissue and turbulent abnormal flow from the aorta toward the left atrium
Findings consistent with severe aortic regurgitation and heart failure
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported fever
No reported chills or night sweats
No reported peripheral stigmata of endocarditis such as petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, or painful finger lesions
Two brief episodes of diarrhea are not typical manifestations of endocarditis

data.diagnosis: Acute severe aortic regurgitation due to destructive aortic-valve disease
data.description: Acute severe leakage of the aortic valve causes a sudden volume overload of the left ventricle and left atrium, rapidly producing pulmonary edema, low forward cardiac output, tachycardia, and cardiogenic respiratory failure. In this case, valve destruction from infection or aortic-root pathology would be a likely cause.
symptoms_in_common: Nonproductive cough consistent with pulmonary congestion
Echocardiographic evidence of marked turbulent flow associated with the aortic valve/aortic root
symptoms_not_in_common: Right shoulder and flank pain are not typical primary manifestations
Six months of intermittent back pain is not typical of isolated acute aortic regurgitation
Diarrhea is unrelated
Recent asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection is not a typical direct cause

data.diagnosis: Infected aortic pseudoaneurysm (mycotic aneurysm) with systemic arterial septic embolic disease
data.description: A bacterial infection involving the aortic wall or aortic root may produce pseudoaneurysms, dissection-like defects, rupture, and embolic vascular lesions. Multifocal abnormal arterial findings on CT can occur when endocarditis or bacteremia seeds arterial walls.
symptoms_in_common: Right shoulder, flank, and back pain, which may reflect aortic inflammation or embolic vascular injury
Progressive shortness of breath from associated valvular destruction and heart failure
Cardiac murmur suggesting associated valve involvement
CT findings concerning for multifocal arterial/aortic abnormalities
Recent dental procedure as a possible bacteremia source
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented fever or bacteremia in the provided history
No reported focal neurologic deficit or limb ischemia
Diarrhea is not a typical feature unless it represented the original infectious exposure
Asymptomatic prior COVID-19 infection does not specifically support this diagnosis

data.diagnosis: Aortic dissection or intramural aortic injury with secondary severe aortic regurgitation
data.description: A tear or injury involving the ascending aorta and aortic root can disrupt aortic-valve support, cause acute aortic regurgitation, and lead to heart failure. Extension into thoracic or abdominal aortic segments may cause back, flank, or shoulder pain and abnormal CT angiographic findings.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive dyspnea and respiratory failure if severe aortic regurgitation develops
Aortic and branch-vessel abnormalities on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: The pain course was subacute over several weeks rather than classic abrupt tearing chest pain
No reported severe central chest pain
Recent dental cleaning would not be expected to precipitate dissection
Diarrhea is unrelated

data.diagnosis: Large-vessel vasculitis or inflammatory aortitis, such as Takayasu arteritis
data.description: Inflammatory disease of the aorta and its major branches can cause arterial wall thickening, stenosis, aneurysm formation, and aortic regurgitation. Takayasu arteritis primarily affects young women and may involve the thoracic and abdominal aorta.
symptoms_in_common: Back, shoulder, and flank pain that could reflect aortic inflammation
Aortic regurgitation and cardiac murmur can occur with aortic-root involvement
Dyspnea and heart-failure symptoms can occur if severe aortic regurgitation develops
symptoms_not_in_common: Rapid progression to severe respiratory failure over days is less typical without a major complication
No reported constitutional symptoms such as prolonged fever, weight loss, or fatigue
No reported pulse asymmetry, limb claudication, bruits, or blood-pressure discrepancy
Recent dental cleaning is not relevant to inflammatory aortitis
Echo findings suggesting a destructive aortic-root communication favor infection over primary vasculitis

data.description: 56-year-old man with a 7-day history of worsening epigastric pain with nausea and belching. Past history: splenectomy after trauma, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, and Bell’s palsy; prior abdominal CT (2007) showed multiple abdominal nodules consistent with splenunculi. He had started orlistat for weight loss about 10 days before symptom onset. On examination, he was haemodynamically stable, temperature 37.5°C, with epigastric and left iliac fossa tenderness; rectal examination was negative. Blood tests showed mild neutrophilia and elevated CRP, with normal liver, renal, amylase, and lipase results. Symptoms persisted and inflammatory markers worsened despite analgesia and high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy.

data.diagnosis: Torsion with infarction of an accessory spleen (torsed splenunculus)
data.description: An accessory spleen can twist around its vascular pedicle, causing venous obstruction, ischemia, and infarction. This can produce acute abdominal pain and inflammatory changes on CT, particularly in a patient with known splenunculi after splenectomy.
symptoms_in_common: Known multiple abdominal splenunculi after splenectomy
CT appearance of a focal inflammatory lesion with adjacent mesenteric inflammatory change
symptoms_not_in_common: Belching
Recent initiation of orlistat

data.diagnosis: Infarction of ectopic splenic tissue (splenosis or accessory spleen infarction without complete torsion)
data.description: Ectopic splenic tissue after traumatic splenectomy may undergo spontaneous vascular compromise or infarction, producing localized abdominal pain and an inflammatory response.
symptoms_in_common: Previously documented multiple intra-abdominal splenic nodules
symptoms_not_in_common: Belching
Pain predominantly described as epigastric rather than left upper abdominal
Recent orlistat use

data.description: Mesenteric panniculitis is inflammation of mesenteric fat that can cause abdominal pain, nausea, raised inflammatory markers, and CT evidence of increased mesenteric attenuation or a focal inflammatory mesenteric mass.
symptoms_in_common: CT evidence of mesenteric inflammatory change
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt progression over only 7 days is less typical
Known splenunculi provide a more specific alternative explanation
Belching
Recent initiation of orlistat

data.diagnosis: Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastritis
data.description: Inflammation or ulceration of the stomach or duodenum commonly causes epigastric pain, nausea, dyspeptic symptoms, and belching. It may not respond immediately to proton pump inhibitor treatment if another process is present or if complications develop.
symptoms_not_in_common: Left iliac fossa tenderness
Rising CRP and neutrophilia are not typical in uncomplicated disease
Persistent worsening symptoms despite high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy
CT mesenteric inflammatory abnormality
Known intra-abdominal splenunculi

data.description: A 12-year-old female presented to the Emergency Department with a 48-hour history of abdominal pain localised in the hypogastrium, which had progressively worsened in the last few hours. The patient mentioned previous episodes of less intense abdominal pain. Considering the clinical suspicion of acute appendicitis, an abdominal ultrasound was requested.

Accumulation of menstrual blood within the vagina caused by congenital obstruction at the hymen. Ultrasound typically shows a large midline pelvic cystic structure with homogeneous low-level internal echoes.
symptoms_in_common: Previous recurrent episodes of less intense abdominal pain
Large midline pelvic fluid-containing structure with internal echoes on ultrasound

data.diagnosis: Hematometrocolpos from a transverse vaginal septum
data.description: Congenital vaginal obstruction from a transverse septum may cause retained menstrual blood in the vagina and uterus, producing cyclic or progressively worsening pelvic pain and a pelvic mass.
symptoms_in_common: Previous episodes of abdominal pain suggesting recurrent or cyclic symptoms
Pelvic cystic distension with echogenic fluid compatible with retained blood
symptoms_not_in_common: No menstrual history, primary amenorrhea, or cyclic timing of pain was provided

data.description: Distension of the vagina, with or without uterine distension, by retained fluid due to congenital genital outflow obstruction. Contents may appear simple or mildly echogenic on ultrasound.
symptoms_in_common: Large pelvic fluid-filled structure on ultrasound
symptoms_not_in_common: The internal echoes suggest blood products rather than simple fluid
No urinary retention, constipation, or vaginal discharge was reported

data.diagnosis: Obstructed hemivagina and ipsilateral renal anomaly (OHVIRA syndrome)
data.description: A congenital Müllerian anomaly, usually involving uterine didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina, leading to hematocolpos and recurrent pelvic pain after menstruation begins; it is often associated with a same-side renal anomaly.
symptoms_in_common: Adolescent female with recurrent pelvic pain
Ultrasound appearance potentially compatible with retained blood in an obstructed vaginal cavity
symptoms_not_in_common: No uterine duplication, obstructed hemivagina, or renal anomaly was stated
No menstrual history was provided

data.description: Inflammation of the appendix causing acute abdominal pain, usually beginning centrally and later localizing to the right lower quadrant, often with nausea, vomiting, fever, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Acute progressive abdominal pain over 48 hours
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is localized to the hypogastrium rather than the typical right lower quadrant
Previous recurrent episodes of abdominal pain are less typical
Ultrasound demonstrates a large pelvic cystic structure rather than an inflamed appendix
No fever, nausea, vomiting, or anorexia was reported

data.description: An 8-year-old Korean boy with severe global developmental delay and multiple exostoses. Developmental delay was first noted at 3 months of age with incomplete eye contact and poor head control. He had hypotonia, ptosis, nystagmus, and microcephaly. By age 6 years, he had marked growth retardation and facial features including sparse eyebrows, prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nare, down-turned mouth, and high-arched palate; he remained unable to sit or walk independently. At age 5 years, testing showed severe intellectual disability. Multiple exostoses were first observed at age 6 years as protrusions of the right wrist and knee. Chromosome analysis showed a normal 46,XY karyotype.

A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome caused by loss of material from chromosome 11p11.2, typically including EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It is characterized by multiple exostoses, parietal foramina or skull defects, developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, craniofacial differences, and growth impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple exostoses involving the wrist, knee, and other long bones
Severe global developmental delay and severe intellectual disability
Early hypotonia and poor head control
Craniofacial differences including sparse eyebrows, prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nares, down-turned mouth, and high-arched palate
Skull imaging findings consistent with enlarged parietal foramina or ossification defects
Chromosomal microarray finding involving EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A
symptoms_not_in_common: None; the overall clinical, radiographic, and genomic findings are highly characteristic

data.description: An autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, most often caused by pathogenic variants in EXT1 or EXT2, characterized by multiple cartilage-capped bony outgrowths near the growth plates of long bones.
symptoms_in_common: Exostoses near the wrist and knee
Growth retardation or short stature can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe global developmental delay
Severe intellectual disability
Early hypotonia and poor head control
Microcephaly
Ptosis and nystagmus
Characteristic craniofacial abnormalities
Parietal skull ossification defects/enlarged parietal foramina
Deletion involving ALX4 and PHF21A in addition to EXT2

data.diagnosis: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia due to ALX4-related parietal foramina
data.description: ALX4-related disorders can cause enlarged parietal foramina and other calvarial ossification defects, sometimes accompanied by craniofacial differences. Isolated ALX4-related disease does not usually cause multiple exostoses or profound neurodevelopmental impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Skull imaging findings consistent with parietal foramina or delayed calvarial ossification
Craniofacial differences including prominent nasal bridge and hypoplastic nares
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple exostoses
Severe global developmental delay
Severe intellectual disability
Marked hypotonia
Profound inability to sit or walk independently
Ptosis and nystagmus
Growth retardation
Deletion involving EXT2 and PHF21A

data.description: Loss-of-function variants or deletions involving PHF21A can cause developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, behavioral abnormalities, and characteristic craniofacial features. Skeletal exostoses and parietal foramina generally require involvement of neighboring genes such as EXT2 and ALX4.
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple exostoses
Parietal skull ossification defects/enlarged parietal foramina
The combined EXT2 and ALX4 gene deletion

data.description: 15-year-old boy with congenital neutropenia due to an ELA2 mutation and refractory anemia with excess blasts 2, referred for bone marrow transplantation. Since infancy, he had recurrent bacterial skin and lung infections with low absolute neutrophil counts (200–1,000/μL) requiring granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and antimicrobials. He presented with multiple nonpruritic skin ulcerations on the right abdomen, scalp, and left ankle, present for several weeks. Labs while on granulocyte colony-stimulating factor showed normal neutrophil, lymphocyte, and eosinophil counts, markedly elevated IgG, and normal IgE.

A severe, highly contagious form of scabies with a very high mite burden, often occurring in immunocompromised patients. It can present with widespread crusted, erosive, ulcerated, or hyperkeratotic lesions and may have little or no itch. The biopsy image demonstrates a mite within the stratum corneum.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple persistent skin ulcerations and erosions on the scalp, abdomen, and ankle
Nonpruritic lesions, which can occur in immunocompromised patients with crusted scabies
Immunocompromised state due to congenital neutropenia and refractory anemia with excess blasts
Histology showing a mite in the stratum corneum
Dermal inflammation and ulceration on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: History of recurrent bacterial lung infections since infancy
Congenital ELA2-associated neutropenia
Refractory anemia with excess blasts 2
Markedly elevated IgG

data.description: A superficial infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei mites that typically causes intensely pruritic papules, burrows, and excoriations, often involving the finger webs, wrists, waistline, genital area, and ankles.
symptoms_in_common: Skin lesions involving the abdomen and ankle
Mites identified within the stratum corneum on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of pruritus
Ulcerative and extensive scalp lesions rather than typical papules and burrows
High-risk immunocompromised state suggesting crusted rather than classic scabies
Recurrent bacterial infections since infancy
Congenital neutropenia
Refractory anemia with excess blasts 2
Markedly elevated IgG

data.description: Ecthyma is a deeper ulcerative bacterial skin infection, usually caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus, producing crusted ulcers. It is more likely in patients with impaired host defenses.
symptoms_in_common: History of recurrent bacterial skin infections
Underlying neutropenia and impaired immune defense
Inflammatory infiltrate and ulceration on skin biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Mite visible in the stratum corneum
Multiple lesions with morphology suggestive of a parasitic infestation
Nonpruritic lesions are possible but do not specifically support ecthyma
Normal neutrophil count at presentation while receiving granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
Markedly elevated IgG

data.description: A necrotic ulcerative skin infection classically associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia in severely neutropenic or critically ill patients. Lesions often evolve rapidly into hemorrhagic bullae and necrotic eschars.
symptoms_in_common: Potential susceptibility to Pseudomonas and other invasive bacterial infections
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions present for several weeks rather than rapidly progressive necrotic lesions
No reported fever, sepsis, or systemic toxicity
No described black necrotic eschars or hemorrhagic bullae
Mite identified in the stratum corneum on biopsy
Normal neutrophil count while receiving granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
Markedly elevated IgG

data.description: 16-year-old male with 4 weeks of weakness, malaise, anorexia, nausea, fever, and vomiting. No rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, or herbal medicine use. Exam showed pallor, bilateral pitting pedal edema, and hypertension (160/90 mmHg); otherwise unremarkable. Labs: hemoglobin 90 g/L, leukocytes 6600/cu mm, platelets 2×10^9/cu mm, 3+ proteinuria with 24-hour urine protein 2.4 g, hematuria with RBC casts, blood urea 130 mg/dL, and creatinine rising from 3 to 10 mg/dL over 7 days. ANA and ANCA were negative, hepatitis B/C and HIV tests were negative, complement levels were normal, and imaging/fundus examination were normal.

A rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis characterized by severe glomerular inflammation and crescent formation, usually with little or no immune-complex deposition. It may occur despite negative ANCA testing and can rapidly cause kidney failure.
symptoms_in_common: Rapidly rising creatinine from 3 to 10 mg/dL over 7 days
Hematuria with red blood cell casts
Malaise, weakness, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and fever
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear systemic vasculitic features such as rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, pulmonary hemorrhage, or upper-airway symptoms

data.description: A clinical syndrome of rapidly declining kidney function over days to weeks, usually associated with nephritic urinary findings and glomerular crescents on kidney biopsy.
symptoms_in_common: Creatinine increasing markedly within one week
Constitutional symptoms including fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting
symptoms_not_in_common: Proteinuria is substantial but not in the nephrotic range
No reported oliguria or anuria
No pulmonary symptoms or hemoptysis

data.diagnosis: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease (anti-GBM disease/Goodpasture-spectrum disease)
data.description: An autoimmune disorder in which antibodies target the glomerular basement membrane, causing severe crescentic glomerulonephritis and sometimes pulmonary hemorrhage.
symptoms_in_common: Hematuria with red blood cell casts
symptoms_not_in_common: No hemoptysis, cough, or other evidence of pulmonary hemorrhage
Anti-GBM antibody result is not reported
Fever and prolonged constitutional symptoms are less characteristic as dominant features

data.description: IgA nephropathy is an immune-complex glomerulonephritis that commonly causes hematuria and may rarely progress to a rapidly progressive crescentic form with acute kidney failure.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid renal impairment can occur in crescentic IgA nephropathy
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported preceding upper-respiratory or gastrointestinal infection
No history of recurrent visible hematuria
Severe systemic symptoms with fever and vomiting are not classic primary features

data.diagnosis: Thrombotic microangiopathy, including hemolytic uremic syndrome or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
data.description: A disorder of small-vessel platelet-rich thrombosis that can cause acute kidney injury, hypertension, anemia, and thrombocytopenia; renal biopsy may show glomerular and arteriolar thrombotic injury.
symptoms_in_common: Acute kidney injury with rapidly increasing creatinine
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented hemolysis markers such as schistocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, or indirect hyperbilirubinemia
No neurologic symptoms
No preceding diarrheal illness
RBC casts are more characteristic of inflammatory glomerulonephritis than thrombotic microangiopathy

data.description: A 44-year-old man was hospitalized because of jaundice. Physical examination revealed normal findings except jaundice, and his past medical history was unremarkable. Complete blood count showed hemoglobin of 15 g/dL, white blood cell count of 8,200/μL with differential of 79% segmented neutrophils, 15% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, and 1% eosinophils, and platelet count of 248,000/μL. Liver function test showed elevation of total bilirubin (15.3 mg/dL), direct bilirubin (9.4 mg/dL), and alkaline phosphatase (298 IU/L). Immunohistochemical stains showed tumor cells positive for leukocyte common antigen (CD 45) and negative for CD 3,4,5,8,10,21,23,56 and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showed neither significant abnormalities nor evidence of myelodysplasia or leukemic infiltration.

A rare aggressive malignancy of mature histiocytes/macrophages that may arise in the liver and infiltrate the porta hepatis or intrahepatic bile ducts, producing obstructive jaundice. Tumor cells are typically CD45-positive and lack B-cell, T-cell, NK-cell, and precursor lymphoid markers.
symptoms_in_common: Marked elevation of total and direct bilirubin
Imaging evidence of biliary obstruction near the hepatic hilum
Tumor cells negative for T-cell, NK-cell, and immature lymphoid markers
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No weight loss or night sweats reported
No hepatosplenomegaly or palpable abdominal mass reported
Normal complete blood count

data.diagnosis: Primary hepatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
data.description: An extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma involving the liver, sometimes presenting as a hilar or periportal mass that compresses bile ducts and causes cholestatic jaundice. Most cases express CD45 and B-cell markers such as CD20 or PAX5.
symptoms_in_common: Possible hilar/periportal infiltrative lesion causing biliary obstruction
Absence of bone-marrow involvement can occur in primary hepatic lymphoma
symptoms_not_in_common: B-cell marker positivity was not reported
No fever, night sweats, or weight loss reported
No lymphadenopathy reported
No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly reported
Normal blood counts

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bile ducts. Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma commonly causes obstruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts, leading to painless jaundice and a cholestatic liver-test pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging appearance consistent with biliary obstruction at or near the hepatic hilum
symptoms_not_in_common: Tumor cells are CD45-positive, which is not typical of cholangiocarcinoma
Tumor cells lack reported epithelial-marker positivity
Histology shows a predominantly hematolymphoid-appearing infiltrate rather than malignant biliary epithelial glands
No constitutional symptoms or abdominal pain reported
